0cf52862aa541a17: NEW YORK: The sale of a Vincent van Gogh masterpiece, reportedly opposed by the descendants of its former Jewish owner, who sold it during the Nazi era, will proceed as planned on Wednesday, auction house Sotheby's told AFP.

"Chataigniers en fleurs" (Chestnut Trees in Blossom), painted in 1890 in Auvers-sur-Oise, France, is expected to fetch US$180 million, which would set a new record for the Dutch post-Impressionist and make it the most expensive work sold so far this season.

The heirs of influential German publisher Samuel Fischer, who acquired the painting in Paris in 1909, object to its sale in 1936, arguing that his family parted with it because of financial losses suffered under the Nazis, The New York Times reported.
Gunnar Schnabel, their Berlin-based lawyer, is calling on Sotheby's to prove that the painting was sold at its market value and that the family would have sold it regardless of the political context.
Schnabel did not respond to an AFP request for comment.

Sotheby's said in a statement on Monday that it had "undertaken extensive research into the ownership history of Chataigniers en fleurs", which was consigned to a gallery owner in Amsterdam between 1932 and 1933 and sold for 68,000 Swiss francs in June 1936.
That "research to date has not established that the painting was sold under duress" or below fair market value, Sotheby's added.
The auction house said it was still in dialogue with the Fischer heirs and was "committed to working towards a mutually satisfactory resolution".
A meeting between both sides was scheduled for Monday in New York, The Times reported.
3573dfdca747a184: BERLIN: Florian Wirtz scored twice and Brajan Gruda contributed a goal and two assists as Germany cruised to a 5-0 win over the Netherlands in Berlin to reach the Nations League quarter-finals on Monday.
Derry Scherhant and Nico Schlotterbeck also got on the scoresheet as the Germans cut the visitors to shreds in the most impressive match of Jurgen Klopp's six-game stint as coach.
It was Germany's biggest win over their neighbours since a 7-0 victory in 1959.
"We hope that we can make it fun for the fans. It was definitely fun for us, especially in the second-half," Wirtz told German broadcaster ARD.

The Dutch defeat was the first since their coach Xavi Hernandez took charge but, despite Greece's 1-0 win over Serbia on Monday, they also qualified for the final eight, although the last German goal dropped them to second in the group.
The Netherlands offered little in attack after Germany's second and missed injured captain Virgil van Dijk at the back, with the hosts cutting through a flimsy defence at will.
So often criticised for a lack of end product since his big-money move to Liverpool in 2025, Wirtz has scored in four in his past four games for Germany.
Germany knew only a victory would give them a realistic chance of reaching the quarters, with coach Klopp describing the match as a "final."
The game, a rematch of the 1974 World Cup final won by Germany in Munich, began with both sides risk averse and reluctant to move forward.
The Dutch had the first good chance when Jurrien Timber found Crysencio Summerville unmarked on the penalty spot, but the winger lost his footing before getting a shot away.
Just after the half hour, the Berlin-born-and-raised Scherhant latched onto a cross from Freiburg teammate Philipp Treu but hit the far post.
Nine minutes later, Scherhant had another chance from the same blade of grass and this time curled a lovely effort across the face of goal and inside the post.

The Germans continued their assault on the Dutch penalty area after the break, Wirtz adding another with a solo effort on the hour. The Liverpool winger dribbled from left to right and back centrally before lifting a shot in off the left post from the penalty arc.
Schlotterbeck headed in from a Gruda free-kick with 65 minutes gone.
The RB Leipzig winger laid on another goal six minutes later when he tore down the right and found Wirtz, who hammered in off the bottom of the crossbar.
In his first Germany match on home soil, Gruda then added one of his own, tapping in a Scherhant shot which rebounded off the post.
"We don't mind who we play. We want to play attacking football. We want to score goals and dominate the opponent. And I think we did that perfectly," said Wirtz.
"We want to keep going next year. We want to get better. I think we've taken some great steps in our development as a team."

A QUARTER of teens globally engage in basically no physical activity — not even an hour of exercise a week — the World Health Organisation (WHO) said, warning that this significantly raises health risks.

WHO's new global estimates found that when asked, one in four adolescents aged 11 to 17 report no active days — defined as at least 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous physical activity — in the previous week.
The study, published in 'The Lancet Global Health', draws on hundreds of population-based surveys from 140 countries and territories, involving more than 3.2 million teens, WHO said.
WHO warned that "physical inactivity is a major risk factor for heart disease, type 2 diabetes and some cancers".
"Helping young people develop active habits early in life is critical to protecting their health and reducing the global burden of these diseases," it said in a statement.
The organisation lamented the lack of progress, with physical activity among adolescents remaining "virtually unchanged" in the past 15 years, urging societies to step up.
"For 15 years, the world has made almost no progress in getting young people moving, and girls are being left furthest behind," WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said in the statement.
WHO highlighted a stubborn gender gap when it came to physical activity among teens, with girls far less active than boys in almost every country and region.
There were also stark differences between nations.

While 40 per cent of adolescents in countries like Namibia, Nepal and the Philippines reported no active days, more than 30 per cent of youths in Bangladesh and Serbia reported daily physical activity, the report showed.
"The answer is not to tell adolescents to try harder. It is to build schools, streets and communities where moving, playing and being active is safe, easy and normal," Tedros insisted. — AFP
9f2c7ffc477ebffc: WASHINGTON: American users of several major banking apps and online portals reported outages on Monday, according to monitoring site Downdetector.com, with one institution ruling out a cyberattack as the cause.
Among those affected were Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase and the popular money transfer app Zelle.
Downdetector said outage reports peaked at around 2pm Eastern Standard Time (1900 GMT) before subsiding.

JPMorgan Chase said in a statement posted on X that it "has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems", adding that "there is no evidence this is cyber-related".
"It is taking longer than usual to service some customers," the statement continued, with the banking giant vowing to restore service by the end of the day on Monday.
"Where we were party to a transaction involving other banks, those banks may have been impacted, but this is not a systemic issue," JPMorgan Chase added.
The outage initially sparked concerns about a possible cyber-related issue.
Last month, cryptocurrency platform Binance was the victim of a hack involving US$6.3 billion in stolen funds, the largest ever in crypto.
More recently, French bank Credit Mutuel Arkea was the target of a cyberattack, losing around 100 million euros.

ROME: Brazilian World Cup winner Ronaldinho played his first competitive match in 11 years at the age of 46, starting for Italian third-tier side Ravenna in their derby against Forli on Sunday.
Wearing the number 10 shirt, Ronaldinho played the entire first half. At the interval, he took a lap of the pitch at the Stadio Bruno Benelli, waving to supporters as they stood to applaud him.
Ravenna beat Forli 2-0 in the Serie C clash. Ronaldinho played a part in Giulio Donati's 36th-minute opener and Simone Rabbi added the second in the 58th.
"It was lovely to be here, playing, having the build-up in the dressing room," Ronaldinho told Sky Sport Italia.
He said he had enjoyed playing alongside team mates who had grown up watching him.
Ronaldinho had last played professionally for Fluminense in September 2015 and formally retired in 2018.
Ravenna, whose president Ignazio Cipriani is a long-time friend of the Brazilian, announced his signing in June, with Ronaldinho also taking a stake in the club.
The former AC Milan forward won the World Cup with Brazil in 2002, the Ballon d'Or in 2005 and the Champions League with Barcelona in 2006.
"It went by too fast, that has always been football for me," he said.
Asked whether he might make another appearance for Ravenna, Ronaldinho said: "Now if the President calls me, I'll be back." — REUTERS
ef7467ac203db3eb: NEW YORK: Football star Jude Bellingham has a trophy case of accolades to his name.
But the England and Real Madrid attacking midfielder has been elevated to the pantheon of US pop culture immortality with his own extra-large Calvin Klein underwear billboard in Manhattan.

Measuring 75 feet by 55 feet (22.9 by 16.8 meters), the giant billboard overlooking one of the Big Apple's busiest shopping havens has drawn crowds of admirers. It also highlights the outsize cultural impact the football World Cup had on the US, which cohosted the tournament with Mexico and Canada.
Bellingham is pictured holding his signature arms-stretched celebratory pose and sporting only a pair of white Calvin Klein hip briefs for modesty.

"We were just in the area, and then my little sister, she was like, 'I got to see the Jude Bellingham poster' - especially after they beat Mexico in the World Cup, right?" said store manager George Lozano, 30, whose sister Jackie, 24, snapped a photo on her phone.

"I personally wouldn't think (most Americans) would recognise him. I think it's still growing. It's growing in terms of the US... support for football. But I think now this would definitely help, right?"
Bellingham became a breakout social media sensation during the summer World Cup for his youthful good looks and prowess on the pitch.
Bellingham's selection for Calvin Klein's landmark SoHo billboard puts him alongside cultural titans including Bad Bunny, Jeremy Allen White and Justin Bieber, who bared nearly all before him.

"I like him but he's not my favorite," said French tourist Roxane Marin, 33, of Bellingham, who helped steer England to a famous 6-4 victory over France in the third-place playoff with an inspired 98th-minute solo spectacular.
"I watch football, but I can't remember if I saw that match," she added to AFP after taking a close-up of the billboard.
Marin insisted she had happened upon the billboard by chance, "but I think there are people who come on purpose."

70b8ec7923d501cb: NEW YORK: A broad selloff dragged US stocks lower on Monday as fallout from Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO soured enthusiasm for AI stocks, raising the stakes for the chipmaker's earnings report on Tuesday and Anthropic's initial public offering later in the week.
The risk-off sentiment gathered momentum as the session progressed, with all three major US stock indexes losing ground.
The Nasdaq suffered the steepest percentage loss, as the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index weighed on the tech-heavy index.
"It's the back-and-forth in this market of the AI-related stocks catching a bid versus this rotation trade," said Ross Mayfield, investment strategy analyst at Baird in Louisville, Kentucky.
"Over the last couple of weeks, it's like a day-to-day thing where, you know, some days the AI names absolutely rip and then the very next day, you know, they're in a freefall," Mayfield said.
"There are signs underneath the surface that investors aren't panic-selling and running away from the asset class altogether, but are probing other corners of the equity market," Mayfield added.

Nvidia's losses extended after Huang's resignation following allegations of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, adding to concerns over the emerging technology's rapid expansion and potential risks.

Huang's departure prompted the Trump administration to issue a new rule restricting China's access to the best AI chips from companies like Nvidia ahead of US president Donald Trump's expected meeting with his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping.
It marks an abrupt reversal of fortune for the sector. In mid-June, the SOX index was up 106.6% year-to-date.
However, that luster has faded in recent months, reducing its 2026 gain to around 43%, still about four times the gains of the broader S&P 500 so far this year.
That retreat helped pull the Nasdaq more than 10% below its all-time closing high reached on Oct 6, confirming the index is in a correction.
Analysts expect Nvidia to post a 90.4% year-on-year earnings jump on revenue of US$109.10 billion.
According to preliminary data, the S&P 500 lost 143.26 points, or 1.89%, to end at 7,418.41 points, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 620.16 points, or 2.47%, to 24,516.11.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 721.40 points, or 1.38%, to 51,626.15.
Warsh remarks, rate-hike probability

US Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh said on Monday that technologies will have a significant impact on the economy, but the possible scenarios range from rising growth with broadly shared gains to higher unemployment and a potential slowdown if anticipated investment returns prove disappointing.
Minutes from the Federal Open Market Committee's latest meeting, due for release on Wednesday, could offer clues on the policy outlook ahead of next month's interest-rate decision.
Markets are pricing in a near-certain 96.0% likelihood of a 25-basis-point rate hike in December, according to CME FedWatch.
Among individual stocks, chipmakers Intel and Micron both slumped, as did neocloud provider CoreWeave and rival Nebius.
Hyperscalers Alphabet, Amazon and Meta also closed sharply lower on the day.
Dell and Super Micro Computer posted steep losses.

da4aa92ae4e76484: WASHINGTON: US president Donald Trump on Monday signaled he would welcome Jensen Huang being reinstated as chief of the AI chip giant Nvidia, after Huang resigned last week amid a spy scandal.
"I would certainly not mind seeing that," Trump told reporters as he headed on a trip to China when asked if he thought Huang should return at Nvidia.
"I think he learned a big lesson," he added.
Trump also referred to a campaign to bring back Huang, with tech tycoon Elon Musk and an Uber co-founder among more than 158,000 signatories of an open letter.
"A lot of people are asking Jensen, they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn't a bad idea," Trump said.
Trump also raised fresh doubts over allegations that Alice Huang, a woman with whom Huang had an affair, was spying for China after all.
"I don't know that she is a spy. Usually what happens with that is that, any woman coming to the country that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she is a spy," Trump said.
"China plays games with us and we play games with them," he said.
Trump dismissed reports that state secretary Marco Rubio had flagged intelligence to him indicating that Alice Huang was a spy, saying: "I haven't heard that".
Huang was a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, which US investigators suspect of illegally channeling Nvidia's technology to China.
The Nvidia scandal has caused tensions in the White House over the sale of advanced American AI chips to China.
US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick's department has been accused by voices led by treasury secretary Scott Bessent of failing to properly enforce export controls on the most powerful chips.

The commerce department on Monday closed a loophole on Chinese access, issuing a rule aimed at stopping Chinese companies from using advanced American AI chips housed in data centers in other countries.
Trump said that Lutnick and Bessent "have two different views. One view is you don't want to insult China. We have a very good relationship with China, and you don't want to insult them.
"The other view is just go down and dirty and do what you have to do. You can't say either is wrong or right, we'll let you know," he said.
However, Trump appeared once again to defend Huang, a frequent guest at the White House who accompanied the US leader on his trip to China in May, over the chip sales.
"Jensen obviously has two things going: he has a family situation which is a rough deal, and what he wants to do is to sell chips," Trump said.
"We prohibited him from selling the important chips, the modern day chips. But frankly, selling the other chips is a good thing, not a bad thing," he added.
3df83f6028082983: BRUSSELS: French Football Federation (FFF) president Philippe Diallo will run for the Fifa presidency in next March's election with the support of the Uefa member associations represented on the executive committee and the Fifa Council, Uefa said on Monday.

Fifa president Gianni Infantino, who will seek reelection as the head of global football's ruling body, has faced widespread opposition since his aborted attempt in July to bring private investors into a new Fifa commercial entity holding rights linked to competitions including the World Cup.

"At a meeting held today and chaired by Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin, the national associations ... invited Philippe Diallo, president of the French Football Federation (FFF), to stand as a candidate in the Fifa presidential election in March 2027 and unanimously pledged their full support," a Uefa statement said.
Diallo has accepted the invitation to stand and his candidacy is due to be formally ratified by the FFF Executive Committee on Tuesday.
"Against the backdrop of serious concerns over the direction of Fifa, the national associations called for renewed unity and trust within the global football community," Uefa said.

"They also called for a Fifa that places the development of the game in every region of the world at the heart of its mission, upholds the highest standards of governance and works in close partnership with its member associations, confederations and football stakeholders.
"They expressed their full confidence in Philippe Diallo to provide the leadership needed to achieve this ambition."
Uefa's executive committee met on Monday to find a candidate ahead of Wednesday's deadline, as they look to oust Infantino, who is seeking a fourth term in the election in Rabat on March 18.
Diallo and France withdrew Infantino support

Diallo has been head of the FFF since 2023. He was initially appointed interim president in January 2023, following the resignation of Noel Le Graet, and was elected five months later until the end of 2024.
The 63-year-old, who was re-elected in December 2024 for a four-year term, joined the FFF in 2021 and became vice-president later that year.

In September, the FFF withdrew its support for Infantino's reelection bid, with Diallo saying that "the trust placed in the Fifa president has been broken", adding that France's decision formed part of a broader movement within Uefa.
"We will need to be ready by then to put forward a candidacy capable of winning the Fifa presidency," Diallo said.
Japan Football Association Honorary president Kozo Tashima this month announced his intention to run for Fifa's top position.
Last month, former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega was the first candidate to publicly declare his intention to challenge fellow Swiss Infantino.
Candidates require the backing of five national associations to stand in the election.
Infantino crisis
Infantino was elected Fifa president in 2016 after a corruption scandal ended Sepp Blatter's reign. In 2023, Infantino stood unopposed and was re-elected by acclamation.
Despite repeated calls for his resignation since his failed Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, the 56-year-old maintains he has overwhelming support from member associations around the world.
Uefa initially threatened to boycott Fifa tournaments, before receiving assurances that plans to sell stakes in the World Cup and other major competitions will not be revived.
Fifa announced Infantino's FFE plan without prior consultation with member associations, and his senior advisor, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned three days later.

Even before the FFE proposal, Infantino had come under fire during the World Cup over the decision to suspend a ban imposed on US forward Folarin Balogun after an intervention by US president Donald Trump.

Trump was awarded the Fifa Peace Prize in December last year during the World Cup finals draw, another Infantino decision which drew criticism and will be reviewed by Fifa’s Football Social Responsibility Committee.
Infantino's relationship with the Trump administration is set to come under further scrutiny once the Democrats take control of the House of Representatives in January.

Infantino's candidacy received a significant boost in October when the head of Asian football publicly endorsed him, while support from several Fifa confederations leaves him well placed among the organisation's 211 member associations.
36f69556c90ac80f: FRANKFURT: US electric carmaker Tesla said Monday it will invest €3 billion (US$3.4 billion) to expand its German factory, which will eventually have capacity to produce one million driverless Cybercabs annually.
The investment at the only European factory run by Elon Musk's company stands in stark contrast to other players in Germany's struggling auto sector, which have been downsizing aggressively.

The expansion also comes despite resistance from residents and activists worried about the environmental impact, and with billionaire Musk increasingly controversial in Germany due to his backing of the far right in last year's elections.
"This will lay the foundation for the world's most technologically advanced Tesla factory here in Gruenheide," a town outside Berlin, the company said in a statement announcing the investment.
Tesla's Gruenheide "Gigafactory" was opened in 2022 after a tumultuous two-year approval and construction process, and was given permission to expand by local authorities two years ago.

However, the manufacturer scaled back some of its original plans after local residents opposed them in a non-binding poll, with concerns including proposals to raze large areas of woodland and increased traffic in the area.
Activists staged frequent protests, camping out in treehouses in woods near the factory in an effort to block the expansion.
The plant was also forced to halt production briefly in March following damage to power lines in an arson attack claimed by a far-left group.

Germany's powerful IG Metall union has accused the carmaker of poor working conditions and covert redundancies, all enabled by the lack of a collective agreement to protect workers - almost unheard of in the country's automotive industry.
Tesla has previously declined to respond to AFP's requests for comment on the claims.
Despite this, IG Metall's regional leader Jan Otto said in a statement that the expansion was "good news" which would "enable the creation and safeguarding of more jobs".
The need for more staff "opens up completely new opportunities for our colleagues in the plant to assert their demands and ideas about good working conditions", Otto said.
'Enormous significance'
Under the investment plans announced Monday, a new facility will be constructed where up to one million Cybercabs a year will eventually be produced, according to Tesla.
The two-seat vehicle with no steering wheel or pedals was unveiled in October 2024, and has been deployed in some US cities as part of Tesla's "Robotaxi" service.
Construction of the facility is set to begin in the first half of 2027, with production slated to start in 2029, it said.
The factory expansion will also create new jobs in a wide range of areas, said Tesla, adding it was already seeking hundreds of new workers to help with the plant's ramp-up.
It currently employs around 11,000 staff.

Musk has become a highly controversial figure in Germany due to his links to US President Donald Trump, and his support of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which leads national opinion polls.
Tesla sales plunged in Germany last year as Musk's popularity plummeted.
Nevertheless Dietmar Woidke, leader of Brandenburg state where Tesla's plant is based, welcomed Monday's announcement, describing it as "a decision of enormous economic significance".
Germany's auto giants are mired in a long decline due to fierce Chinese competition, high costs of production at home and a choppy shift to making electric cars.
Volkswagen, Europe's top carmaker, is in the process of cutting tens of thousands of jobs and Mercedes announced last week it would halt all investments in Germany and was weighing factory closures.
"Especially in economically difficult times, this is a strong signal: Germany is still an attractive location for major industrial investments," said Woidke.
4fd433437958eed7: Johannesburg: Premier League duo Nicolas Jackson and El Hadji Malick Diouf scored on Monday as Senegal beat Sudan 4-2 to virtually clinch a place at the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations tournament.
Cameroon trounced Namibia 3-0 and Benin snatched a late 1-0 win over the Central African Republic to move close to qualification for the marquee African competition.
Senegal, Cameroon and Benin have 10 points each from four matches and could all be confirmed as qualifiers on Tuesday depending on the other result in their groups.
Cameroon and Senegal are former Afcon champions while the furthest Benin have progressed is the round of 16 at the 2025 tournament.
Jackson came to Africa last week having scored nine goals in all competitions for Aston Villa this season. He opened the scoring in a 4-1 home win over Sudan last Thursday.
He also broke the deadlock with a fourth-minute goal away to Sudan, who hosted the match in South Sudan because of a civil war in their homeland.
Defender Diouf, who moved from relegated West Ham United to Brentford during the close season, doubled the lead midway through the first half.
Sudan staged a second half comeback to draw level after 75 minutes through goals from substitute Al Gozoli Nooh and Salaheldin Adil.
But a late Senegalese rally saw Pathe Mboup restore the lead, then set up Paul Mendy to score in added time.
Senegal won the final of previous edition of the Afcon 1-0 in extra time over hosts Morocco last February.
But CAF declared Morocco champions because most of the Senegalese team temporarily left the field to protest a penalty, which Morocco missed when play resumed.
Senegal have asked the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) in Switzerland to overturn the CAF ruling and a decision is expected this month.
It took Cameroon 12 minutes to score away to Namibia through Mahamadou Nagida. Goals from Ryan Fosso and Saidou Alioum in the second half completed the victory.
Benin left it late to secure maximum points with debutant Ede Oloko netting in added time. The goal condemned the Centrsl African Republic to a fourth straight loss.
Elsewhere, Zimbabwe outplayed Equatorial Guinea 3-0 in Harare, Guinea beat Eritrea 3-1 in Cairo and a Jordan Ayew penalty earned Ghana an unimpressive 1-0 win over Somalia in Essipong.
In the six matches on Monday, Zimbabwe were the only host nation to actually play at home. Central African Republic, Eritrea and Namibia do not have international-standard stadiums.
A civil war that erupted in April 2023 prevents Sudan playing in Khartoum and Somalia cannot stage Afcon qualifiers due to security concerns in the Horn of Africa state.

dcb04fc1a47117d7: LONDON: Crystal Palace appointed Thomas Frank as their new manager on Monday, handing the Dane the daunting task of lifting the struggling club off the bottom of the Premier League table.

The Frenchman was unable to build on the legacy of his predecessor Oliver Glasner, who oversaw the most successful period in the club's history.
Glasner led the south London club to their first-ever major trophy, beating Manchester City to win the FA Cup in 2025, and won the Uefa Conference League last season.
"It's an honour to sit here and be in charge of this fantastic football club. I'm really, really looking forward to it," Frank said in a Palace statement.

"Crystal Palace is an iconic club in England and in the Premier League. I will do everything I possibly can to help and support the players and everyone around the place and I'm really looking forward to meeting them."

Frank, who has signed a two-and-a-half-year deal, enjoyed great success during seven years at Brentford, leading the Bees into the top flight for the first time in 74 years in 2021 and establishing the club in the Premier League.
His work in west London earned the 53-year-old a move to Tottenham in June 2025 but he lasted just eight months as Spurs struggled.
Palace hope Frank can rekindle the highs of his time at Brentford with similar resources at Selhurst Park.

"I'm delighted to be able to welcome Thomas to Crystal Palace," said Palace chairman Steve Parish. "He has a proven track record of both creating winning teams and improving players, making him the perfect fit for our club."
Sage paid the price after four straight league defeats left Palace at the bottom of the table.
He was hindered by the departures of Maxence Lacroix to Chelsea and Daniel Munoz, who reunited with Glasner at Nottingham Forest.
Palace have the worst defensive record in the Premier League, shipping 24 goals in 10 matches.
They will be hoping for an instant improvement as they prepare to face relegation rivals Coventry and Hull in their next two league games.
They also sit 21st in the 36-team Europa League table with four games of the league phase remaining.

4c52bb5ce7762fca: Attackers are using open source AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate their attacks on banks, governments, energy and healthcare providers, and other critical sectors around the globe, according to security alerts from the FBI and Amazon Threat Intelligence.

Between October 3 and November 5, Amazon’s MadPot honeypot threat sensors detected two ARTEX campaigns: one that allowed thieves to steal AI credentials at “industrial scale” to gain free access to models, and a second that generated deepfake videos to trick live selfie checks.
In the first one, miscreants used AI agents to steal API keys, and then feed these keys into the ARTEX framework’s model gateway to power more agents searching for more AI model access keys.

“Agents validated identities through each provider’s token and identity services, enumerated storage, assessed permission scope, and went after managed AI model services, secrets and parameter stores, and application identities,” AWS Chief Information Security Officer CJ Moses wrote in a blog post on Friday.

Targets included LLM gateways and proxy platforms such as One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API, and LiteLLM, and AI application builders Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat, and Ollama.
This campaign also used cloud credentials to gain stolen access to the models.

In a second campaign, attackers used ARTEX to create real-time deepfake videos to trick identity verification (KYC) checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges, and forged ID photos to pass document checks.

“The agents reverse-engineered one vendor’s liveness protocol in detail, documenting the face-detection event stream it sends, how it tracks face position during the check, and the coordinate system it uses to tell the user where to move,” Moses wrote.

The agents did manage to complete the full movement sequence with the face positioned within 7 pixels of the target, but this feat was not enough, as the vendor’s server-side verdict rejected the deepfake in every attempt.

In a separate session, agents built a real-time deepfake video pipeline on a single consumer-grade GPU using an open-source face animation model. This video achieved 11.5 frames per second, which Moses said is “close to what a live video check expects.”

Meanwhile, agents also worked on the ID document checks, building synthetic camera metadata whose image dimensions matched the real values inside the JPEG file, and preserving the original camera compression tables that are usually replaced by re-saving an edited image.

While the end goal was stealing cryptocurrency, the campaign illustrates how ARTEX runs several sessions simultaneously, with multiple agents working toward the same result. “One searched for ways to cash out, one worked on clearing account balances, one set up the deepfake video pipeline, and one carried out the verification bypass,” Moses wrote.
None of the attack techniques are new, but both of these campaigns show how AI agents can boost the speed and persistence of the attacker.

“The agents succeeded where basic security hygiene was missing, including default or hardcoded credentials, keys left in code and public artifacts, unauthenticated interfaces and inference endpoints, and unpatched software,” Moses added. “Getting those fundamentals right remains the most effective defense.”
The FBI weighs in

The FBI also hammered this message in a separate Friday alert noting “ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours.”

The federal cops cited the August attacks against South Korean financial institutions that stole personal data belonging to about 67,000 people. The FBI also highlighted a September ARTEX campaign that targetedd ConnectWise Cloud Backup customers in a supply chain attack that ultimately compromised more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft tenants.
After these security breaches became public, the original ARTEX developer removed the GitHub repository in October.

However, forked and localized variations plus a commercial version remain, and as of November 4 internet scanning service Censys identified 1,465 hosts running an exposed ARTEX console. And the total number of deploymentsis “likely significantly higher when including systems behind firewalls or in private networks,” according to the FBI.

The feds urged all organizations – especially those operating internet-exposed applications, self-service portals, cloud infrastructure, and partner or supplier systems – to implement a series of mitigation measures outlined in its Flash alert.

These include reducing external attack surfaces by restricting sensitive services to trusted networks, private connectivity, or dedicated administrative paths, and moving enterprise applications behind zero-trust access policies and permissions. ®

49b793be636601e9: After two years of experimentation, the Chrome team shipped the HTML-in-Canvas API with Chrome 157. With it comes a new vision of how Web pages could be designed, for better or worse, allowing richer, more interactive elements but also more opportunities for annoying ads.

“Previously, when creating visually demanding web apps, you had to choose between standard HTML elements and raw canvas contexts,” enthused one Google DevRel in a tutorial. “HTML-in-Canvas eliminates these trade-offs.”

The Web API has been submitted for inclusion in the WHATWG HTML Living Standard, the ever-updating standard formerly known as HTML5 – for all the technologies that officially make up HTML (including Canvas itself).
A Web API for the browser’s rendering engine

Originally developed by Apple and standardized in 2014, the canvas tag is an HTML element that offers a space to render fluid graphics via JavaScript drawing commands. It creates a dedicated grid on screen, within which JavaScript can use a set of Canvas methods to draw lines, curves, text, gradients, and images. Or, the user’s GPU, via WebGL or WebGPU, can use the canvas to render 3D images and other custom effects.
The downside of Canvas is that the regular HTML controls didn’t work inside the canvas itself. Formatting any text had to be done by hand. Interactivity was out, as were accessibility aids.

Primarily developed by the Google Chromium team, HTML-in-Canvas allows JavaScript to place HTML commands within the canvas element, thanks to an attribute option within Canvas. If the canvas tag includes a content attribute of "drawable," the browser’s rendering engine prepares the HTML content inside the box so JavaScript can render it.

While fully supported by Chrome and Chrome Android beginning with release 157, none of the other major browsers support the API yet (Microsoft Edge 157 – which is made of Chromium – unofficially appears to support at least some HTML-in-Canvas actions as well).
The Web’s about to get lit
Google posted a few possibilities of what can be done with HTML-in-Canvas.

Developers can wrap HTML controls onto a 3D object. In one example, the user can turn the pages of a virtual book and even copy text out of the book itself. A video, complete with a set of controls, can be wrapped into an odd-sized canvas. The spec seems to work particularly well with JavaScript plug-ins, allowing coders to create entire 3D environments with Three.js, or to create charts with D3.js.
Enthusiasts are already hacking against the spec with mad abandon.
Developer Wes Bos put a notes app in the canvas, then used it as target practice by overlaying the app with some Duck Hunt-styled game code.
HTML-in-Canvas “opens up the door to a lot of stupid use cases … but also a lot of really creative, interesting things where you can apply stylistic effects to HTML,” Bos explained on X.

A trippy demo from html-in-canvas.dev shows a dragon slithering through the opening chapter of an online book, with the text smoothly reflowing in its wake. Try to shoo the beast off with your cursor and it will burn the virtual text with its fiery breath.
The source code reveals that “Margin Dragon” was rendered in 881 lines of vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript code.
Another demo on the sample site is a “mouse-driven elastic displacement effect,” in which a “radial bulge” and drop shadow follow the cursor across the canvas.

Of course, such stylistic enchantments will not always be used for whimsy. Inevitably, unscrupulous marketers will discover powerful new ways to annoy us about all the virtues of late-stage capitalism.
“The world is not ready for HTML-in-Canvas,” a punter wrote on X.
Here be dragons

As per norm, HTML-in-Canvas has plenty of bugs (and it hasn’t even gone cross-platform yet). In some cases, the CSS doesn’t get painted on where it should, and timing with the reactive frameworks could be better synchronized.
And there is a lot for the lowly web maintainer to learn.

The core developers resolved the issue of canvas copying sensitive cross-origin data where it oughtn’t (as per CORS), but the API does not indicate when it declines to copy the data, leaving the community to file bug reports of what appear to be silent failures.
Likewise, developers must learn to properly document on-screen bounding boxes to keep accessibility tools like screen readers and click targets operating properly in 3D environments. ®

46cac4ef45279ad2: A new Top500 list of supercomputers has dropped, but little has changed. China remains uncontested with the most powerful supercomputer on the biannual ranking, and the US is not even close behind.

The Middle Kingdom's LineShine super tops the list, boasting 2.2 exaFLOPS as measured by the High Performance Linpack (HPL) benchmark. That's roughly 22 percent ahead of Uncle Sam’s biggest iron, Laurence Livermore National Laboratory’s El Capitan.

But LineShine may not be the most efficient. Using 42.2 megawatts, LineShine’s lead comes at the expense of a noticeably higher power bill; not that that makes much of a difference. Number one is number one, and to add insult to injury, the National Supercomputing Centre in Shenzhen (NSCS) did it in spite of US export controls denying them access to American GPUs. The entire super is powered by 45,360 LingKun LX2 CPUs, each with 304 Arm v9.2 cores clocking to 1.5 GHz.

The US is unlikely to reclaim the number one spot any time soon, though not for lack of trying. Under the Genesis Mission announced late last year, the Department of Energy is on track to deploy at least nine new supers. It just so happens that most of these will be smaller or AI-focused machines, with few truly large systems.

Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s (ORNL) Lux supercomputer, built in collaboration with HPE and AMD, is one such example. Delivering 220 petaFLOPS of double-precision grunt in HPL, it’s certainly a potent system. Just two years ago it would have been a top 10 supercomputer, but it''l have to settle for number 14 on this fall’s Top500 ranking.

Now, if you’re willing to turn the resolution slider down to FP4, peak performance jumps to somewhere north of 20 exaFLOPS. That’s fine for AI inference and even some training, but for running multi-physics sims on America's nuclear deterrent, the DoE has traditionally gone for something a bit bigger.

ORNL’s upcoming Discovery system will certainly have enough grunt to give LineShine the boot. Details on the HPE Cray based system remain thin, but we do know it’ll be powered by a combination of AMD Venice CPUs and Instinct MI430X GPUs.

Unlike most of the GPUs sold today, the MI430X hasn’t forsaken double-precision grunt for low-precision AI throughput. Each of these multi-die chips is estimated to deliver north of 200 teraFLOPS of FP64 matrix math. According to the DoE, Discovery will deliver somewhere between 3x to 5x the performance of Frontier, which would put its Rpeak somewhere between 5.1 and 8.5 exaFLOPS at FP64.

As impressive as that might sound, China has proven that once you take power out of the equation, all it takes to claim the number one spot is scale. And if there is one thing LineShine does well, it’s scale.

In GPU-accelerated systems like El Cap, you’re lucky to push HPL to within 70 percent of the system’s theoretical roofline. But LineShine isn’t GPU-accelerated. Sure, with 16 HBM stacks, the LX2 looks a lot like a GPU, but it's really just an enormous CPU with enough vector and matrix units to put more than a few modern GPUs to shame.
With enough of them – by which we mean 22,680 dual-socket nodes – NSCS catapulted China to the top of the Top500 for the first time in nearly a decade.
Not the benchmark it used to be
The US has no shortage of systems capable of eclipsing El Capitan or even LineShine’s performance if someone were motivated enough to get HPL running on them.

SpaceXAI’s 300 megawatt Colossus supercomputer in Memphis, Tennessee, boasts 200,000 Hopper GPUs each good for 34-67 (vector/matrix) teraFLOPS of FP64 grunt. Even assuming an abysmal 25% efficiency, the cluster should be more than capable of breaking three exaFLOPs in HPL.

It might need 10x the power of El Capitan, but the thing is, beyond winning points with the White House — a ship that has almost certainly sailed for Elon Musk after the DOGE fiasco — renting out the cluster to Anthropic to train and run Claude is a far more lucrative endeavor.
The same could be said of any number of AI clusters, from Meta’s Prometheus to OpenAI’s Starship.
It used to be that the systems to summit the Top500 were among the largest computers humanity has ever built. But this hasn’t been true in some time.
The US is starving for compute. HPL or even its sibling High-Performance Gradient Conjugate just aren’t the benchmarks to beat any longer.
The new battleground isn’t nuclear proliferation; it’s one of AI models, agents, and the means to harness them.

We’re not talking about tokens, LLMs, or chatbots, but the ability to harness these models to automate laboratories and formulate and test hypotheses long after the scientists they serve have gone home for dinner.
It’s why the US’s Genesis mission puts such a strong emphasis on AI.

AI-driven labs present an opportunity for researchers to iterate faster. Rather than running hundreds or thousands or simulations trying to find a needle in a haystack, a task for which a bigger iron is warranted, AI analysis and automation could focus that search.

High-performance computing (HPC), and by extension the Top500, will remain relevant as long as more FLOPS means more simulations per unit of time. But these systems can only move as fast as the men and women who operate them. ®

9ccf8665576aaeb3: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world.

These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry’s critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech).

Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post.

But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress.

On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead.

It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)
The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control.

But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China.

It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further.

What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell.

But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good.

The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers. That was important, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit. If Huang is out, who is next?

3ec3fbaaa5e4180c: It’s been eight years since NordPass released the first edition of its most common passwords of the year list, and the world has learned nothing about password security in the meantime.
NordPass’ eighth edition of its most common passwords list, as culled from data breaches, was released Monday, and it looks suspiciously like the previous ones in the worst possible way.
“Once again, ‘123456’ is the most commonly used password in the world,” NordPass said in the report. “That makes it seven out of eight years this password has stood at the top of the leaderboard.”

Even when 123456 wasn’t number one, it was still near the top of the heap, as the top three passwords in the list remain unchanged in the eight years NordPass has published its list: 123456, admin, and 12345678. It’s not like the rest of the most common passwords are showing any variety either.

According to NordPass, the only real shuffling among the 10 most popular passwords was the entry of the worryingly short 1234 into the top ten and the migration of the ever-popular password “password” down slightly in the top 10 from 6th to 7th place.
“We still have a lot of work to do to spread awareness about password safety,” NordPass concluded of that data – and there’s no more pressing time than the present.

AI adoption has made password cracking an easier exercise than ever, with more credentials being sucked up in more data breaches at a faster pace. AI has also made cracking hashed passwords a snap too. In other words, if you’re reusing a password that’s been exposed in a breach, even if it’s just a hash that was exposed, you’re more likely than ever before to have another account compromised.
The best advice NordPass gives is to move away from passwords toward biometric authentication or passkeys and you're insane not to enable MFA.
But for the places you still have to use passwords, there are a few things to avoid – like the 200 passwords in NordPass’ list, for example.
Beyond that, NordPass also recommends steering clear of pop cultural trends.

“Fandoms make for terrible passwords,” NordPass notes. There are several reasons for that – namely the fact that they follow trends, meaning that “minecraft” password in the early 2000s was a simple one to add to a password stuffing dictionary, just like “skibiditoilet” in recent years.
The one thing that connects all those pop-culture passwords is that “they all could be cracked in seconds,” NordPass said.

We’re sure our readers are conscientious about their online habits, carefully protecting their accounts with the proper security measures and ensuring each and every password is unique, long, complicated, and random. Unfortunately for you smarties reading El Reg, the person down the hall whose security you’re responsible for may not be so disciplined, so be sure you’re enforcing good practices – Nord knows the average user just isn’t doing it despite years of begging and reminders. ®

ff0169702f8be68d: The researcher who sounded the alarm over Dirty Frag earlier this year has uncovered another Linux kernel flaw, and this one lets attackers crash entire servers remotely without so much as a password.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-99288 and dubbed NoisyTCP, was discovered by security researcher Hyunwoo Kim, who says it affects almost all Linux distributions. The flaw dates back to October 2015 and went unnoticed until this year, when Kim found and patched it.

Attackers don't need to log in or get their hands on any credentials to cause trouble. They can simply knock the server over, although there's no evidence yet that the flaw can be used to steal data or hijack a machine.

The bug is buried in Linux's TCP networking code. Two parts of the kernel can trip over each other while processing incoming traffic, leaving one trying to use memory that's already been freed. When that happens, Linux can panic and take the whole machine down with it.

Kim says there's no need for any special server configuration either. Services such as Nginx, Apache, and SSH can be vulnerable straight out of the box. An attacker needs access to an open TCP port on a system that processes incoming network traffic across multiple receive queues or CPUs.

Perhaps more concerning for administrators running containerized workloads, the damage isn't necessarily limited to the application being attacked. Because the flaw sits in the Linux kernel, crashing a web server inside a container can take down the underlying host and anything else running on it.

Kim found that the attack was particularly effective against virtual machines. During testing, he managed to crash Nginx, Apache, and SSH servers running on QEMU/KVM virtual machines in between five seconds and two minutes.
Physical hardware put up more of a fight. Even after tailoring his exploit to the target machine, Kim needed roughly 14 hours to crash a bare-metal server running Nginx.

Kim has a knack for finding holes in Linux. Back in May, he uncovered Dirty Frag, a kernel bug that allowed local users to gain root privileges. That one caused headaches for administrators when a working exploit went public before patches were ready.

His latest discovery, NoisyTCP, has another potentially nasty trick up its sleeve. Kim identified a second exploitation path involving a use-after-free condition, although pulling it off is considerably more difficult than simply crashing a server.

In his advisory, Kim says he has developed a limited exploit targeting virtual machines in a lab environment but has yet to demonstrate a general-purpose remote code execution attack. For the moment, the confirmed impact is remote denial of service.

A fix was committed to the upstream Linux kernel on November 3, but administrators will need to check whether their distribution has shipped an updated kernel. Red Hat has rated the vulnerability Important, assigning it a CVSS score of 7.5.
For those unable to patch immediately, Kim suggests two temporary workarounds: disabling TCP SYN cookies or restricting incoming packet processing to a single receive queue.

Neither is particularly appealing. Disabling SYN cookies reduces protection against SYN flood attacks, while limiting packet processing can hurt network performance. The former also needs to be applied separately to containers using their own network namespaces.

Kim published the details on November 15, once the disclosure embargo was lifted. The bug had been hiding in plain sight since 2015, leaving Linux servers vulnerable to remote crashes for 11 years. Not bad for a flaw that doesn't even require a login. ®

2cb18a210c5dea98: Canonical is offering Ubuntu Pro users an opt-in channel for AI-generated security patches, deploying bots to help tackle the growing pile of vulnerabilities other bots are uncovering.

Canonical's VP for "Excellence Engineering," Pierre Guillemin, gave the second keynote at the recent Ubuntu Summit, introducing the Edge archive, an optional repository of security fixes generated by the company's Surge framework.

As the announcement describes it: "We built Surge, a multi-agent orchestration framework for CVE remediation and backporting, and have reached a high level of confidence in its capabilities. We will not automatically upload Surge-generated fixes to our stable releases, but from today they are available to Ubuntu Pro users in the new Edge archive."

Edge offers patches before extended testing and qualification are complete, allowing users to assess them themselves. Canonical says updates delivered through the normal security channels will remain human-validated.
Ubuntu Summit now runs twice a year. Last week's Ubuntu Summit 26.10 followed a rather unfortunately timed server outage for the company.

At the previous such event in June, the company announced a move into agentic AI, but this new one is bolder still. Guillemin noted that "October 2026 saw almost as many CVEs as all of 2025." Surge is a "multi-agent orchestration framework" to remediate vulnerabilities in Ubuntu's userspace. In other words, not the kernel, but even so, it is ambitious.

The idea is to use a group of different LLMs to triage new vulnerabilities, find existing fixes, use multiple competing models to backport them to the versions in Ubuntu, and run automatic testing on them. Then a different group of "judging models" will evaluate the fixes and look for consensus. When candidates are chosen, they pass through normal Ubuntu package testing. If there are edge cases, low confidence scores, deadlocks, or other problems, then the process will be escalated to the staff of Canonical's security team.

It's an attempt, as Guillemin put it, "to use AI to fight AI" – cooperating groups of LLMs patching their way through the ever-increasing flow of security holes. Even so, this is a remarkably courageous tactic (at the risk of using a famous British euphemism).

It's an opt-in feature of Ubuntu Pro, Canonical's security and support subscription – although as we reported in 2022, Pro also has a free tier, so security researchers and the community can try Edge out, study it, and report their findings.

We do sympathize with companies struggling against a rising tide of bot-powered security hole discovery. In theory, corporate funding can pay for faster fixes than a volunteer community can offer, but even for commercial vendors these are testing times. As we reported when Debian turned 30, surveys suggest that Ubuntu is about a third of the world Linux user base. Some of those users will be intrepid enough to try this, and that will end up being informative for the whole FOSS world.

Those with long memories will remember the last time Canonical used the same edgy nomenclature. Back in July 2013, it launched a crowdfunding campaign for an Ubuntu smartphone. The campaign didn't raise enough money. ®

24c11abe66a97610: LearnWorlds, a software and learning course platform, says an attacker sent 13,000 phishing emails to customers over seven days by using automated tools to open free trial accounts. The company insists its systems were not breached.

Panos Siozos, Co-founder and CEO at LearnWorlds, said the miscreant created around 570 free trial accounts on the platform between November 7-14, which they used to issue fake copyright infringement notices to customers.
"We have found no evidence of unauthorized access to existing customer schools or personal data held for our customers and their end users," he told The Register.
According to Siozos, the attacker bypassed the platform's per-customer limit on trial subscriptions and exploited its welcome email feature to send the phishing emails.

"In each trial they added their own list of target addresses and rewrote the standard welcome email as a fake copyright notice," he said. "Adding those users triggered the welcome email from our sending address."

The first email was sent on November 7, after which the company detected the suspicious signups and blocked the first sender on November 9, although the attacker returned to send a second wave of emails within 40 minutes.
LearnWorlds removed all the trial accounts by November 10 and one paid account, which was used to launch more emails, on November 14.

"In total, around 13,000 emails were sent to addresses on external recipient lists supplied by the sender," said Siozos. "The trial accounts sent 9,853 between November 7-9, and the paid account sent 3,723 on November 14.
"We can’t tell how many people clicked, because the link was disguised to hide clicks. The recipient addresses were the sender’s own list."
The CEO confirmed that LearnWorlds has since enhanced its bot checks and is placing holds on new accounts if their emails trigger fraud flags.

"We have also examined the novel patterns the attackers used to create more advanced scoring mechanisms. We have reported the phishing website so it can be taken down. Further measures are currently being examined.
"Anyone who signed in on the fake page should change their Google password and review their account’s recent security activity."

The company's confirmation follows suspicions of foul play aired by users on social media. User reports included copies of the emails they received, which demanded urgent responses to fake copyright infringement claims related to YouTube content.
Among the more prominent recipients of the copyright infringement email notices was Marcus Hutchins, of WannaCry fame, who claimed he received an email from the company’s official mail server.

The email, a copy of which Hutchins posted to X, referenced general intellectual property and copyright infringements but failed to specify any specific issues. The email prompted the recipient to click a YouTube link to see the “supporting documentation submitted by LearnWorks.”

The link predictably turned out to be a YouTube redirect link, taking recipients to a separate website that presents them with a real Google OAuth page. If the user completed the authorization flow, it would have handed attackers control of the target’s Google and YouTube accounts.

“The site is designed to look like an official YouTube webpage that enables users to review copyright claims against their channel,” Hutchins wrote. “It contains both the YouTube and Google branding, as well as a very similar theme to the official YouTube one.”

0ae7983049f12656: Nine countries including the UK have signed a US declaration pledging to secure supply chains for AI tech, as pressure grows for tighter export controls following the high-profile resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

The US is firming up its Pax Silica initiative on AI and supply chain security. Under the San Francisco declaration, signed on November 15, the coalition says it is entering a new phase that turns shared principles into a working partnership with shared responsibilities.

Pax Silica was announced in December last year, ostensibly for the participants to work together on vital parts of the global technology supply chain, including frontier foundation models, compute and semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, minerals refining and processing, and energy.

But the list of participants was notable for not including one country – China – leading many to suspect that Pax Silica is yet another effort by Washington to squeeze out its main rival in the global technology and economic stakes. Hong-Kong based South China Morning Post refers to it as Trump's "campaign to China-proof AI and chip supply chains."

The latest declaration states that "the security of our peoples cannot be separated from the security of our economies and those of our closest partners," and sets out what must be protected, as well as committing to "protect it together."
It asserts that protection should cover key foundational technologies essential to economic security, listing "software, materials, knowledge, components and inputs…essential to AI supply chains."

This includes anything that "theft, illicit transfer, or acquisition by hostile actors would confer a meaningful military or intelligence advantage, or undue economic leverage over the participants, or whose unauthorized transfer or misuse could pose significant risks to the economic and national security of the participants."
Also listed is the protection of critical infrastructure such as ports, terminals, transport, communications, and logistics networks, and the ICT and energy infrastructure these depend upon.
The declaration was jointly released by the US administration, and the governments of Australia, India, Israel, Japan, South Korea, Qatar, Singapore, United Arab Emirates, and the United Kingdom.

"The know-how to design a chip, the machine that makes it, and the port that ships it can all be in different countries," the US under-secretary of state for economic affairs Jacob Helberg told the Financial Times.
"What makes the San Francisco Declaration historic is that Pax Silica partners have agreed to treat the security of those technologies and the infrastructure behind them as a shared responsibility."
This move comes amid reports that both Republican and Democrat lawmakers want to push through further measures to prevent China from accessing advanced chips for AI processing.

It follows the recent news that Jensen Huang, the now former CEO of top GPU maker Nvidia, admitted to an affair with a woman suspected by the US of being a spy for Beijing. She worked for a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed that bought Nvidia hardware and was also suspected of making it available to Chinese users. US, Singaporean, and Malaysian police investigations are still probing whether chips were diverted or accessed remotely by Chinese firms.
American efforts to control Chinese access to its technology started under the first Trump administration, and continued under President Joe Biden’s leadership.
A report out last week claimed US export controls are not stopping AI labs in China from using restricted Nvidia chips, and many of their cutting-edge models were trained using Blackwell GPUs.
It is understood that President Trump is to meet with China's premier Xi Jinping this week for bilateral talks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen. ®

b2955c38ff71d9a1: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors.

For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses.

AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built.

We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do. We will do it by fencing it in with hard limits that are enforced outside its reach. In OpenAI’s case, the safeguards sat inside a system the agents could edit. But a fence the agents can simply move is not a fence.
Where traditional definitions of trust fall short

Recent MIT Technology Review coverage has approached this problem from other directions. One contributor argues that having a human in the loop is an insufficient solution because humans are fundamentally unable to understand AI systems’ intentions and advocates instead for interdisciplinary research and collaboration between academia, government, and the tech industry. And a story on reverse game theory describes using incentives to keep models from deviating from the rules, even when no one understands how they work on the inside.

Both articles acknowledge that we cannot understand or watch every AI decision. Our instruments of trust, including requirements, testing, certification, safety margins, interlocks, and pass/fail criteria, all depend on our ability to bound a system’s behavior. This is the determinism paradox.

With generative and agentic AI, behavior is shaped by training data, architecture, prompts, context, retrieval sources, and the environment. Inputs change, models are updated, tools change, and agents interact. Small variations propagate into outcomes nobody designed. The problem is not randomness; it is that the space of possible behavior is too large to enumerate in advance. Trust must therefore be engineered around boundaries rather than predicted outputs. The goal is not deterministic AI, but bounded, observable, and controllable AI. Trust also cannot be a one-time test. Traditional assurance certifies a product at a point in time, but AI keeps evolving after deployment, and a system that has passed every test can drift outside the conditions that made those tests meaningful. Trust must be continuously earned.

Safety engineering has been accounting for some of this variability for decades. For example, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission determine the likelihood of failures in complex systems, and Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP) showed that accidents can emerge from interactions among working components, people, and organizations. But AI raises the stakes, because just a single component can now interpret, infer, and act. The stakes rise further as AI moves from browsers into vehicles, robots, medical systems, industrial controls, and data centers, where a wrong answer can become a life-threatening event.
Building trust that scales

It’s clear that a person rubber-stamping thousands of AI actions an hour is not an acceptable—or scalable—safeguard against risk. But the remedy is not to remove people from the loop; it is to put human judgment where it counts: setting limits in advance and approving the rare actions that have serious consequences while hard constraints handle the rest.

Therefore, trust has to move upstream into architecture. The central questions become: What authority are we willing to give AI, under what conditions, and supported by what evidence? And what happens outside those conditions? That is very different from asking whether a model scored 94% on a benchmark.

The determinism paradox does not mean AI cannot be trusted. It means trust needs a different architecture. Instead of making every output predictable, make the boundaries predictable. An AI medical assistant may be probabilistic in its diagnosis, but deterministic rules govern whether it can change a prescription. An industrial AI may find many ways to optimize a process, while fixed limits keep it within pressure and temperature bounds. An agent may decide how to complete a task, while permissions, transaction limits, and human approvals determine what it is authorized to do.
Let AI be probabilistic inside the box and make the box itself deterministic wherever consequences matter. Leaders can put this into practice by asking five questions:
What authority does AI have? Define not only what it can do but what it is allowed to do, separating interpretation, recommendation, decision, and execution.
Is the function of AI proportional to the consequence? A marketing copilot and AI controlling industrial equipment need different assurance thresholds.

Are we taking the appropriate steps toward autonomy? For example, there needs to be a plan to move from having AI interpret while humans decide, to AI making recommendations, to then taking action with approval, and ultimately to having supervised autonomy, but only as AI can safely work at each step.
Are we testing the system or merely the model? Unexpected interactions emerge among models, data, agents, APIs, and human workflows.
Are we continuously earning trust? Monitor drift, failures, near-misses, and model changes throughout the lifecycle.

The winners in AI will be those who solve the determinism paradox—giving AI enough freedom to create value while engineering boundaries strong enough to make what it does with that freedom trustworthy. Invention earns attention. Trust earns adoption.

bbbda7c9a3961001: October ’26 might be remembered as a seminal moment for software developers and application security teams. AI agents are investigating unfamiliar systems, testing ways to get in and adjusting their next move when an attempt fails. Anyone with a credit card can use that capability to come after your application.

Coding agents and their tool integrations have introduced new entry points and surface areas that can be exploited. Pillar’s OpenCode disclosure in October showed how a malicious Model Context Protocol (MCP) server could execute commands on a developer’s Windows or WSL machine during authentication. A server-supplied URL reached a shell without tricking the model. In the same month, the discovery of the two PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, remote code execution bugs in the PHP runtime uncovered with the help of OpenAI’s models, brought new urgency to securing longstanding code across much of the internet.

Microsoft revealed that an agent moved from searching GitHub for exposed credentials to stealing Azure Key Vault data in five minutes. When its cloud API requests failed, the agent corrected the API versions and tried again until they succeeded.

A report by Anthropic described individual operators using agent frameworks for multi-victim campaigns that previously required specialist teams. Agents carried out reconnaissance, exploitation and data theft across targets in parallel, making sophisticated operations accessible with less hands-on work.

In a recent analysis, Tomasz Tunguz estimated the model cost of a 100-million-token attack workload using GLM-5.3, a low-cost model: 100 million tokens × $0.902 per million = $90.20. That is roughly 98% to 99% below the $5,000 to $10,000 frontier-model estimate cited by Bank for International Settlements (BIS) for a comparable cyber attack. Tunguz’s figure covers model usage only, not the full cost of an attack. Even still, it shows how trivially cheap it is now for attackers to go after any codebase, with the spend falling from thousands of dollars to under $100.

These new agentic attacks should make every team take another look at the code they’ve been running for years. Engineering and security teams need to find and fix weaknesses in their own applications before an attacker with an army of AI agents gets there first.
Security has to become every developer’s responsibility

Traditional AppSec checks such as rule-based static analysis, dependency scanning and secret detection are no longer enough on their own. Developers, engineering leaders, and security teams also need defensive AI agents that trace attack paths, uncover missing safeguards and business-logic vulnerabilities, and help fix them.

Developers’ responsibility doesn’t stop at the code they’re writing now. An application already in production without known vulnerabilities might still get exploited by an AI agent looking for ways to skip a permission check or business rule. The gap only shows up when a request is traced through the codebase and checked against what users should be allowed to do.
A new approach to securing your code

CodeRabbit Secure uses semantic analysis to understand your codebase and reason about it the way a security engineer would, tracing requests and checking whether permissions and business rules are enforced. Agents investigate potential attack paths and verify findings independent of the developer or agent that wrote the code, while CodeRabbit Agent generates reviewable fixes.
Three main use cases that improve your code security: this works across the SDLC:
reviewing each commit in a new PR and flag its security risks;
finding vulnerabilities across the repo with a Deep Scan;
rechecking code with incremental scans and validating findings at runtime.
Find vulnerabilities already in committed code

Deep Scan examines the repository, including older paths outside the latest PR. Agents map entry points, access controls, and sensitive operations, then investigate across functions and files. Linked repositories, when configured, supply context from shared services and libraries. A separate agent challenges each suspected vulnerability, checking reachability, exploitation conditions, and safeguards that could disprove it.
I tried CodeRabbit Secure Deep Scan against ast-grep and was impressed by its precision. Proving vulnerabilities before flagging them makes every finding far more actionable.
Herrington Darkholme, creator of ast-grep
Review incoming changes before merge
PR security reviews assess each incoming change, including agent-generated code, for vulnerabilities that are reachable and exploitable in the existing application.

CodeRabbit’s Security Architecture Review examines how architecture-level changes affect permissions, sensitive data flows, and trust boundaries. The Security Blast Radius map connects changed components to their dependencies and the code that relies on them, helping reviewers trace the potential security impact beyond the PR diff.

On GitHub, administrators can enable CodeRabbit Security check and require it through branch protection or a ruleset. It blocks merges when PR security comments at or above the configured severity threshold remain unresolved.
Recheck code as it evolves and validate findings at runtime

Each Deep Scan builds an attack surface map of the repository, showing which security-relevant entry points have been verified, which have gone stale as the code changed, and which have never been examined. Delta scans then check changed files and areas of the map that are out of date or unverified, so teams know how much of the codebase has been security-reviewed and when it was last reviewed. Individual findings can also be rechecked to determine whether a fix addressed them.

For eligible Deep Scan findings on GitHub Cloud with CodeRabbit Cloud, runtime verification generates a reproduction guide and can run it in an isolated environment to confirm whether the vulnerable path is reached. Results are “reproduced”, “not reproduced” or “inconclusive” for the tested revision and environment, however a failure to reproduce may not mean the finding is fixed.
