9af9c51a7fd2f67a: From Abd Rahim Romle and Ainur Rabiyatul Abd Rahim

A Malaysian applying for a licence, renewing a permit, or seeking government assistance should not have to navigate several websites, remember multiple passwords, or repeatedly submit the same information. Yet for some, accessing public services can still feel more complicated than it should.
We have become good at introducing digital platforms. The more important question is whether these platforms are making life easier for the rakyat.

Malaysia's digital transformation has brought improvements to public administration. Online apps, electronic payments, and digital records have reduced the need for physical visits and made many services more convenient.
These achievements deserve recognition. However, digital progress should not be measured simply by the number of apps launched or systems developed.
A government service is only successful when people can use it easily, reliably, and without unnecessary frustration.

Consider a small business owner applying for an operating licence. The application may be available online, but if the process still requires repeated document submissions, unclear approvals, or visits to different departments, digitalisation has merely changed the location of the bureaucracy.
The same applies to a parent seeking educational assistance, or an elderly person accessing healthcare services.
For these Malaysians, convenience matters more than the technology behind the system.

The 13th Malaysia Plan (2026-2030) places digital transformation and public service efficiency among Malaysia's development priorities. The challenge is ensuring that these ambitions translate into improvements that citizens can experience.

One persistent concern is fragmentation. Different agencies may operate separate systems with different registration requirements, procedures and user interfaces. While each platform may serve an administrative purpose, the combined experience can become confusing.
Citizens should not have to understand the organisational structure of government simply to obtain a service.

A more effective approach would focus on integrating services around people's needs. For example, starting a small business involves several administrative requirements. Instead of expecting entrepreneurs to navigate multiple agencies independently, government systems should provide clearer guidance and better coordination.
Similarly, families applying for assistance should not repeatedly provide information already held by public institutions, subject to appropriate privacy safeguards.

Another challenge is digital inclusion. Not every Malaysian has reliable internet access, the latest smartphone, or sufficient digital literacy to navigate complicated applications. Older citizens, rural communities, and people with disabilities may face additional difficulties.
Digital transformation should, therefore, preserve accessible alternatives while improving online services.

Three priorities deserve attention. First, government agencies should evaluate digital platforms through citizen experience rather than technological output. Processing times, successful applications, accessibility, and complaint resolution should become central performance indicators.

Second, greater emphasis should be placed on interoperability and administrative simplification. Agencies must improve information-sharing and eliminate unnecessary procedures before transferring them online.

Third, public servants should receive continuous training to provide responsive assistance across both digital and physical service channels. Technology cannot compensate for unclear procedures, weak coordination, or poor communication.

Importantly, public feedback must play a stronger role in evaluating service quality. When citizens report difficulties, their experiences should inform system improvements rather than disappear into administrative complaint channels.

Malaysia does not necessarily need another app whenever a service problem emerges. Sometimes, improving an existing platform, simplifying a form, or ensuring that someone answers a telephone call would make a greater difference. The objective should never be digitalisation for its own sake.

Malaysia's ambition to become a competitive digital economy depends partly on building public institutions that are efficient, trustworthy and responsive. A well-designed digital government should save citizens time, reduce costs, and make essential services easier to access.

The rakyat do not judge government efficiency by how many digital platforms exist. They judge it by whether applications are processed promptly, information is clear, and problems are resolved without unnecessary obstacles.
Malaysia's next public sector breakthrough may not require another digital platform. It may simply require making the services we already have work better for everyone.

Abd Rahim Romle is an associate professor and deputy dean at the Ghazali Shafie Graduate School of Government at Universiti Utara Malaysia. Ainur Rabiyatul Abd Rahim is a Master of Teaching English as a Second Language candidate at Universiti Putra Malaysia.

2ef03f377757f8dc: MELAKA: Asean member states must strengthen collective military readiness before crises emerge, amid an increasingly complex and unpredictable regional security landscape.

"Collective readiness cannot be built when a crisis is already unfolding. Instead, it must be developed well before a crisis erupts," he said.

81b21a83da89693c: CHINA doesn't need to clear Europe's trade barriers. It can build inside them.

Chinese firms are establishing production and supplier networks across Central and Eastern Europe, which could enable them to gain more control over the technologies and inputs that European manufacturing needs.
China is increasingly challenging the European Union in the advanced manufacturing sectors that helped the EU weather the first China shock, which reshaped global manufacturing in the 2000s.
Chinese firms are competing with the EU in chemicals, machinery, advanced equipment and autos — and increasingly coming out on top on price and quality.

The EU trade deficit with China has nearly quadrupled over the past decade, from around 100 billion euros in 2014 to over 370 billion euros last year, or roughly one billion euros a day, according to Eurostat data.

France and Germany are seeking to push back with stronger trade defences, but import curbs will achieve little if Chinese investment, ownership and control of critical technologies recreates the same vulnerabilities inside the single market.
Central and Eastern Europe (CEE) appear to be key to China's growth strategy in Europe.
For example, Slovenia's goods deficit with China rose from 2.5 per cent to 16 per cent over that period. Investment and corporate ties deepened that exposure.

Last year, Chinese foreign direct investment (FDI) flows into the EU approached 16.8 billion euros, and the cumulative value of Chinese investment in the bloc was about 95 billion euros, according to Eurostat and Rhodium Group data.
While most legacy Chinese FDI in Europe centred on Germany, France and the Benelux countries, the focus has shifted east in recent years.

CEE has attracted more than half of Chinese FDI into the EU and Britain since 2021, according to an analysis by the Rhodium Group, with an even larger regional share when the Western Balkans are included.
Hungary has attracted the largest share of new investment since the Covid-19 pandemic, hitting 44 per cent in 2023 and 23 per cent last year.

The investment surge in CEE has largely been driven by mega-projects in the electric vehicle (EV) supply chain. Chinese EV and battery manufacturers CATL, BYD and Sunwoda are all establishing major Hungarian operations.
Slovakia has attracted investment from Chinese battery tech firm Gotion and will be the site of a new plant owned by Volvo Cars, the carmaker majority-owned by China's Geely Holding.

Meanwhile, Serbia, which has significant steel and copper assets, has signed contracts with Chinese auto firms Minth, Shanghai Automotive Chassis, BMTS Technology and Xingyu Automotive, envisaging around one billion euros in investment and nearly 1,700 car-parts jobs.
The deals also include a new robotics factory in Sabac, billed as Europe's first humanoid robot mass production base.
These investments can create jobs, spur growth, and accelerate the energy transition, but they may also erode EU competitiveness over time.
Outsourcing key advanced manufacturing technologies to Chinese entities risks deepening Europe's dependence on external supply chains and weakening domestic innovation and research and development.

Europe is seeking to limit China's access to its consumer markets and industries, but the current Franco-German push for faster defensive trade action and tougher investment screening across the bloc appears to be too little too late.
Europe's flagship proposal, the Industrial Accelerator Act, leaves manufacturers' key competitiveness gaps unaddressed.

Moreover, its screening mechanism would largely leave unexamined Chinese control via ultimate ownership, foreign subsidies and supply-chain concentration — some key issues when looking at CEE's growing dependence.
There is also the problem of fragmentation across the bloc. Investment deals might be in one country's interest but could weaken the bloc's collective negotiating position with Beijing.

To address this, the continent would likely need a permanent European economic security coordination mechanism to unite trade, competition and national screening authorities that could identify risks before investments become irreversible.
Yet the chances of forming such a body at a time of growing political fragmentation within EU countries seem slim.
And, ultimately, protectionism cannot compensate for the region's structural problems, including expensive energy, fragmented capital markets and slow industrial innovation.
For that, the region would likely need to create a true energy union and invest in technological innovation.
Building trade walls buys time, but not true change.
The writer is director of the Geoeconomics Program of the Center for the Study of Democracy

81186c1a62923f38: The contact details of 22 million people were accessed after a cyberattack on a subsidiary of France's postal service, officials say.

La Poste confirmed to The Register that an attack in September had resulted in full names and postal addresses being stolen by cybercriminals.The attack targeted the systems of Maileva, a business mail platform that's part of Docaposte, the digital services arm of La Poste.
Customers use Maileva for hybrid post services. They upload the documents they need to send to Maileva, which then prints and posts the letters on behalf of the customer.
According to Maileva itself, the service has more than 70,000 registered users and is trusted to send more than 180 million documents per year.
The digital assault was first reported by French cyberattack-tracking website Cyberattaque late last week, revealing that Maileva notified customers of an attempted intrusion in late September.
The letters mentioned the cybercriminal attempting to send emails using customers' official, trusted addresses, a situation which resulted in Maileva service disruption for six days.
A number of Maileva customers issued public statements confirming the attack in October.

Cornouaille's occupational health and safety service, for example, said the attack targeted Maileva's tracking database. It went on to say that senders' usernames and email addresses were also compromised, and that recipients' genders were exposed too, adding to the potentially affected data types that La Poste confirmed over the weekend.
Maileva told the organization it was not aware of any compromise of documents uploaded to the platform, nor did the attacker alter or destroy any data.
However, the disclosures of other customers suggested that each may have been affected differently.

In the case of the Foch hospital in Suresnes, whose debt recovery partner Kiwee was a Maileva customer, the names of documents sent to recipients may have been exposed, which may have indirectly revealed details about medical conditions.

According to Cyberattaque, the attacker also potentially accessed the contents of payment reminder letters, which in turn revealed additional details such as invoice numbers and amounts, and treatment dates.
Another case involving social housing provider Flandre Opale Habitat reportedly exposed details from letters dating back ten years.

La Poste said in a statement to The Register: "All teams are working hard to provide the best possible support to Maileva's clients and remain committed to rigorously and professionally implementing the necessary measures to ensure the security of its own operations and those of its clients."
The attack on Maileva is the second major cyber-related disruption La Poste has handled in the space of a year.

On December 22, 2025, the organization fended off a DDoS attack, which went on to affect mail operations for days, including online parcel tracking and its banking arm’s online services, right at its busiest time of the year.
La Poste described the DDoS attack as "unprecedented in its scale and power," and while it had mostly subsided by December 24, the attackers restarted it in the early hours of New Year’s Day.

The organization said the second wave comprised "several billion connection attempts per second," sent from several million IP addresses. More than 300 cybersecurity specialists were involved in defending and remediating the attack. ®

a655dd629143cd1e: A RESOUNDING Democratic takeover of Capitol Hill did more than rattle Asian chipmakers. It set off a macro realignment of foreign policy, energy and trade that could create new winners and losers across Asian markets.
The "blue wave" in the United States midterm elections on Nov 3 triggered an anti-artificial intelligence (AI) market shock, sending the tech-heavy Nasdaq to its steepest fall in 19 months.
Investors feared that incoming Democratic leaders would subject AI companies to stricter scrutiny, including over data centre construction and tax breaks.
Asian equities led the regional retreat in the week of the vote. South Korea's KOSPI and Taiwan's TAIEX each tumbled 12 per cent, dragging the broader MSCI Asia ex Japan index down five per cent.

While Asian markets have recovered some ground, investors remain on edge after an October tech selloff driven by valuation concerns and doubts about the payoff from AI investment, fears since amplified by turmoil at Nvidia, a key engine of the AI boom.
The ramifications of the US elections for Asia extend well beyond data centres.

First, there is US policy in the Middle East. Democratic congressional control could pressure the White House to de-escalate the US-Iran war. Indeed, President Donald Trump said the US was unlikely to strike Iran while negotiations continued, a far cry from the more hawkish rhetoric before the elections.
Markets appear to be pricing in this policy shift. Since the midterms, benchmark Brent crude oil has fallen for a second straight week, dropping nearly 19 per cent to below US$96 a barrel.
Cheaper energy could offer relief across Asia.

Historically, around 80 per cent of oil and 90 per cent of gas transiting the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint was destined for ‌Asian markets, meaning this year's Middle East conflict has hit the region particularly hard.
The countries that stand to benefit the most from falling fuel prices include Japan, South Korea and India.

In addition to weighing on inflation and helping boost growth, declining oil prices should also be positive for Asian energy importers' trade balances, which, all else being equal, could help boost their currencies.
But this is where countries may see greater divergence.

North Asian economies have seen their trade surpluses balloon over the past year on the back of massive AI exports. So, if oil prices and AI demand decline together, the latter could offset the former, leaving large tech exporters as net losers.
That shouldn't be the case for their less tech-exposed neighbours.

Currency markets illustrate the divide. Since Nov 3, South Korea's won and the Taiwan dollar have underperformed their major Asian peers, whereas the Indian rupee, heavily exposed to oil prices but not to tech hardware exports, has appreciated sharply.
A widely held view in the US, echoed by leaders on both sides of the aisle, is that elevated prices were a major factor behind the Democratic landslide.
Policy focused on improving affordability could, therefore, become more prominent in both parties' agendas.

Tariffs played a role in cost-of-living concerns, so the election results may reduce the likelihood that Trump ratchets up his aggressive trade policy, even if he could persist via executive authority.
Given bipartisan concerns about China, trade pressure on Beijing may not ease.
But this could benefit other Asian countries that supply consumer goods, such as Vietnam, Bangladesh, Thailand, Indonesia and India.
Another key affordability issue was healthcare. Efforts by Democrats to lower healthcare costs could accelerate demand for generic drugs and outsourced manufacturing.

India could be well positioned here. The country's generic manufacturers, including Sun Pharmaceutical Industries, produce roughly 20 per cent of the world's generic medicines and already supply about 40 per cent of US demand for generics.
However, nothing is certain. Should Trump leverage his executive powers to escalate Middle East conflicts, any projected relief from inflation or high energy costs would immediately vanish.

Furthermore, if strategic competition with China pushes Washington to loosen domestic constraints on AI development, capital could pivot rapidly back to North Asian hardware exporters, relegating markets like India to the sidelines.
For now, navigating Asia requires recognising that Washington's policy shifts reach far beyond the AI supply chain.
Writing for Reuters, the writer is founder and chief executive officer of Emmer Capital Partners Ltd and the former head of Asia-Pacific Equity Research at BNP Paribas Securities

a0f6bb2263066289: AT the tail end of the 49th Asean Summit in Manila yesterday, the bloc made progress on a slew of collaborations on artificial intelligence, the digital economy and maritime security.

However, like in previous years, Asean barely moved the needle on Myanmar's civil conflict, military crackdowns and persecutions, preferring to uphold "constructive and principled engagement", a position that won't settle the humanitarian crisis in the country.
About 3.6 million people are displaced inside Myanmar while 1.5 million refugees and asylum seekers, Rohingya in particular, have mostly fled to Malaysia.
Since the 1980s, Malaysia has taken in 126,000 Rohingya registered with the United Nations refugee agency, UNHCR, and thousands more who are undocumented.
With third countries slow or reluctant to share the load, Malaysia has had to tighten security and registration, allow conditional access to temporary work and pursue repatriation.
Other than the refugee crisis, transnational crime is rife within Myanmar in the form of cybercrime, fraud, human trafficking, forced labour and illegal gambling.

According to reports, these criminals have netted US$1.4 billion since 2015. China has aggressively cracked down on syndicates operating in the Kokang region, executing 11 of its core figures in January.

However, action against major syndicates has inadvertently created smaller, more mobile criminal groups that conduct online scams. This is why Asean must act now, with Malaysia taking the lead in a joint anti-scam task force linking police, financial intelligence units, immigration authorities and cybersecurity agencies.

This task force should run joint investigations under agreed procedures for arrests and evidence collection and be able to freeze suspicious bank accounts, cryptocurrency assets and other illicit proceeds.
It should support common extradition and prosecution of offenders while providing repatriation, legal aid and psychological support for victims.

Decades of Asean's tenet of consensus and non-interference has regularly excused inaction, but this task force needs teeth. Malaysia is in a position to lead because many of its citizens have lost money and their lives to these criminal networks.

Besides, our National Scam Response Centre provides a good working model. Asean must also rope in China and the United States, on top of global and regional banks and technology platforms, as scam syndicates operate not just within Southeast Asia.

To make enforcement work, there has to be political will. Member states must be committed to tracking the evidence, even when it leads to investigations and indictments of "influential" individuals or businesses.
That, more than any summit communiqué, will show whether Asean can actually protect its people.
1b4297afbc04034b: JOHOR BARU: About 170 students from five schools in Johor have completed a three-month programme to learn traditional Indonesian dances and graduated at a ceremony today.
Organised by the Indonesian Consulate-General in Johor Baru, the initiative aimed to strengthen cultural ties between Indonesia and its neighbouring countries.
The students showcased dances representing various Indonesian regions during the graduation ceremony.
Indonesian Consul-General Sigit Suryantoro Widiyanto said cultural diplomacy played an important role in strengthening ties between communities beyond formal government and economic relations.
"While diplomatic and economic relations can be built through agreements on paper, bonds between people are nurtured through the language of art and culture.
"The historical, geographical and shared cultural ties between Indonesia and Malaysia, particularly with Johor, must continue to be strengthened through tangible initiatives.
"Cultural preservation cannot be taken for granted. It must be introduced and passed down to the next generation," he said.
He hoped the programme would continue in the coming years and eventually become an annual initiative involving more schools, with support from the Johor government and state education authorities.
The programme, which began in September, involved students from SK (P) Sultan Ibrahim, SK Larkin 2, SK Ngee Heng, SMK Majidi Baru 2 and Austin Heights International School.
They received training from Indonesian dance instructor Ghasanni Ashabul Jannah, better known as Nona JJ, from West Java.
Among the dances performed were Bajidor Kahot from West Java, Mappadendang from South Sulawesi, Tari Piring, Dayak dance and Ondel-Ondel from Jakarta.
The students also performed Malaysian dances, including Zapin Melayu and Gramiyam, highlighting the two-way cultural exchange promoted by the programme.

Johor Unity, Heritage and Culture Committee chairman P. Pannir Selvam, who attended the ceremony, said the initiative went beyond teaching dance by exposing young people to different cultural traditions.
He said exposure to arts and heritage helped nurture mutual understanding, tolerance and respect among communities.
e914d5022a22c74e: ISLAMABAD: Pakistan’s imprisoned former prime minister Imran Khan appealed Monday to the country’s top judges, seeking their help in getting urgent medical treatment for himself and his wife, and alleging that authorities had failed to implement an earlier court order to transfer him to a hospital in the capital, Islamabad, The Associated Press (AP) reported.

In an open letter and conveyed to the judges through his lawyer, Imran said his blood pressure had risen sharply and that doctors had warned him he was at risk of a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest.

According to the letter released to the media by Imran’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party and lawyer Salman Safdar, the former premier said that his wife, Bushra Bibi, also needed further eye surgery and could permanently lose her sight without it.

Imran has been in prison since 2023 after being convicted in a graft case. He was removed from office in a parliamentary no-confidence vote in April 2022. Despite his legal troubles, Imran remains a central and popular figure in Pakistan, and the PTI wants his release.
Imran's wife is also serving a prison term on graft charges.
Tariq Fazal Chaudhry, a Cabinet minister, disputed Khan’s account, saying he was receiving regular medical care and accusing him of seeking political advantage.

In a post on X, Tariq said Imran has been taken to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences in Islamabad eight times for examinations, where his health and blood pressure were found to be satisfactory.

He said Imran received meals of his choice and had access to books and television. The government was responsible for ensuring Imran’s medical care and protecting his legal rights, as it was for every prisoner, Tariq said.
The latest development comes days after authorities allowed Imran's lawyers to see him at the prison.
“Today, I ask only that my wife and I be treated,” he said according to the letter. “I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive.”
The letter was addressed to the chief justices of Pakistan’s Supreme Court and other courts.
“I appeal to Your Lordships on the most basic grounds of human compassion: give me justice before it is too late,” Imran said.

Earlier this year, Salman, Imran's lawyer, told the Supreme Court that the former premier had lost roughly 85 per cent of vision in his right eye. The government at the time denied the claim, and one of Imran’s sisters said his eyesight had significantly improved following medical treatment, which authorities say is ongoing.

The government of prime minister Shehbaz Sharif has said that Imran is not being held under a government order but as a “convicted prisoner” serving sentences imposed by the courts following judicial proceedings.

The government has rejected allegations that Imran was being held in solitary confinement or denied contact with his family, saying Imran had received more than 900 visits since his imprisonment in 2023.

<!--kg-card-end: html--> When writer and musician Samantha Shokin noticed her cover of a public domain Bulgarian folk song had been copyright struck on YouTube, she assumed it would be easy to fix. It wasn’t. And trying to figure out what happened led her to discover an AI content mill that is running 500 slop-filled channels and abusing YouTube’s automated copyright detectors.
“Any human would agree with me that there’s something clearly wrong here that needs to be fixed, but I can’t get in touch with a human being,” Shokin said.
Shokin’s journey is a modern nightmare that highlights the ways AI can be weaponized against human creators, and the ways people fall through the cracks of big tech’s automated systems.

During the pandemic, Shokin recorded a 50 second version of the Bulgarian folk song ‘Bre Petrunko’ and uploaded it to SoundCloud, where it didn’t get much traction. Two years later, she uploaded it to YouTube and watched as her cover grew in popularity, gaining 125,000 views in four years.

Last summer, she noticed an uptick in comments on the video. Unbeknownst to Shokin, her version of “Bre Petruinko” had become popular among DJs and electronic artists and had been sampled in dozens of songs. Someone in the comments pointed her towards one of the more popular tracks. “I look up this video and it’s something that has millions of hits [...] and 30 seconds into this track I hear my own voice and I was utterly shocked. I didn’t know how to react,” she said (the video has more than 4 million views).

“The first thing that comes to mind is, ‘Oh my god, someone stole my voice and didn’t credit me,’” she said. Shokin said she talked to a lot of DJs and figured out how they’d gotten her voice. They’d purchased a pack of samples from a company called Loopmasters that was selling her version of “Bre Petruinko” as part of its “Folk Legends” set.

“I got in touch with the distributor and they were deeply apologetic. They were unaware that this had happened and they immediately tried to make right of the situation and granted me royalties on the sample pack,” Shokin said. “At that point, countless DJs and music producers had been using my voice for their own tracks, unbeknownst to me. At least I’m aware and at least I was making something off of it and I was satisfied with that. I didn’t love the way that it came about, but whatever, they tried to make right of the situation.”

But Shokin’s “Bre Petruinko” saga wasn’t over. Last month, she opened YouTube and noticed her original recording was gone. A company called Media Nov Records had issued a copyright strike against her song, and YouTube had taken it down.She thought it would be easy to get this reversed. It’s a public domain folk song and she had the original recordings and a history with a distributor. “If I just explain it to YouTube, they’ll understand,” she thought.

Media Nov Records advertises itself as a “distribution company” that that partners with artists to release their music on digital platforms. But a lot of its website focuses on rights management and copyright protection. “At Media Nov, we go above and beyond to safeguard your musical creations. Our comprehensive rights management system leverages cutting-edge technology and legal expertise to ensure you receive the royalties you deserve,” it said on its website.

YouTube uses automated systems to work through copyright claims. When someone files a claim against a video, the company tends to automatically approve it. The original uploader can file a “counterclaim,” where they argue that the video should stay up, or that it should not be demonetized.

Shokin filed two counterclaims, but neither worked. “It's unclear to us whether you have a valid reason for filing a counter notification, so we won't be able to honor your request,” YouTube said in its last denial. It told her to contact the copyright holder; in this case, it was a public domain song and so there was no actual “copyright holder,” just Media Nov, which was claiming to hold it.

“I tried emailing them,” she said. “I tried calling them. There doesn’t appear to be a working phone line. I got in touch with [Loopmaster, which was selling her recording]. They tried getting in touch. I’m being ignored by everybody, by YouTube, by this media company that, like, the website seems to be entirely AI-generated, and all I want is to talk to a human about this.”

Media Nov’s site boasted about its use of automated DMCA takedowns, YouTube content ID management, and AI-powered content recognition. “Our advanced AI identifies your music across platforms ensuring accurate tracking and protection,” it said. The company says it has been in existence since 1996, but Archive.org’s Wayback Machine doesn’t show much of a web presence until last year. Its website is basic and barebones.

The company has two addresses on its website. One is an apartment building in Los Angeles on Marina Del Rey. The other is the Black Church in Dublin, Ireland — a cathedral that’s been converted into an office space. The site listed a Los Angeles phone number that was busy every time 404 Media tried to call it.

According to corporate paperwork filed in Ireland and reviewed by 404 Media, Media Nov Records was founded a little more than a year ago. Its listed address is the Black Church in Ireland but both of its shareholders gave addresses in Turkey.

404 Media found four different YouTube pages managed by Media Nov Records. Each contained hundreds of videos — many with AI-generated art assets and music. The songs are sometimes cross posted between the different channels and are mostly looping electronic beats. Think low effort “lofi beats” knock offs. The art assets are footage of sports cars, anime girls, and AI-generated pictures of women. The songs are cross posted on multiple channels and often generate fewer than 100 views. Each also has few YouTube shorts that revolve around “random acts of kindness.” A Douyin (the Chinese version of TikTok) watermark is present in some of these videos.

For example, recent YouTube shorts on its flagship page include a basic beat playing over an AI-generated woman mopping the floor of a store while being berated by her AI-generated boss. Another features an AI-generated woman crying over a well, and a crew of men rescuing her child. One of its other pages looks like this:

Media Nov Records told 404 Media that it operates 500 of these channels and “works with various artists, content creators, and music partners.” The company did not initially return emails or phone calls from Shokin or Loopmaster, but responded to an email from 404 Media.

It said it would look into its copyright claim of Shokin’s track. “We remain willing to review the relevant ownership documentation, original audio files, and supporting evidence to investigate the copyright claim thoroughly. If an error is identified, we are committed to taking appropriate corrective action promptly,” it said.

After 404 Media requested comment, Media Nov Records responded to Shokin and asked her to provide “relevant documentation supporting her ownership of the recording, including original audio files, recording evidence, original publication dates, and any other supporting materials,” which is a wild request considering that it has nothing to do with her recording and does not own the copyright.

The company told 404 Media that Shokin and Loopmaster’s emails had gone to its spam folder. “Regarding ‘Bre Petrunko,’ we would like to clarify that the musical composition and arrangement rights associated with Philip Koutev’s work must be distinguished from the rights in any individual sound recording. Media Nov Records also holds certain rights relating to the relevant musical content,” the company told Shokin in an email reviewed by 404 Media.

“Bre Petrunko” is an old folk song with no known writer. It’s primarily sung and most performances of it do not use instruments. Philip Koutev is a Bulgarian composer who popularized a version of the song in 1963. He died in 1982 and the copyright for that particular version is held by the Smithsonian. There are also many other versions of the song on YouTube, some with millions of views.

“Recording your own cover or performance does not automatically establish ownership of the underlying composition or arrangement. Likewise, rights in the underlying musical work do not automatically establish ownership of your particular recording,” Media Nov said.

“It’s ironic that they’re in the copyright business,” Shokin said. “It’s not the arrangement that’s in question. It’s the voice and performance [...] they clearly have no clue what they’re talking about.”

It's unclear why Media Nov Records brought Koutev into the conversation. 404 Media asked which song or work in its catalog triggered the copyright notice against Shokin but Media Nov Records did not respond.

“That makes it really ridiculous,” Alfred Steiner, an artist and copyright lawyer, told 404 Media. “If it’s her voice and her playing instruments, what could she possibly be infringing if it’s a folk song from the 19th century?”

The situation between Shokin and Media Nov Records sounded odd to Steiner. “I've seen lots of providers where you say ‘I have the rights’ and basically say nothing more than that, and they put it back because they’re taking a risk now. They’re harming her. If they just put it back, they’re at no risk,” he said.

“It sounds, to me, like a small company — despite the fact that they represent or run 500 YouTube channels — that are understaffed and is using a lot of different tools, probably a lot of AI, to identify tracks that are ostensibly owned by its clients and then automatically filing takedown requests,” he said. “They’re probably taking down far more than they have the right to take down.”

Minutes after it sent Shokin an email asking for proof she’d recorded the song, Media Nov Records followed up in an email addressed to both 404 Media and Shokin. “Following our review, Media Nov Records has decided to retract the copyright removal request for Samantha Shokin’s video. We are taking this step because the video has not generated revenue or received views, and we do not consider maintaining the removal request necessary at this stage,” it said. “However, this decision does not constitute a waiver of any rights we may hold. We intend to initiate appropriate legal proceedings regarding the underlying copyright dispute.”
Around 24 hours later, Shokin’s original video was back up. A spokesperson for YouTube confirmed that it reinstated the video after the claimant withdrew their complaint.
“It sounds like they got scared and feel like this is not a battle worth fighting,” Shokin said after seeing the email from Media Nov Records.

“Submitting a takedown request for rights that you don’t have can subject you to liability which includes actual damages and costs and attorney’s fees,” Steiner told 404 Media. “Doing this on a slipshod, shotgun approach is inadvisable from my perspective. Of course, if all of the people you end up offending are small parties and don’t have the resources to respond through the court system, and you are a fly-by-night entity that is hard to pin down and nobody knows who you are [...] it can be difficult to get a remedy.”

Shokin said she felt vindicated but was unhappy that it took a journalist emailing Media Nov Records to get them to listen to her. “They got my emails and they got Loopmaster’s email and they were just ignoring it because they only decided to respond because they got scared that it’ll be bad press,” she said. “It’s just not great all around. The whole system is broken. It feels like a broken system.”

e71b89da3f15416f: PETALING JAYA: A dentist was fined RM70,000 by the sessions court here today after being found guilty of two charges of employing an individual who was not registered as a dental practitioner and allowing the person to perform dental procedures at her clinic two years ago.
Judge Noor Ruzilawati Mohd Noor imposed a fine of RM30,000 for the first charge and RM40,000 for the second, with six and seven months' imprisonment respectively in default of payment.

Dr Tong Soo Huan, 38, was charged with employing an individual who was not registered as a dental practitioner under the Dental Act 2018 at a dental clinic in Jalan SS21/1 here at 12.50 pm on May 6, 2024.
The charge was brought under Section 68 of the Dental Act 2018, which provides for a maximum fine of RM300,000 or imprisonment for up to six years, or both.

She was also charged with allowing an individual who was not registered under the Act to practise dentistry at her clinic on the same date and time, under Section 69(a) of the same Act, which carries the same maximum penalty.

According to the facts of the case, on May 6, 2024, a team of enforcement officers from the Selangor State Health Department conducted an inspection at Dr Tong's clinic and found a female staff member scanning a patient's teeth using an iTero Element intraoral scanner.

The inspection found that the staff member was not registered with the Malaysian Dental Council (MDC) as a dental practitioner, while Dr Tong, who was a registered dental practitioner, failed to produce the staff member's annual practising certificate when requested by the enforcement officers.

Earlier, Health Ministry (MOH) prosecuting officer Dr Haznita Zainal Abidin urged the court to impose substantial fines for both charges in the interest of public safety and patient protection, noting that the offences were of a strict liability nature and involved the integrity of the dental profession.

"The accused not only failed to ensure that a registered dental practitioner was on duty throughout the clinic's operating hours, but also deliberately instructed and allowed a clinic staff member whose only qualification was the Sijil Pelajaran Malaysia (SPM) to perform dental procedures, namely intraoral scanning using specialised medical device equipment at the accused's premises.

"An oral scanning procedure using an intraoral scanner (iTero Element) requires a high level of expertise to operate. Based on testimony from the Medical Device Authority, the device can only be operated by qualified medical or dental practitioners," she said.

Dr Haznita said the sentence should send a strong message and serve as a stern lesson to the accused and the entire dental practitioner community in Malaysia not to take shortcuts to cut costs or disregard the law by delegating clinical duties to staff without professional qualifications.
However, lawyer Rejinder Singh, representing Dr Tong, appealed for a lighter fine, arguing that his client was a first-time offender and had no previous record of offences under the Dental Act 2018.
"The offence committed was a technical violation and did not involve any criminal element, as a patient had come to the clinic for treatment while Dr Tong was out for lunch at the time.
"The accused is aware of her actions and regrets not exercising greater vigilance in supervising the clinic staff. She has pledged to ensure stricter control measures in the future," the lawyer said.

5bdecafd2c8a4d92: WASHINGTON: The Trump administration on Monday issued a rule that will further restrict China's access to the best AI chips from companies like Nvidia, just as President Donald Trump began a trip to China to meet with President Xi Jinping.

The new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres in countries like Malaysia and Thailand will hurt Chinese companies who use those datacentres to access advanced AI chips to train their AI models.

The rule shows the commerce department is scrambling to show it is cracking down on Chinese access to sensitive American technology, following reporting that the agency turned a blind eye to the smuggling of advanced Nvidia AI chips to China.

It also comes as Trump is set on Thursday to meet with Xi in China's southern city of Shenzhen, the site of this week's Apec summit. Trump often unleashes punitive tech threats or action against Beijing ahead of such meetings.

The new rule requires companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to cut down on them being illegally diverted.
The timing of the rule also coincides with increased pressure on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to bolster US export controls of advanced chips to China.

08350c681e0f0d0f: MANILA: Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim has dismissed speculation of a Cabinet reshuffle, saying the government remains stable and focused on delivering its policies.

"The government is stable now, policies are discussed comprehensively in the Cabinet, and I work with ministers from various parties.

"We work, share, discuss and have a common position, including on sensitive bilateral, multilateral and Asean issues," he told a media conference on the sidelines of the 49th Asean Summit and Related Summits here today.
On Loke's resignation, Anwar said he respected the DAP leader's principled stance, although he had earlier asked him to reconsider.
"He, on principle, asked me to accept his resignation, which I have yet to do. But I respect his position because it is important to him to uphold the principles he stands for," he said.

Loke announced his resignation on Nov 10 following the Kuala Lumpur High Court's decision allowing former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak to serve the remainder of his prison sentence under house arrest.
Anwar dismissed claims of government instability as part of a political campaign, saying the administration would remain focused on delivering for the country.
413220c7807ddb35: Most victims of last week's Microsoft outage lost access to their email, but 15 unlucky guests at a German hotel got a dose of chlorine when a warning about dangerous levels never reached staff.

The incident, first reported by German broadcaster WDR, happened on Friday at Hotel Ling Bao, part of the Phantasialand theme park in Brühl, Germany, where a malfunctioning automatic dosing system pumped too much chlorine into the swimming pool.

The hotel's monitoring system spotted the problem and emailed staff a warning about the excessive chlorine levels. Unfortunately, Microsoft's Outlook service was caught up in a global outage, meaning the warning never arrived.

Brühl Fire Department said the problem started when a technical fault caused the pool's dosing equipment to pump in more chlorine than it should have. Chlorine gas then escaped into the swimming area, leaving guests needing medical attention.

Paramedics checked over 15 people at the hotel, and five were taken to hospital. Four suffered minor injuries, while one was moderately injured and needed further treatment. The fire department sent about 40 personnel to the scene, and crews spent roughly two hours dealing with the incident.

The incident came as Microsoft was battling a major outage that began on Thursday, November 12, and dragged well into Friday. Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, and other Microsoft 365 services were knocked offline, leaving businesses unable to access email and documents. The disruption wasn't confined to office workers unable to check their inboxes, with hospitals, police forces, and government departments reporting problems accessing the Microsoft services they use for day-to-day operations.

Redmond has since blamed the outage on a bug introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade. It sat there until a later network change set it off, and the failures then spread across the company's infrastructure. Microsoft ruled out both cybercriminals and AI as culprits, and has issued the customary apology.
At Phantasialand, though, a broken inbox was the least of anyone's worries.

The chlorine dosing equipment went haywire independently of Microsoft's troubles, but the email warning staff about the problem apparently never arrived. Whether the hotel had a backup alarm, or anything capable of shutting off the chlorine supply automatically, remains unanswered.

Why a hotel would rely on Outlook to deliver warnings about dangerous chlorine levels is anyone's guess. Email can be delayed, filtered into spam, or simply disappear when Microsoft's infrastructure throws a tantrum, none of which is particularly helpful when you've got a pool with guests breathing in noxious gas. ®

032a89b87c0f8cb4: KOTA BARU: The recent election victories in Negri Sembilan and Melaka could serve as a catalyst for stronger political cooperation between Perikatan Nasional (PN) and Barisan Nasional (BN).

Pas deputy president Datuk Seri Tuan Ibrahim Tuan Man said the outcomes should be leveraged to strengthen mutual understanding, cooperation and public confidence in both coalitions' ability to provide better leadership and governance.

"The victories should be utilised to expand mutual understanding, strengthen consensus and build public confidence in the ability of both coalitions to offer better leadership and administration to the country," he said.

67a303343be3f57a: COLOMBO: The FBI will help Sri Lankan law enforcement detect cyber scammers who have shifted illicit operations to the island following a crackdown in Southeast Asian countries, the US embassy said Monday.
Police say scam networks have increasingly moved operations to Sri Lanka – an attractive destination owing to its relaxed visa regime and reliable, high-speed internet.

"FBI personnel will work with Sri Lankan law enforcement partners on investigative techniques, digital forensics and case development" in a bid to disrupt transnational criminal networks operating out of the South Asian nation, the US embassy in Colombo said in a statement.

An FBI team will spend a week in Sri Lanka this month training local investigators and helping to identify victims, trace criminal activity and build stronger cases against those responsible for online scams, the embassy added.
Fraud compounds, where scammers lure internet users into fake romantic relationships, cryptocurrency investments and betting platforms, have flourished across Southeast Asia.
Initially targeting largely Chinese speakers, the criminal groups behind the compounds have expanded their operations into multiple languages.
Those conducting the scams are sometimes willing con artists, while others are trafficked foreign nationals forced to work.
Officials say the networks operating in Sri Lanka target victims across Asia, including in India, Vietnam and the Philippines, but there are growing concerns that Sri Lankans could be next.
Since the start of the year, Sri Lankan police have arrested more than 1,100 foreigners, mainly from China, Vietnam and India, for alleged involvement in cybercrime.
Sri Lanka has also sought help from China, which pledged closer cooperation on combatting cybercrime.
Beijing's embassy in Colombo said in March that activity in Sri Lanka had risen following enforcement actions in Cambodia, Myanmar and the United Arab Emirates. — AFP

be969b177c93d70f: PETALING JAYA: Cargo transport is expected to be the main driver of East Coast Rail Link (ECRL) revenue growth, with its contribution projected to more than triple to RM214 million in 2029 from RM68 million in 2027.

Deputy transport minister Hasbi Habibollah said the increase is expected to lift total projected ECRL revenue from passenger and cargo services to RM418 million in 2029, up from RM260 million in 2027, Bernama reported.
Citing a consultant study conducted between 2020 and 2025, he said passenger revenue is projected to rise from RM192 million in 2027 to RM198 million in 2028 and RM204 million in 2029.
Cargo revenue is expected to grow from RM68 million in 2027 to RM71 million in 2028 and RM214 million in 2029, in line with the phased opening of the alignment and cargo facilities.
"In the long term, cargo services are expected to be the main contributor to ECRL revenue, with a target of around 70% from cargo and 30% from passengers once operations mature.”
Hasbi said this when winding up the committee-stage debate on the Supply (Budget) Bill 2027 and the 2027 Development Expenditure Estimates motion for the transport ministry in the Dewan Rakyat today.

He said the ECRL is also seen as a strategic long-term infrastructure investment expected to generate economic spillover effects through increased trade, industrial area and transit-oriented development, new investments, and stronger logistics links between the east coast and west coast.
On the ECRL fare structure, Hasbi said the government has yet to finalise special fare rates for those registered under eKasih and Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah recipients.
"However, the government is offering a 50% fare discount for senior citizens, persons with disabilities and children, as well as 40% for students.
"Proposals for family fare packages and fare caps during festive seasons will also be studied.”
Separately, he said the proposed Trans Borneo Railway project will be brought to the Cabinet for consideration.
The Dewan Rakyat later passed the transport ministry’s 2027 operating and development expenditure estimates totalling RM7.07 billion by a voice vote after a debate involving 21 MPs.
The Dewan Rakyat sitting resumes tomorrow.
0633b8e1172b9f38: PETALING JAYA: Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim says his administration remains stable and focussed on implementing government policies and fulfilling its responsibility to the people, rather than entertaining speculation about a Cabinet reshuffle.
Anwar said there was no pressing need for a reshuffle, in response to calls and speculation following DAP secretary-general Loke Siew Fook’s resignation as transport minister.
“The government is stable. Policies are discussed comprehensively in the Cabinet, and I work with ministers from various parties.

“We work, discuss and share common positions, including on sensitive bilateral, multilateral and Asean issues,” Bernama quoted him as saying on the sidelines of the 49th Asean Summit in Manila, the Philippines today.
Anwar said he respected Loke’s decision as a matter of principle, despite having previously asked him to reconsider his decision.
“Loke has asked me to accept his resignation, which I have yet to do. But I respect his position because it is important to him on the basis of the principles he upholds,” he said.

Loke stepped down as transport minister on Nov 10 following a High Court order allowing former prime minister Najib Razak to serve the remainder of his SRC International prison sentence under house arrest.
Anwar said avenues for political discussions were always open, including through formal and informal meetings with party leaders and members of the administration, to address differences of opinion.
He dismissed claims that the government was unstable, describing them as politically motivated.

“(These claims) are being blown out of proportion as part of a campaign agenda. For now, we must stay on course and continue working. What is important is that we give our best for this country,” he said.
Last Friday, Anwar said the “political temperature” in the Cabinet remained under control despite tensions arising from remarks made by several leaders in the unity government.
He said the political climate usually heats up slightly during elections, but returns to normal once the polls are over.
Deputy prime minister and Barisan Nasional chairman Ahmad Zahid Hamidi also recently reaffirmed his support for Anwar, saying there was no reason for any BN minister to resign from the Cabinet.
f7a3a5d0cb686a0f: MADRID: Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva met leftist ally Pedro Sanchez in Madrid on Monday, with his recent election comeback offering encouragement to the Spanish leader ahead of a snap vote on Nov 29.
Lula, 81, secured re-election in Brazil in October after overcoming conservative rival Flavio Bolsonaro, overturning a first-round deficit to win a closely fought run-off.
The result came despite opinion polls in the final days of the campaign pointing to a Bolsonaro victory.
Sanchez has repeatedly cited Lula's victory as evidence that he too can defy opinion polls, putting him behind right-wing parties.

"It happened in Brazil. It has just happened in the United States. And it will happen soon in Spain," the Socialist said after the Democrats secured a landslide victory in the US midterm elections earlier this month.
Sanchez, 54, and Lula have developed close political ties in recent years and are among the most prominent figures of the international left.
The two leaders embraced and shook hands outside the Moncloa Palace, the Spanish government's headquarters, before heading inside for talks on Monday.
Lula is concluding an international tour that has taken him to Turkey for the COP31 climate talks and the Philippines for a regional summit.
Sanchez's Socialists had initially announced that the two leaders would take part in a discussion at a trade union headquarters in Madrid on Monday, but later cancelled the event.
Lula, who underwent treatment for throat cancer in 2011, has opted not to deliver scheduled speeches in recent days because of vocal fatigue.
Sanchez is also due to meet Uruguayan President Yamandu Orsi on Monday, another of his allies on the Latin American left, at a time when conservative parties are gaining ground across the region.

6368ac2908033cb4: SAN FRANCISCO—When Ars first drove the new Mercedes-Benz CLA last year, the automaker also gave us a sneak preview of its next driver assist. Called Drive Assist Pro, it’s for collaborative partially assisted driving, and from the passenger seat at the time, the demo was impressive. Now the automaker is getting ready to start rolling out Drive Assist Pro to customers with cars running the new MB.OS operating system here in the US and in Germany, and it let us have some time behind the wheel.

While most automakers want a reputation for safety, Mercedes has long used passive and active technology to do so in its products. It was one of the first OEMs to introduce airbags, and a decade later started adding active safety systems like anti-lock brakes, electronic stability control, and adaptive cruise control. And so, by giving the car’s electronics the ability to control the brakes and throttle, we arrive at the first level of assisted driving—called “level 1” in automotive engineer-speak.

“Level 2” assisted driving, where the car also controls the steering as well as the acceleration and braking, got famous with Tesla Autopilot. But the first lane-keeping assists predate it by almost a decade in passenger cars, when Toyota introduced a system in 2004. The human driver behind the wheel is still in charge, responsible for situational awareness (and anything that arises from a lack thereof), with the idea that long drives become less tiring and a little more effortless when the car does the boring job of keeping a constant speed or a constant distance to the car ahead and between the white lines.
0c510f0e83b9b096: A suspected Russian-speaking operator used an AI agent to turn security patches into working exploits with no human in the loop – a first such occurrence, according to the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) – before ultimately stealing data from victim organizations.

Google documented this attack in its fourth-quarter 2026 AI threat tracker, and said it marks a significant advance in how attackers use LLMs for fully autonomous vulnerability discovery and exploitation compared to Q3.

In this case, the threat hunters found an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent vulnerability research and weaponization framework that integrates with multiple frontier and local models. The framework, called exploit_agent, used Russian-language tooling, and was configured to conduct continuous differential analysis of “popular web application software,” according to the report.
This includes comparing code before and after security updates, identifying potential vulnerabilities, developing exploits, and then automatically executing them without any human involvement.

The server also contained data stolen from victim organizations, and “multiple” post-compromise scripts that allowed attackers to perform nefarious activities including internal reconnaissance, brute-forcing, installing webshells, and removing other attackers’ webshells.

“Victim telemetry on the server suggests the operator was specifically interested in targeting French websites associated with the media and entertainment industries, as well as the education sector,” according to the report.

The report also documents other instances of attackers moving beyond manual LLM prompting during cyberattacks and instead deploying autonomous, multi-agent offensive security frameworks to carry out multi-stage intrusions. These include both financially motivated cybercriminals and cyber-espionage groups.

In addition to the recent attacks involving the open source penetration-testing tool ARTEX, attackers have also used other AI-powered offensive frameworks, including CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, HexStrike AI, and PentAGI. In another instance, GTIG observed attackers using PentAGI alongside proxy services to target the aerospace sector.

“We have observed several threat actors separately experimenting with use of these frameworks and harnesses, including financially motivated, as well as suspected espionage threat actors with a PRC nexus,” the Googlers wrote. “Given the low barrier to entry, ease of integrating new exploits, and massive scaling potential, we believe it is highly likely that threat actors will continue to use these frameworks in campaigns targeting organizations globally.” ®
e1b3eccce9b1092f: Celestial AI’s dream of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) at a distance will soon be a reality as part of a new collaboration between Marvell Technology and system integrator Penguin Solutions to build a photonic memory fabric.

Marvell acquired the underlying technology for the fabric from Celestial AI for $3.5 billion in February. It comprises a memory expansion module with two stacks of HBM3e totaling 72 GB along with support for eight channels of DDR5 stacked atop a silicon photonic interposer with 7.2 Tbps (900 GB/s) of bidirectional bandwidth.

“What we provide in this appliance is what we call a Photonic Fabric memory module… We provide these modules to Penguin, and they build the box, do all the power management, do the software, and all the management layer,” Preet Virk, senior VP of Marvell’s photonic fabric biz, tells El Reg.
Penguin’s first appliances based on the tech will support 16 of these memory modules for up to 16 TB of DDR5 and 1 TB of HBM, with future systems capable of scaling to twice the DDR5 capacity.

With 57.6 Tbps of bandwidth distributed via a Marvell-designed optical fiber shuffle, each appliance supports up to 16 servers either via a network interface card, or via co-packaged (CPO) or near-packaged optical (NPO) modules.

If you’re not familiar, CPO modules are typically integrated directly into the compute or switch ASIC, while NPO modules are a sort of half measure. They connect electrically to the host, whether that’s a CPU, GPU, or some other ASIC, and the rest of the fabric optically. NPO is expected to play a major role in the next generation of rack-scale systems from Nvidia and AMD, as it provides better serviceability and lower blast radius than baking photonic chiplets directly into CPUs or GPUs.

Through a software layer, which we’re told was developed by Penguin, each system can access the entire shared memory space, similar to how systems connecting to network-attached storage would have access to the appliance's full capacity.

As we understand it, a lot of this functionality is made possible today through CXL 3.1 compatible NICs and host CPUs, like AMD’s shiny new Venice CPUs. However, for NPO- and CPO-based memory, Virk tells us that CXL can be bypassed entirely.
The implications of this tech should be obvious. If memory can be shared and pooled across multiple servers, each of those servers doesn't need as much of its own DRAM, possibly saving some money.

In addition to facilitating communications, Virk says, the software also allows for several memory tiering modes by which customers can expose the resources to connected systems. For the most part, these follow typical CXL memory tiering conventions, with the exception of an HBM cache-through mode that Virk says will enable users to extract the performance of HBM with the capacity of DDR5.
This mode essentially treats the HBM as a read/write cache. Frequently accessed files are written to and read from HBM first before being pushed into standard DDR5 as they get stale.

Marvell and Penguin are positioning the new memory appliance as an alternative to storage-based key value (KV) cache offload. AI inference generates large KV caches, which are used to track model state across chat sessions, and long-running agents. Depending on the context length, these caches can be both computationally expensive to recompute and large to keep in memory.

Because of this, inactive KV caches are often offloaded to DRAM or flash memory, since it’s faster to store and copy them than to recompute them if and when a session is restored. Marvell contends that by offloading KV caches from HBM directly to these memory appliances, customers can achieve better performance and higher memory utilization.

Beyond AI-adjacent workloads, this technology also has potential to reduce the amount of DRAM required for individual systems, a concept we explored in greater depth earlier this year, and one that Meta has already embraced in its own datacenters.
Marvell expects Penguin’s first generation of Photonic Fabric memory expansion systems to arrive sometime in the second half of next year. ®

Spencer GreenOne of the most quintessential American things is having roasted turkey on the table at a Thanksgiving feast. While that remains the norm, Americans are eating much less of this kind of poultry today than in the past. Annual consumption has fallen by more than 25% over the past three decades, while demand for chicken has soared. I’m a business school professor who has written about the economics of various holidays. I find turkeys fascinating, because even though I live in an urban area, a large group of wild turkeys has taken over my backyard. And I can offer several good explanations for the turkey slump. Receding since the late 1990s Domesticated turkeys, unlike their wild cousins, are a big business. More than US$5 billion worth of the birds were sold in 2025. That’s no chicken feed. However, it’s the latest sign of the industry’s decline. U.S. consumers are drifting away from eating turkey. Back in 1995, the average American consumed 17.7 pounds (8 kilograms) of turkey each year. By 2025, consumption had fallen to just 13.2 pounds (6 kg). While turkey consumption started to recede in the late 1990s, it began accelerating around 2008, when the Great Recession was underway. Occasionally, turkey production ticks upward a little, as happened in 2026 as demand for niche products like turkey jerky rose, but the long-term picture is one of steady decline. It’s not like Americans are eating less poultry overall. Chicken consumption has steadily grown during this turkey slump, rising about 50% from 69 pounds (31 kg) in 1995 to 104 pounds (47 kg) in 2025. In other words, we’re eating almost eight times more chicken than turkey. Well, at least the 95% of Americans who aren’t vegetarian or vegan are. More costly at every step in the supply chain Government agencies, researchers and some pundits have identified two possible explanations for why Americans are eating less turkey. First: pocketbook concerns. Turkey often costs more than chicken, except when it goes on sale just before Thanksgiving. Over the past 25 years, wholesale turkey prices per pound averaged about 10% higher than chicken, according to U.S. Department of Agriculture data. That price, which is what big retailers typically pay, affects what you owe at checkout. For example, just before the 2026 Thanksgiving sales began, a Bell & Evans fresh whole turkey was going for $4.99 a pound, while a Bell & Evans fresh whole chicken cost $3.49 a pound at my local supermarket. That’s $1.50 a pound difference, which is significant in an economy where many people feel economically pinched. Nationally, you will see similar price differences, with fresh turkey being more expensive than fresh chicken. So, why is turkey pricier than chicken? Both turkeys and chickens are fed a diet of corn and soybeans. However, turkeys consume a higher percentage of soybeans. And soybeans currently cost about twice as much as corn. The latest data shows turkey feed costs are up almost 80%, without accounting for inflation, since 2000, while chicken feed costs have climbed only 60%. Too big for more families The second reason has to do with the size of today’s families. The typical Bell & Evans whole chicken my grocery store sells weighs approximately 4 pounds, while its fresh turkeys tend to range between 10 and 12 pounds. Big birds are handy if you have a lot of mouths to feed, but American families have shrunk over time. Today the average household includes only 2.5 people. The extra half-person does not represent children who are picky eaters or people who don’t like eating meat. It just means the typical family has between two and three people. That means cooking a 10-pound turkey results in 4 pounds of food per person, which is far more than almost anyone who is not a competitive food eater can consume. Cooking a 4-pound chicken, however, results in a more manageable 1.2 pounds of poultry per eater after getting rid of the bones, which make up about a quarter of a chicken. In simple terms, buying a whole chicken often results in one or two meals per person. Cooking a whole turkey often yields enough meat to produce meals for an entire week. Raymond Baker carves a turkey in 1948 while his wife and 16 kids surround him. Getty Images There are two more factors to consider. First, a 10-pound turkey costs a lot more than a 4-pound chicken. A 10-pound fresh bird at $4.99 a pound sets you back almost $50, while a $3.49-per-pound chicken that weighs 4 pounds costs under $14. Last, bigger birds take longer to roast. Cooking a 10-pound turkey in an oven takes about three hours, while a 4-pound chicken takes about two. That extra hour is a big burden in an increasingly time-pressed society. In case you were wondering, the world record for eating a turkey is held by Joey Chestnut. He gobbled down 9.35 pounds of turkey off the bone in 10 minutes in 2014. Please do not try that at home. What about wild turkeys? If you need to save money on turkey this holiday season, you should consider buying a frozen one. They are much cheaper. But can you save even more by going turkey hunting? Given all the large wild turkeys roosting in my backyard, I looked into what it would take. I live in Massachusetts, where hunting wild turkeys before Thanksgiving is legal. For much of the fall, hunters are allowed to use only bows and arrows. Beyond needing to be a proficient archer, they also have to purchase a sporting license, a turkey permit and an archery stamp for $95 each year. Having learned about that, I’m sticking to buying my turkeys in the supermarket. Jay L. 36ae6e814e5b9164: The transcript from this week’s, MiB: Vanguard CEO Salim Ramji, is below.

You can stream and download our full conversation, including any podcast extras, on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, and Bloomberg. All of our earlier podcasts on your favorite pod hosts can be found here.
Masters in Business: Salim Ramji, CEO of Vanguard Interview transcript · Bloomberg Radio
[00:00:02] Bloomberg Audio Studios, podcasts, radio, news.

[00:00:07] BARRY RITHOLTZ: This week on the podcast, yet another fascinating conversation. I sit down with Vanguard’s CEO, Salim Ramji. Previously he was at BlackRock, helping to oversee iShares and indexing. He’s got a fascinating background, and really is one of the people in the wealth management industry who is so uniquely situated to see all of these different things that are going on.

What a great perch to observe the future of wealth management. I thought this conversation was fascinating, and I think you will also. With no further ado, my conversation with Vanguard’s Salim Ramji. Salim, welcome to Bloomberg.
[00:00:58] SALIM RAMJI: Well, thanks, Barry. It’s great to be back. I think we did this about half a dozen years ago, right?
[00:01:02] BARRY RITHOLTZ: In the middle of peak COVID. It was a frightening time.
[00:01:07] SALIM RAMJI: It’s nice to be in a studio.
[00:01:09] BARRY RITHOLTZ: Yes. I want to talk about your career and what led you to Vanguard. But I have to start by asking about your academic background.
Bachelor’s in economics and politics from the University of Toronto, and then a master’s in law at Cambridge. And I’m assuming a master’s at Cambridge is like a JD here, is that right?
[00:01:19] SALIM RAMJI: Yeah, kind of.
[00:01:33] BARRY RITHOLTZ: Was the original career plan becoming an attorney?

[00:01:37] SALIM RAMJI: Neither of my parents finished high school. My dad used to run a grocery store that I worked in as a kid. And from my parents’ point of view, they just wanted me to go to college. I don’t think there was any great original plan other than I thought going to college would be a good thing. I was drawn to the law, and ultimately my first job was at a law firm in London, in part because there were so many exciting and interesting things happening in the world of law and business in the early nineties in Europe at the time.

And so that, for me, was a compelling piece. But I wasn’t one of these kids who, from the age of 10, wanted to be a lawyer. It was more—it felt like a really interesting time, with markets liberalizing and lots of new markets opening up all over the world.

[00:02:41] BARRY RITHOLTZ: I’m curious how your upbringing affected how you look at money. You mentioned you worked in your dad’s grocery store; both your parents were immigrants working and living in British Columbia. How did that affect your relationship with money and work?

[00:02:56] SALIM RAMJI: It probably—some of these things you don’t really truly understand until years later. But we didn’t always have a lot of financial security growing up. And I’m at a company that cares very deeply about people’s financial security, and you can sometimes abstract that away in terms of what it means.

But at least for me, I know what having it is, and I know what the absence of it is. Obviously, having some financial security is far better. And I think it really drove home for me the real importance, at a very personal level, of what financial security means in somebody’s life or somebody’s family, and the importance of it to so many other things: the general happiness of the house, the levels of stress in the house, the freedom to be able to do things once you’ve attained it.
