faa3285f0524450b: PAIPORTA, Nov 16 — Maria Laura Bustamante had barely finished furnishing the home she had just bought with her husband in the Spanish town of Paiporta when floods swept through the area, destroying the flat.

The disaster also destroyed the Latin Grammy-nominated couple’s home recording studio, where Bustamante and her husband, Alejandro Rivas, professional musicians who perform together, worked on their music.

Spain’s deadliest floods in a generation devastated the eastern region of Valencia in October 2024, sweeping away cars, submerging roads and buildings, cutting off residents and claiming more than 230 lives.
The couple and their young daughter spent the following months living in the nearby city of Valencia while their flat was being repaired.

“I used to find it difficult to imagine that climate change could affect us or force us to leave our homes,” Bustamante, 40, told AFP on the terrace of her home in Paiporta, one of the hardest-hit towns. “It seemed a long way off.”
The experience inspired the couple to write “El rio no tiene culpa” (The River Is Not to Blame), a song reflecting on climate change and criticising the authorities’ handling of the floods.
It also strengthened their conviction that action is needed to tackle climate change, an issue that has struggled to gain traction ahead of an early general election on November 29.
The floods and recurring wildfires, including July blazes west of Madrid that forced nearly 60,000 people to flee, have highlighted the risks posed by extreme weather.
And the election campaign is unfolding against the backdrop of the COP31 United Nations climate conference in Turkey, which ends on Friday.
Yet surveys suggest climate change remains a low priority for voters.
Housing, the economy and immigration are the issues most likely to influence voters’ choices in the election, according to a survey by pollster Invymark for Spanish television channel laSexta.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A picture taken on October 27, 2026 in Valencia’s Paiporta district shows the Paiporta Auditorium, which remains closed off since the floods on October 29, 2024. — AFP pic
‘Like a tsunami’

The floods initially increased the proportion of people in Valencia who believed climate change was affecting their region, but the effect had faded just six months later, according to an academic study published last month.

However, this shift did not translate into greater support for climate policies, one of the study’s co-authors, University of Barcelona political scientist Jordi Munoz, told AFP, describing the finding as “paradoxical”.
Part of the reason, he said, was that the political debate after the disaster focused on inadequate prevention measures and delays in delivering aid, rather than on climate change itself.
The regional government of Valencia was heavily criticised for not sending out flood alerts to cellphones until 8.11 pm on October 29, 2024, when flooding had already started in some places.
“When the alarm went off, the water was already up to here,” Maria Guillermina Spiekermann, 51, told AFP, gesturing to just above her waist as she described the flooding at her home in Picanya.
“It was truly apocalyptic. Cars piled four or five high, fallen trees and destroyed houses. It looked like a tsunami had hit.”

Her home and bookstore were destroyed, but she questioned the role of climate change, arguing that the region had experienced major floods in the past and that better infrastructure could have prevented much of the damage.
‘Same policies’
Scientists say human-driven climate change is intensifying autumn storms in eastern Spain, as warmer Mediterranean waters fuel evaporation and heavier rainfall.
Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has repeatedly called for a cross-party pact on what he describes as the “climate emergency”.
But on the campaign trail he has made scant mention of the issue.
During a 22-minute speech at a rally in Valencia earlier this month, he referred to the issue just once, describing greenhouse gas emissions as “one of the main problems” affecting the region.

Climate change has featured little in the right-wing opposition Popular Party’s campaign, which has focused on deteriorating public services, particularly rail since last month’s deadly collision, which killed 69 people.
In Paiporta, the public library entrance remains bricked up after flood damage, while pupils at a local primary school still attend classes in prefabricated buildings.
Raul Camacho Segarra, spokesman for neighbourhood volunteer groups set up after the 2024 floods, questioned whether authorities had learned any lessons about climate risks since the disaster.
“It seems incredible that, in a climate crisis, they continue to pursue the same policies,” he said, pointing to continued construction on farmland and in areas vulnerable to flooding. — AFP
efed5b133b094876: SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 16 — Anthropic has become an AI giant valued at US$1 trillion (RM4.1 trillion) and it is now aiming for a record-breaking stock market debut, even if its original ambitions have been watered down somewhat.
The San Francisco-based firm faces three threats: rivals that are catching up, prices that are collapsing, and bills that keep climbing.
Anthropic spelled out the risks in its Wall Street prospectus, the document that lays out its vision to potential investors.
The first is commoditization: “the degree of differentiation among advanced AI models may narrow,” the company warns.

Additionally, Anthropic says that “substantially all” of its revenue comes from its AI tools. Unlike Google or Meta, it has no advertising empire to fall back on if business takes a hit, and no cloud business like Microsoft’s.
Investors have already grown nervous.

In mid-August, shareholders were floating a valuation of US$2 trillion. But quarter-on-quarter growth slowed from 145 per cent in the second quarter to 45 per cent in the third, cooling expectations to around US$1.3 trillion.
Cheap and open
So-called open AI models, which anyone can download and modify, are approaching the capabilities of closed models such as Claude or ChatGPT, which are available only through their owners’ services.
Open models lag their closed counterparts by only about four months on average, according to research institute Epoch AI.
They include Kimi K3.1 Pro from Chinese company Moonshot, which costs half as much as Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic’s current flagship.
And among paid models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, none has stayed on top for long.
Anthropic also acknowledges it is holding itself back: its safety measures “could slow our capability gains relative to competitors that do not adopt similar constraints.”
Still, the company says each new version of Claude has boosted sales. More than 80 per cent of its revenue last quarter came from models less than six months old.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

In this file photo taken on September 29, 2026, co-founder and CEO of Anthropic Dario Amodei (centre) looks on as US Speaker of the House Mike Johnson speaks to the press after a meeting with technology executives about artificial intelligence at the White House in Washington, DC. — AFP pic
Prices collapsing

When products look alike, prices fall. According to Morningstar, the price of having AI process the same amount of text at the same level of performance has dropped 97 per cent, from US$17 at the end of 2024 to 50 cents today.
Anthropic itself cut the price of Claude Opus by 20 per cent in September, and OpenAI cut the price of one of its flagship models by a factor of five in July.
The effect is already visible at Vercel, a developer platform that routes requests across AI models.
In August, more than half of the text it handled was processed by open models, up from 13 per cent in April.
Even so, Anthropic still captured nearly two-thirds of spending on the platform.
Even a 90 per cent price cut would not shrink total spending on AI as long as usage keeps growing at its current pace, said Malik Ahmed Khan, a senior equity analyst at Morningstar.
‘Triple whammy’
Anthropic’s costs, by contrast, are largely locked in. To stay ahead, each new Claude model has to be bigger than the last, trained on more data using more computing power.
Since late 2025, the company has committed to paying at least US$417 billion to rent chips and servers.
That is nearly 13 years of sales at its first-half 2026 pace, and the total could nearly double if cancellable or planned contracts are included.
These commitments are due no matter the state of its business, Anthropic warns.
The bet involves the entire industry: Google and Amazon are at once Anthropic’s shareholders, its suppliers and its resellers.

If AI turns out to be less profitable than expected, the International Monetary Fund fears a “triple whammy” from these intertwined investments: falling stock prices, debts that are harder to repay, and promised revenue that never materializes.
The independent research firm New Constructs called the listing “an unprecedented test of investor gullibility.”
To pay these bills, Anthropic is counting on money from the stock market, which is not unlimited.
SpaceX, Elon Musk’s rocket and AI company, raised record sums there in June, while Google and Meta, which are pouring fortunes into data centres, are also seeking fresh capital.
OpenAI, whose chief Sam Altman called a listing “ill-advised” this year, has chosen to wait until 2027, giving it time to see how Wall Street treats its big rival. — AFP
996137738c87c0da: SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 16 — Founded five years ago by a breakaway group from OpenAI, Anthropic is now preparing a stock market listing that will be the biggest test yet of AI’s long-term financial viability.
Here are five things to know about the company behind the Claude chatbot.
OpenAI exiles
Anthropic’s leaders learned to build AI at OpenAI, the ChatGPT maker, where they became known for their work on safety.
Dario Amodei joined the then-nonprofit in 2016, where he ran its safety team and a team studying “scaling laws.” Scaling laws describe how AI models gain ability as they are trained on more data.
His younger sister Daniela joined OpenAI in 2018 and became vice president of safety and policy.
After disagreements with OpenAI leadership over how AI should be built, the Amodeis and several colleagues left in December 2020 and launched Anthropic four weeks later.
The bitter rivalry between the two San Francisco-based companies has continued since.
Siblings and housemates

Chief Executive Dario Amodei and Daniela, the company’s president, grew up in San Francisco’s Mission District. Their father was a leather craftsman and their mother managed public library renovations.

According to the New York Times, two other Anthropic cofounders were the Amodeis’ housemates in San Francisco before the OpenAI years: physicist Jared Kaplan, now chief science officer, and researcher Chris Olah, whom Dario Amodei had once tutored in math.
The remaining three cofounders also came from OpenAI. Sam McCandlish is Anthropic’s chief architect and was previously chief technology officer.
Tom Brown oversees the computing infrastructure. He was among OpenAI’s first 20 employees.
Jack Clark heads the company’s public benefit work and founded the Anthropic Institute, an internal think tank. He is a former technology journalist who joined OpenAI in 2016.
Rationalists and effective altruists
Dario Amodei’s thinking was shaped by two related movements.
The first is rationalism, associated with AI thinker Eliezer Yudkowsky, which holds that AI could become powerful enough to destroy society.
The second is effective altruism, which aims to make charitable giving as efficient as possible.
“Effective altruists” also supplied Anthropic’s early money. Facebook cofounder Dustin Moskovitz and Skype cofounder Jaan Tallinn backed the first funding round.

Sam Bankman-Fried invested US$500 million through his company FTX in non-voting shares. After FTX collapsed and Bankman-Fried was sent to jail, that stake was sold for US$884 million to repay the exchange’s customers.
Amodei said in 2023 that he did not consider himself an effective altruist, though he was sympathetic to some of its ideas.
Critics including Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang have called him a “doomer.”
Big Tech and big funds
Anthropic’s IPO filing shows that two of its largest backers are Amazon and Google’s parent company Alphabet.
Other participants include Founders Fund, the venture firm started by Peter Thiel, along with Microsoft and Nvidia.
In May, Anthropic raised US$65 billion at a US$965 billion valuation, which put it ahead of OpenAI for the first time.
Former Google chief executive Eric Schmidt is among the earliest outside investors. He put tens of millions of dollars into Anthropic’s first funding round in 2021.
Clash with the Pentagon
In January, the Pentagon, under President Donald Trump’s administration, asked for unrestricted use of Claude, the company’s chatbot.
Anthropic refused to allow two uses: domestic mass surveillance and lethal autonomous weapons.

In February, a furious Trump ordered federal agencies to stop using Anthropic’s technology. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth then directed that the company be labelled a supply-chain risk, a designation normally used for foreign adversaries.
In September the Defense Department posted on social media: “Americanism, not effective altruism.” — AFP
c6c9e05c3c0df856: MIAMI, Nov 16 — Landmarks in Miami are lighting up with its alter ego “Vice City” in the run-up to the much-anticipated launch of the latest installment of the Grand Theft Auto (GTA) video game.
Millions of fans have been waiting for more than a decade for GTA VI, and the city that inspired the series is awash with ads for it ahead of the November 19 release.

Miami-Dade County officials signed a US$3.9 million deal with GTA developer Rockstar Games to place advertisements in iconic locations like the stadium of the Miami Heat basketball franchise and the city’s airport.
The neon-pink inscription of Vice City can also be seen on storage containers on Miami Beach, on giant murals on downtown boulevards, boxing rings and even on coffee cups.
The campaign also evokes the 1983 movie “Scarface,” which was set in Miami.

Outside a Miami Beach location where a violent scene from the movie takes place, there’s a neon-pink classic car with the slogan, “Welcome to Vice City,” and a mannequin resembling the film’s protagonist, Tony Montana, where tourists and fans can pose for photos.
That’s feeding into feverish anticipation from local fans of the video game.
“I grew up in the city. I love Miami and it’s just crazy to see one of my favourite games be based on the place I grew up,” Yarixza Hernandez, a 21-year-old student at Miami Dade College, told AFP.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A ride-share car with a “Vice City” decal drives past a City of Miami police patrol in downtown Miami, Florida, ahead of the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI on November 10, 2026. — AFP pic
High expectations
The stakes are high for Rockstar Games. The last installment, GTA V, which was released in 2013, shifted 230 million copies, making it the second best-selling video game ever.

Although Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar Games’ parent company, has not released sales figures for this particular game, its CEO, Strauss Zelnick, said that pre-orders are reaching “unprecedented levels.”
Market research firm Sensor Tower estimates that pre-orders have already exceeded US$1 billion.
The excitement is palpable among fans.
“It’s like the game people have been waiting for,” said Aldo Gonzalez, a 19-year-old student at Miami Dade College, who competes in esports at the university.
“People have already called off work for like a week to play the game.”
‘Play nonstop’
Videos of people preparing for the launch are doing the rounds on social media.

One man cleans and takes his PlayStation 5 to the barber, and another dresses up as if going on a date. One even sings a verse from Phil Collins’ song “In the Air Tonight”: “I’ve been waiting for this moment all my life.”
Guido Rodriguez, 18, is in that category.
“I’ll probably play the game nonstop until I beat it, honestly, for a couple of days,” he said.
For local devotees, it’s an opportunity to explore a digital version of their city.
The beaches, skyscrapers, canals and neighbourhoods of Vice City are easily recognizable to any resident of South Florida.
College gamer Gonzalez said he plans to attend Vice City-themed parties and show his city to his friends – at least virtually.
Miami-Dade County’s support for the GTA promotion campaign wasn’t without controversy.
County Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz grumbled that the game is built around “criminal activities,” a charge that has been leveled at the series before.
But for gamers like Rodriguez, it’s a way to escape from reality.
“It’s like watching a movie or reading a book, right? It puts you in a different world that you can experience,” he said. — AFP
84377556b27b3648: The US Department of Energy (DoE) is deepening its relationship with HPC-first chip startup NextSilicon.

During Supercomputing 2026 in Chicago on Monday, the Israeli startup revealed that the agency had deployed its second Maverick-2 cluster in the Darwin testbed at Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL).

The deployment comes just six months after Sandia National Laboratories powered on NextSilicon’s first supercomputer, which features 64 nodes and 128 of the company's “runtime-configurable” accelerators.
NextSilicon’s latest DoE system is comparatively smaller, comprising just four accelerators, yet for LANL, the system is arguably more important despite its size.
Darwin, LANL’s chief scientist Galen Shipman, tells El Reg is a “long-lived testbed environment where we bring in newer technologies for evaluation.”
“It gives us the ability to work with the technology much more quickly, and integrate it with other components of our architecture in our environment,” he explained.

Smaller systems like the Maverick-2 cluster now deployed in Darwin allow LANL to validate and port a wider array of codebases to the chips, identify problems, and work with NextSilicon to not only address them, but directly influence the capabilities of future chips, Shipman explained.

In other words, Los Alamos’ interest in Maverick-2 is the first step toward larger scale deployments of NextSilicon silicon in future DoE supers. For this, hands-on access is kind of important as many of LANL’s most important workloads can’t exactly be run on public systems.
A compute chameleon

LANL is one of several labs tasked with ensuring that the US’ nuclear deterrent remains effective decades after underground testing was banned. The lab is also responsible for running simulations on energy sources like fuel candidates for future fusion reactors. Both of these workloads, Shipman tells us, fall into a category called multi-physics simulations.
These workloads aren’t really one workload, but multiple simulations that can have wildly different compute requirements.

A “good example is inertial confinement fusion. At the National Ignition Facility at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, you're using lasers to implode a fuel capsule, and the goal is to generate more energy through yield than you do from depositing energy to the capsule,” Shipman explained. “That's inherently multiphysics.”

There are simulations for the lasers, the hydrodynamics within the fuel capsule, and the chemistry and material interactions taking place during the fusion process. The problem, Shipman explains, is that a system that’s ideal for one of those simulations may not be well suited to others. “Identifying one specific platform that is optimal for that type of simulation is challenging.”

CPUs, he says, are well suited to workloads with large serial sections, irregular access patterns, and jobs that benefit from deep cache hierarchies. Meanwhile, GPUs are fantastic for dense, matrix-multiplication heavy workloads.

"Where NextSilicon fits in is being able to reconfigure to match the workload, on demand,” Shipman said. “The hope is that we won't have to make these rigid determinations upfront like, ‘we need this much CPU or we need this much GPU.’ We can use a much more adaptable, reconfigurable architecture to meet the workflow where it is at.”
A closer look at Maverick 2

Despite some visual similarities to Nvidia’s current crop of GPUs, Maverick-2 is not a GPU. Instead it employs a dataflow architecture which overlaps communication and computation. Rather than waiting for load-store operations to shuffle data around as you would with a conventional CPU or GPU, the chips themselves comprise a grid of arithmetic logic units (ALUs) which are configured to perform an operation like addition or multiplication in the order that they’re needed.
Data is computed as it moves from one ALU to the next, a bit like how a ball moves through a Rube Goldberg contraption.

This can make dataflow architectures extremely efficient in bandwidth-bound scenarios, which has implications not only for HPC and scientific computing but also for AI. It’s why we’re seeing dataflow accelerators, like Nvidia’s Groq, Cerebras’ WSE-3, and SambaNova’s SN50, being deployed as decode accelerators in AI inference clusters. Where NextSilicon stands out is that its designs, so far, have been specifically tailored toward sparse double-precision FP64 workloads.
Real FLOPS are rarely advertised

Programming dataflow architectures, historically, has been a challenging endeavor. To overcome this, NextSilicon claims to have developed a compiler that can decompose any existing C, Python, Fortran, or CUDA codebases into a graph that can run directly on its chips.

So far, NextSilicon has managed to validate its systems against the High Performance Conjugate Gradients (HPCG) benchmark, the LAMMPS molecular dynamics test suite, and the Sparta Monte Carlo simulation suite.

But as NextSilicon CEO Elad Raz notes, the roofline performance of Maverick-2 is different from one workload to another, and so the company has opted not to advertise peak theoretical performance the same way GPU vendors like Nvidia or AMD have traditionally done.

That’s not to say NextSilicon is shy about Maverick’s performance characteristics. Rather than advertising peak performance that the chip may not be able to hit in the workloads its customers actually care most about, it published performance figures across a swath of HPC benchmarks. For example, in HPCG, one of the closest watched HPC benchmarks after High Performance Linpack (HPL), NextSilicon says a single Maverick achieves 600 gigaFLOPS of performance, which it says is on par with contemporary GPUs but at half the power.
That’s just fine and dandy as far as Shipman is concerned. He tells us peak advertised performance is rarely a useful proxy for real-world performance.

“The thing that my team spends the most time on is how do we generate representative proxies, representative kernels; how do we generate specifications that communicate our needs to the broader ecosystem so that vendors like NextSilicon can meet us and co-design with us.” ®

11cf973c0d595b96: For years, enterprises have approached AI as a series of discrete experiments. Now, as AI agents begin to move into the workflows that run the business, that model is starting to look inadequate. Organizations moving from isolated pilots toward AI agents and autonomous workflows are confronting a deeper challenge: rethinking how data, business processes, governance, and people fit together, turning AI from a collection of tools into part of the enterprise operating model.

For Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, that shift begins with treating AI as an enterprise platform rather than a collection of disconnected projects. “AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation,” he says, arguing that companies need a connected, semantically rich layer that reflects their business before they can reliably deploy AI across processes. The stakes also change as AI moves into mission-critical workflows. For some everyday applications, “80% might be good enough,” he says, but in areas such as supply chains or financial close, that level of accuracy is “a very terrible result.”

That foundation also determines which AI applications are worth pursuing. Satinder Pal Singh, associate VP North America for SAP BAIP and SAP AI Strategy at Infosys, frames AI agents as “digital coworkers” and recommends evaluating potential use cases through three lenses: impact, feasibility, and scalability. Companies should identify where an agent can move meaningful business metrics, determine whether their data and talent can support the use case, and then establish whether successful applications can be replicated. “A pilot that can’t scale is just an experiment,” he says.

Scaling also brings governance into sharper focus. Clear policies, access controls, monitoring, and oversight are necessary to ensure agents remain trustworthy and aligned with business requirements. “The absence of governance doesn’t speed up AI adoption,” Singh says. “It creates a risk backlog” that can ultimately force a more disruptive stop and audit.

Those considerations will become more important as AI agents take on more responsibilities as digital coworkers. Both executives see a future in which agentic systems coordinate work across applications, while customer-specific knowledge graphs and governed data become critical enterprise assets. For Singh, the longer-term opportunity is a shift from AI as a productivity tool to “AI as a decision-making partner,” helping leaders understand what is happening, anticipate what comes next, and determine how to respond.

Full Transcript
Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace.
This episode is produced in partnership with Infosys.

Now, the development and democratization of AI tools has the potential to reconfigure how enterprises operate. But, at a time when applications are being scaled up from that initial phase of experimentation, we’re still seeing senior leaders grapple with questions around AI’s value, risk, and the complexity it adds. It’s becoming clear that, unlike past ways of automation, AI requires a real mindset shift. Put simply, the technology can’t simply be added into an enterprise’s existing toolkit. It requires a complete reconfiguration of what’s inside and how it’s used.
Two words for you: conscious configuration.
My guests today are Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, and Satinder Pal Singh, Associate VP for North America, SAP Business AI Platform and SAP AI Strategy.
Welcome, Thorsten and Satinder.
Thorsten Leiduck: Yeah, thank you for having us. Really a pleasure to be here with our valued partner, Infosys. Looking forward to the conversation.
Satinder Pal Singh: Hi, Megan. Thanks for inviting for the conversation today. Looking forward to the discussion.

Megan: Me too. Thank you both so much for being here. Thorsten, if I could start with you. We know that many senior leaders understand the transformative potential in AI, but they continue to struggle with aspects of its implementation. Many projects remain stuck at a pilot phase, for example. When you speak to clients, what are the biggest obstacles they face when it comes to integrating AI into their tech stack?

Thorsten: Yeah. Megan, as you mentioned, AI is on the agenda of every client conversation today, but many customers are really struggling how to convert that interest into an operationalized model and to unlock the value of AI across the enterprise. And the reason is that too many programs start as isolated POCs on different AI technologies and in an inconsistent fragmented data foundation.

This creates a lot of duplication, inconsistent performance, and no clear path to scale. At the same time, leaders are highly concerned about security, observability, reliability of agents, and some ethical implications when those get deployed. This is also shown in some studies. For example, BCG has launched a report, which shows that 74% of the organizations are stuck in pilot mode with no plan to scale. And in an Anthropic survey, data said that 42% are really struggling with getting access to the data and the quality to really, basically, scale the entire AI capabilities across the organization.

The path forward is really to treat AI not just as a project, but more holistically, as an enterprise platform, one that really consistently connects an unified data layer with the process context of the applications, and then embed AI capabilities governed across the entire life cycle. And to make this real, we in SAP launched the SAP autonomous enterprise framework, so organizations can move from pilots to scaled outcomes.

Megan: Yeah, really, to provide that support. And, Satinder, would you agree, why is it that we’re seeing enterprises get a touch of almost AI paralysis here? What’s the mindset shift that needs to happen and, perhaps, why is this something organizations need to be thinking about now, as well?

Satinder: Absolutely, Megan. And, if anything, the picture sharpens when you look at, specifically, at agentic AI. Infosys and HFS research surveyed over 500 global 2,000 enterprises and found only 14% have successfully scaled AI. Eighty-six percent remain in early exploration, proof of concept, or fragmented pilot phases. For a technology at the top of every boardroom agenda for two years, that’s a striking failure rate. And at the core of that 86% is what I would describe as AI as a department trap.

What happens is that an organization creates an AI team or a center of excellence and walls it off from business. That team builds technically excellent pilots the business doesn’t recognize itself in, and you end up with AI solutions searching for problems, rather than the other way around. Mindset shift is clear. Move from treating AI as a technology initiative to treating it as an operating model transformation. AI stops being something IT does for business and starts being something the whole organization does together. Every function, every workflow, embedded from the start.

And what makes this a now problem? Early movers are building an advantage. You cannot close by buying the same platform later. Eighteen months of agent behavior data, calibrated knowledge graph, workforce that has genuinely internalized AI, that is a structural advantage that compounds. Infosys Knowledge Institute AI Maturity Index shows that only 8% of the companies qualify as AI native today, yet they achieve four times the revenue contribution from the AI versus laggards. If you’re not building AI today, you’re not standing still, you’re falling behind at an accelerating rate.

Megan: Right. There’s a real polarization there, isn’t there, between the front-runners and the laggards, as you say. As we shift from pilot to scaled-up applications, perhaps the first step is evaluating when AI is the right tool. AI has quickly become the default solution within many enterprises. Is there a tendency to use it as a bit of a blunt instrument, nowadays, Thorsten? At the outset, how can senior leaders better evaluate what use cases are worthy of their time and investment, in order to strip out some of that later complexity?
Thorsten: Yeah, I think, Megan, what everybody needs to be aware is adopting and rolling out AI across an organization is as much a change management journey as it’s a technology rollout.

Now, when you have this in mind, it makes absolutely sense to put AI in front as many teams as possible, because you want to build formality, and spark ideas, and also people should see the benefit of AI in an organization. When you think about travel assistance, meeting summaries via Copilot, or AI-enabled workflows, increase the productivity, everybody feels this in their real job, in their real daily business. And, obviously, this creates creativity and also provides the organization from a bottom-up perspective with some innovation scale.

Now, however, as majority grows, the conversation, and this is also what we discuss with many of the leaders, and our clients, shifts more to economics and governance. Things like token costs, model performance, security, and accountability become much more relevant. And when you then take the approach and think about AI agents as digital workers that execute specific tasks within a business process, then this means, from an AI perspective, not every task justifies nation.

In some cases, human effort remains more economical or effective. The smart approach, and that’s what we really recommend to our clients, is to start with a defined, maybe small set of high-value use cases with defined success metrics upfront. So, for example, such as cycle time reduction, accuracy gains, or cost of per transaction, or top line improvement, and then scale what works. Those use cases can be tied to a line of business domains or industry scenarios.

And then, what we are doing from an SAP perspective, together with Infosys, we really help customers to be successful. And then, last but not least, in many scenarios, I think, which has been very common pattern in particular around large industry AI use cases, is a joint approach, and we do this with partners like Infosys, but also customers around forward deployed engineering, so that you really define very closely the AI-specific use case with the defined outcomes together with the customer, and deliver this as the initial projects. And then, ideally, scale this to other customers and take it back like a best practice, which can be rolled out to other organizations, as well.

Megan: Right. It’s been really clear, isn’t it, on what you’re looking to achieve and what’s worth your time, as I say. And what would your advice, Satinder, be here, on refining an AI strategy to ensure organizations can focus on those areas, where AI can deliver the highest returns?

Satinder: Sure, Megan. I think Thorsten’s framing of AI agents as digital coworkers forces a precision that agentic AI strategy language often lacks. When you ask which digital coworkers do we need and where do they deliver the most value, the answer starts to become clearer right from the first step. At Infosys, through our Topaz AI-first framework, we push clients through the three lenses simultaneously.

The first one is impact. Where does deploying an agent move the numbers that matter? Revenue, cost, working capital risk. We have built a library of over 300 enterprise use cases across industries, so we never begin from a blank page. The second is feasibility. Given your data foundation platform and talent today, which high-impact use cases can you actually execute? Feasibility determines your sequence. The high-impact use case on a broken data foundation is not viable. When the foundation is right, the results are dramatic. One Infosys engagement cut complex SAP-specification documents from 86 person hours to 6, a 92% reduction.

Third is scalability. Once you have proven a use case with clear ROI metrics, cycle time reduction, accuracy gains, cost per transaction, what’s the architecture that lets you replicate it? A pilot that can’t scale is just an experiment. My practical advice: treat your AI portfolio like an investment portfolio, quick wins that fund the program, medium-term bets, one or two bold, long-term positions that balance keep stakeholders engaged at every stage and not just in year three.

Megan: That’s such a useful framework for people to use there. And given the urgency here, Thorsten, how can organizations approach and manage AI in a more structured, efficient way? To start with, what are the fundamentals that some organizations perhaps miss at the moment? I know Infosys and SAP talk about platform and data, then AI, for example.

Thorsten: Yeah, Megan, I think the fundamental, which many organizations are overlooking, is data and the data is a foundation for AI. Because, at the end, without the data structures and the ability to access the right information at the right time and basically bringing different kind of structured, unstructured data sources together, in a meaningful governed and semantic way, there will be no successful AI. AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation. And I think this is often overlooked, and that’s why I said when you start POCs in different organization, or different parts of the organization with different technologies, it’s very hard to establish an end-to-end consistent model on the data side, as well as on the AI side.

One of the key goals companies need to achieve is, and that’s why we really talk about you need to start with data first and the platform first, is to establish and semantically-rich connected data layer that really reflects your business, so that the agents are really grounded in the company’s reality and not just in generic patterns.

And then, I think, the second element that’s important is accuracy. In the enterprise context, it really matters. For example, what might pass in a consumer setting, where you have 80% accuracy, and even in a workforce environment where you build PowerPoints or you do email drafts, which you then, with a human in the loop, optimize, 80% might be good enough. But, when you really think about mission-critical or business-critical processes in the supply chain, or closing the books, 80% is a very terrible result.

The stakes are much too high and you need to have much more accuracy. And that’s why it’s important that you have business process logic and industry context embedded into the data and the models which build the foundation, if you will, the backbone for every AI and, obviously, for the data in the ERP and the line of business system.

And then, last but not least, the other critical element, and you see this obviously in the news with all the agents going rogue, are governance, compliance, and security. Very critical in an enterprise context. You need to set clear policies, access controls. You need to have monitoring ability, capabilities, to really make sure that what then the AI agenda capabilities or agents are executing is fully aligned, is trustworthy, and scalable.

Megan: Right. Which is quite a lot of things for organizations to be thinking about. Satinder, how do SAP and Infosys work with organizations to streamline some of these processes, perhaps and make unlocking AI’s capability a little bit easier?

SAP brings the platform foundation, business data cloud for the semantically-rich enterprise, generative AI hub for governed LLMXs, and agent hub for the lifecycle governance, enterprise grade from day one. Infosys brings implementation depth, industry context, and use case accelerators. Through Infosys Topaz, we have built over 50 pre-configured AI use cases on Business AI Platform, production-ready configurations deployable without building from scratch. In another account, an AI-powered platform auto-classifies over 120,000 SAP incidents monthly, with zero analyst charge. The combined effect time to value drops from 12 to 18 months, down to four to six months.

What I would emphasize is change management damage. Technology is increasingly deployable, and Thorsten also spoke about it earlier. What’s hard is helping an organization internalize that their agents are digital coworkers, not automations. That mindset shift is 70% of the implementation challenge that platform cannot solve alone, and Infosys and SAP run joint adoption programs addressing both the dimensions in parallel.

Megan: Fantastic. Some great real-world examples there, as well. Thorsten, can you tell us a little bit more about SAP’s Business AI Platform, or BAIP, in particular? How does that work and what sets it apart from other platforms?

Thorsten: Yeah, so SAP Business AI Platform, if you will, is the foundation for our SAP autonomous enterprise framework, which really consists of a unified user interface and is enabled as an agentic orchestration layer, which we call Joule. And you have the autonomous read with all the applications, and then you have the Business AI Platform, which powers the other capabilities, and is closely connected, and is basically organized around three core pillars.

The first one is, really, what we call build. What it means is you provide the respective intent-based development tools, so that customer, or partners like Infosys, can really create and development agents, applications and workflows using best-in-class tools and model to extend SAP’s own assistant, or customizing those, or really building own agents as needed.

Complimenting what Satinder said, it’s really critical for us that we have a thriving ecosystem, who is innovative, and is building innovations, and is complementing our own SAP agentic portfolio. We are focusing on specific areas on the domains, from a line of business industry perspective, where we deliver assistance as part of our organization, but to really then customize them from a last mile execution from really complimenting areas which we don’t cover and really driving the innovation towards the customer, our ecosystem is the multiplier force and Infosys is really playing a leading role here with us, together.

Second is, and we talked about this, is what we call the contextualize and reason pillar, which is literally as a foundation data, we address with SAP Data Cloud and comprehensive data strategy, where we establish an end-to-end data fabric across partner provider platforms, like Databricks, Snowflakes, where we promote and zero copy access to data. 6524a9e79f97deb6: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 16 — Rainfall exceeding 100 millimetres within just over two hours could trigger flash floods in Kampung Melayu Subang and surrounding areas if rivers and local drainage systems are unable to cope with the volume of water.
Selangor Fire and Rescue Department (JBPM) assistant director (Operations) Ashrul Riezal Ashbar said the two main rivers contributing to overflow in the area were Sungai Damansara and Sungai Buluh.

“In areas currently at risk of flooding, the overflowing water comes from Sungai Damansara and Sungai Buluh. In Kampung Melayu Subang, flooding is also influenced by overflow from the local drainage system,” he told Bernama today.

He said the overflow could also affect several other areas, including Shah Alam, Puncak Alam, Paya Jaras and Kampung Kubu Gajah, before flowing towards Kampung Parit Mahang, Ijok, Cerakah and Kampung Bukit Kuching, eventually reaching Kuala Selangor.
In preparation for the Northeast Monsoon (MTL), Selangor JBPM has identified 56 flood hotspots and 232 flood-prone areas statewide.

Klang has the highest number of flood hotspots, with 13, followed by Petaling (11), Gombak (10), Hulu Langat (nine), Kuala Selangor (six), Sepang (three), and Kuala Langat and Hulu Selangor with two each. No flood hotspots have been recorded in Sabak Bernam.

3d53c50388e76f74: SpaceX caught its Starship upper stage returning from orbit on its first attempt, but the Super Heavy booster ended its flight in an explosion after recovery was aborted.
The catch was a remarkable achievement: Starship returned to the same launch tower it had left almost a day earlier, settling into its giant mechanical arms.

Flight 15 began well, with the 33 Raptor engines of the Super Heavy booster launching the stack from Pad 2 at Starbase, Texas. Hot staging followed, and the booster performed its directional flip maneuver.

Thirty-two Raptor engines relit for the boostback burn, intended to return Super Heavy to the tower for another catch. The booster had managed the maneuver on flight tests 5, 7, and 8, but this time something went wrong. "The boostback burn ended early due to low fuel mass," SpaceX said.

The booster automatically aborted its return to the tower and diverted offshore. It completed a landing burn, briefly hovering above the Gulf before its engines shut down and the flight termination system delivered an explosive finale.
Starship reached orbit under the power of its six Raptor engines and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites. Unlike the previous flight's brief orbital stint, this mission lasted almost a day.
Following a deorbit burn, Starship returned to the launch site 22 and a half hours after it left.

Many more development flights remain before SpaceX can deliver its promised fully reusable launch system. NASA's Space Shuttle came close, but the large external tank was expended with every launch, and the orbiters never matched the cadence SpaceX reckons it can achieve with Starship.
SpaceX boss Elon Musk admitted that "many small fixes are needed to achieve immediate reusability (like an airplane)."

Cadence will be key if Starship is going to meet NASA's needs for the Artemis missions. Somewhere between 6 and 22 launches (depending on who you ask) will be required for a lunar mission, and SpaceX has yet to demonstrate in-space propellant transfer between vehicles.
Next year's Artemis III mission also calls for docking tests between NASA's Orion spacecraft and a test version of SpaceX's Starship Human Landing System (HLS) in low Earth orbit.
The booster fumble shouldn't obscure what the engineering teams achieved. Now comes the small matter of doing it again – preferably with both stages intact. ®

0a527adf041c22f5: PETALING JAYA, Nov 16 — A dentist was fined RM70,000 by the Sessions Court here today after being found guilty of two charges of employing an individual who was not registered as a dental practitioner and allowing the person to perform dental procedures at her clinic two years ago.
Judge Noor Ruzilawati Mohd Noor imposed a fine of RM30,000 for the first charge and RM40,000 for the second, with six and seven months’ imprisonment respectively in default of payment.

Dr Tong Soo Huan, 38, was charged with employing an individual who was not registered as a dental practitioner under the Dental Act 2018 at a dental clinic in Jalan SS21/1 here at 12.50 pm on May 6, 2024.
The charge was brought under Section 68 of the Dental Act 2018, which provides for a maximum fine of RM300,000 or imprisonment for up to six years, or both.

She was also charged with allowing an individual who was not registered under the Act to practise dentistry at her clinic on the same date and time, under Section 69(a) of the same Act, which carries the same maximum penalty.

According to the facts of the case, on May 6, 2024, a team of enforcement officers from the Selangor State Health Department conducted an inspection at Dr Tong’s clinic and found a female staff member scanning a patient’s teeth using an iTero Element intraoral scanner.

The inspection found that the staff member was not registered with the Malaysian Dental Council (MDC) as a dental practitioner, while Dr Tong, who was a registered dental practitioner, failed to produce the staff member’s annual practising certificate when requested by the enforcement officers.

Earlier, Health Ministry (MOH) prosecuting officer Dr Haznita Zainal Abidin urged the court to impose substantial fines for both charges in the interest of public safety and patient protection, noting that the offences were of a strict liability nature and involved the integrity of the dental profession.

“The accused not only failed to ensure that a registered dental practitioner was on duty throughout the clinic’s operating hours, but also deliberately instructed and allowed a clinic staff member whose only qualification was the Sijil Pelajaran Malaysia (SPM) to perform dental procedures, namely intraoral scanning using specialised medical device equipment at the accused’s premises.

“An oral scanning procedure using an intraoral scanner (iTero Element) requires a high level of expertise to operate. Based on testimony from the Medical Device Authority, the device can only be operated by qualified medical or dental practitioners,” she said.

Dr Haznita said the sentence should send a strong message and serve as a stern lesson to the accused and the entire dental practitioner community in Malaysia not to take shortcuts to cut costs or disregard the law by delegating clinical duties to staff without professional qualifications.
However, lawyer Rejinder Singh, representing Dr Tong, appealed for a lighter fine, arguing that his client was a first-time offender and had no previous record of offences under the Dental Act 2018.
“The offence committed was a technical violation and did not involve any criminal element, as a patient had come to the clinic for treatment while Dr Tong was out for lunch at the time.

“The accused is aware of her actions and regrets not exercising greater vigilance in supervising the clinic staff. She has pledged to ensure stricter control measures in the future,” the lawyer said. — Bernama

90c0af906a2ad146: TASEK GELUGOR, Nov 16 — The Penang branch of the Domestic Trade and Cost of Living Ministry (KPDN) seized 27,000 bottles of hair dye products worth RM1.08 million suspected of misusing the Malaysian halal logo without a valid Malaysian Halal Certification (SPHM) in a raid on a warehouse in Kampung Selamat here today.

Penang KPDN director S. Jegan said the seizure was made during an inspection conducted at about 1pm following complaints and three weeks of intelligence gathering by the ministry's enforcement officers.

"In the raid, we seized 27,000 bottles of hair dye products stored in the warehouse and detained two company employees, a local woman and a Chinese national man, both in their 30s, to assist in investigations.

"Preliminary investigations found that the products were suspected of displaying the Malaysian halal logo although the company failed to produce valid halal certification documents to substantiate the use of the logo,” he told a media conference at the warehouse here today.

He said investigations also revealed that the hair dye products were imported from China and stored at a warehouse rented by the company before being marketed online through social media and e-commerce platforms such as TikTok, Shopee and Lazada.
Jegan said the company was believed to have been operating for the past six months, with an estimated 600,000 units of the products sold during that period, each bottle of hair dye retailing at RM40.

He said the company's modus operandi included displaying suspected fake halal certificates in advertisements on social media and e-commerce platforms, as well as engaging popular social media influencers and affiliate agents to convince consumers of the products' halal status.

"Our inspection also found that the halal certificate displayed in their promotional materials actually belonged to another company and not the company marketing the products. The Malaysian halal logo was also displayed on the product packaging despite the company not having a valid SPHM for the products,” he said.

He said the matter was particularly concerning as the hair dye was a personal care product used by various segments of society, including senior citizens, and misuse of the halal logo could mislead consumers and undermine confidence in the integrity of the country's halal certification system.
He said further investigations were underway, including efforts to trace the company owner, and the case was being investigated under Section 16 of the Trade Descriptions Act 2011 (Act 730).

He advised consumers to verify the halal status of products through the official website of the Department of Islamic Development Malaysia (JAKIM), particularly before making purchases, and not to rely entirely on sellers' claims or affiliate promotions. — Bernama

c603bb9c607c7dc2: Datacenters made up nearly three times as large a share of UK planning applications in the year to September 2026 as they did three years earlier, with councils receiving 59 submissions.
The figures come from planning data site Plota, whose Q3 2026 Planning Index draws on applications from every council across the UK.

Plota has logged 416 datacenter applications since 2016, though these include extensions and alterations, not just new bit barns. Estimates put Britain's existing fleet at between 477 and 602 facilities.

The peak for volume came in the 12 months to March 2021, when 63 campus applications were filed. However, overall planning applications were also higher then, so datacenters accounted for just 1.1 in every 10,000 filed. In the current period they equate to 1.4 in every 10,000.
The figures show that applications for building new server halls are about as high as they have been over the past decade, and close to their recent peak as a share of all applications.
Even so, the application numbers don't show the dramatic jump that the steady stream of bit barn announcements might suggest. Nor do they tell us how many facilities are actually being built.

Applications did bounce around the middle of 2024, when the current government - and its fetish for all things AI - was elected. But it didn't publish the AI Opportunities Action Plan, which recommended "AI Growth Zones" with streamlined planning to speed up datacenter builds, until the start of 2025.

Plota links the rise to datacenters being recognized as critical national infrastructure (CNI) in September 2024, and a December 2024 update to the planning framework that told councils to identify suitable sites for them.

The facilities are getting larger. One site being built for Equinix near London's M25 motorway will feature three data halls with more than 250 MW capacity, while another planned for Havering in East London could go up to 600 MW. Both were billed as being among Europe's largest campuses.

According to Plota, just 3.3 percent of datacenter applications decided between 2016 and 2024 were refused, against 11.3 percent across all applications. The government has also overturned some local council refusals, controversially, as at a site near Abbots Langley in Hertfordshire last year.
Slough leads Plota's tally of applications since 2016 with 28, followed by Tower Hamlets in East London with 16, Leeds with 12, and West Northamptonshire with 11.

Developers in England can also ask ministers to bring qualifying datacenter projects into the nationally significant infrastructure planning regime, shifting the consent decision from the council to central government. Projects taking that route fall outside Plota's council-based figures.

A recent report found UK ministers met with representatives from 137 different businesses between July 2024 and June 2026 to discuss datacenters, while there were no meetings with environmental or community groups about them. ®

ba680f82382990bd: Elon Musk and a bunch of Silicon Valley heavyweights want Jensen Huang back at Nvidia, and they've decided an online petition is the way to make it happen.

An open letter addressed to Nvidia's board had attracted more than 173,000 signatures at the time of writing, just four days after Huang's departure following revelations about his personal relationships, including an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China.

The campaign, launched under the banner "Stand with Jensen," calls on Nvidia to reinstate its co-founder and former CEO while an independent investigation establishes the facts, give him a chance to respond to the allegations, and publicly explain why he was forced out.

"For thirty-three years, Jensen poured his heart and soul into building Nvidia," the letter reads. "He bet it on ideas that most of the industry dismissed, carried it through years when the bets looked foolish, and stayed long enough to see them change how the world computes.

"Many of us joined because of him. Many of us stayed because of how he treated the work: as something worth getting right, together, at whatever hour it took. This company is the work of his life. That deserves more than gratitude after the fact. It deserves fairness now."

Among the supporters are Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Y Combinator boss Garry Tan, and Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick. More than 8,000 signatories also identify themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to roughly a fifth of its workforce.

However, how many of those signatures are genuine is anyone's guess. The site doesn't verify names or employers, so there's nothing stopping someone from signing as Musk, Huang, or Nvidia's entire board if they fancy it.

The campaign follows Huang's resignation on November 12, ending his 33-year reign at the GPU giant he co-founded in 1993. His departure came after reports of an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who US intelligence suspects of spying for Beijing, and a separate alleged relationship with an Nvidia employee.

Nvidia CFO Colette Kress has been handed the unenviable job of running the company while its board searches for a permanent replacement. Huang's departure has left the chipmaker facing something of an identity crisis, with rivals undoubtedly watching the chaos with interest.

Huang himself may not be ready to hang up his leather jacket. According to the Financial Times, the former CEO has discussed a possible comeback with associates, while an ally is reportedly assembling a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return.
The effort could even involve seeking support from the White House, although Washington appears rather less enthusiastic about the prospect.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that Nvidia needs a "dramatic shake-up" and should look outside the company for its next chief executive. He also wants answers about whether Nvidia knowingly allowed advanced AI chips to reach China in breach of US export restrictions.

None of that seems to have put off Huang's supporters. "He has erred, yes – to err is to be human – but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company," Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick said.
Nvidia reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday, giving investors their first major opportunity to grill management about the leadership crisis.
Whether the board will be swayed by a petition full of unverified names is another matter. Running one of the world's most valuable companies is, after all, not supposed to be a popularity contest. ®

9f3294f3d4e429be: BANGKOK, Nov 16 — A Thai court denied an attempt on Monday by former leader Thaksin Shinawatra to pause the seizure of his assets over a disputed tax bill of more than US$500 million (RM2 billion).
The Supreme Court ordered the ex-prime minister – one of Thailand’s richest people – last November to pay back taxes over the 2006 sale of shares in his telecoms firm.

Thaksin then sought a temporary injunction against the Revenue Department to stop it from seizing his assets to pay the bill, which the tax court said was around THB17.5 billion (around US$515 million).
The request was dismissed, according to a court statement on Monday. A mediation between Thaksin and the Revenue Department before the tax court is set for December.
Thaksin, 77, argued in court last month that he had already settled the bill for the tax-free sale of Shin Corp to Singapore’s Temasek Holdings.
The 2006 deal, which netted the Shinawatra family a US$1.9 billion windfall, sparked protests and became a lightning rod for opposition to Thaksin’s government.
He was ousted in a coup later that year and went into exile for more than a decade, during which time he was convicted of corruption.
Thaksin was arrested when he returned in 2023 but sent to hospital and then freed. He finally saw the inside of a jail last year, serving eight months before his release in May.
The Shinawatra clan has for two decades been a key foe of Thailand’s pro-military, pro-royalty elite, who view their populist brand of politics as a threat to the traditional social order.
However, the political dynasty has faced a series of setbacks, including the court-ordered removal of Thaksin’s daughter, Paetongtarn, as prime minister in August 2025 over an ethics breach.
Their Pheu Thai party also had its worst election result in February, slipping to third place, but was still included in the ruling coalition of conservative Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul. — AFP

abb0e23108d956a4: HOLLYWOOD, Nov 16 — Hollywood royalty Glenn Close and Ridley Scott both received an honorary Oscar on Sunday, the first golden statues of their decades-long careers, at a lavish gala bringing together industry elites.
Screen legend Close, 79, has been tipped for Academy Awards eight times during her five-decade career, including for her roles in “Fatal Attraction” and “Dangerous Liaisons.”
British director Ridley Scott, 88, known for box-office hits including “Alien,” “Blade Runner” and “Gladiator,” is a nine-time nominee but had also never won the award.
The honorary Oscars, awarded annually by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, celebrate cinema legends for their careers and contributions to the film industry.
US actor John Malkovich, who is tipped for Oscars glory for his role in dark comedy “Wild Horse Nine,” introduced Close as “a friend and a treasured colleague.”
“She is a true master,” said Malkovich, who starred alongside Close as the arch seducer in “Dangerous Liaisons.”
“Glenn is unafraid to go there, and I love that about her.”
Close, who dedicated the award to her daughter, earned a standing ovation.

“As an outsider, I have never worried about whether I was going to win or not, though some years I thought I might have a chance,” said the actress, who earned her first nomination for 1983 hit “The World According to Garp.”
“I have always felt that the great honour is to be in the room,” she added.
Three-time Best Director nominee Scott received his gong from Matt Damon, who paid tribute to the master of the modern screen epic.
“It is about time we all saw him with an Academy Award in his hand,” said Damon, who worked with Scott on 2015 box office smash “The Martian.”
The director did not attend the event at the Ray Dolby Ballroom in the heart of Hollywood, but expressed his gratitude in a pre-recorded video.
Director Christopher Nolan and actors including Tom Holland, Charlize Theron, Olivia Wilde and Penelope Cruz were among dozens of star attendees.
The 17th edition of the awards, which precedes the Golden Globes in January and the Oscars in March, also paid tribute to legendary animator Floyd Norman.
Norman, who began his career in 1956 at Walt Disney Animation Studio, becoming the studio’s first Black animator, contributed to dozens of films including “Mary Poppins” and “The Jungle Book.”
“On occasion, even movies have a happy ending,” the 91-year-old said.
“This special evening, here’s my happy ending.” — AFP
3411c497853951d7: From Ahmad Zaharuddin Sani Ahmad Sabri
There is something more dangerous in politics than losing an election: winning one without understanding why.
The Melaka state election should be a wake-up call for both Pakatan Harapan (PH) and the Barisan Nasional-Perikatan Nasional (BN-PN) alliance.
BN-PN may celebrate its overwhelming victory, while PH may console itself with retaining a loyal support base. But beneath the celebrations and disappointments lies an uncomfortable reality.

PH has yet to demonstrate that it can significantly expand its appeal among Malay voters. BN-PN, meanwhile, has yet to prove that Malay political consolidation can translate into broader national acceptance.
Let the numbers speak.
In 2021, PH secured 114,457 votes, representing nearly 35.8% of the popular vote. In 2026, its tally increased to 143,273, but its vote share declined to 29.3%.
PH gained almost 29,000 votes, yet lost 6.5 percentage points of electoral support.
That is not an insignificant distinction.
PH is not necessarily losing its existing voters. It is losing the race to win over new ones.
More embarrassingly, all four seats won by PH went to DAP. PKR and Amanah failed to secure even a single constituency.

This raises an uncomfortable question: how can a coalition led by a Malay prime minister, supported by Malay ministers and commanding federal power, struggle so badly to translate that leadership into electoral success in Malay-majority constituencies?
PKR must ask whether its reformist identity still inspires confidence beyond its traditional supporters.
Amanah must explain why its supposedly progressive Islamic alternative has struggled to establish meaningful electoral traction.
A political party cannot survive indefinitely by reminding voters of what it once fought for. Eventually, voters want to know what it has delivered.
Reformasi cannot remain a historical slogan. It must become a measurable improvement in people's lives.
DAP should not celebrate too comfortably either.
Preliminary turnout estimates suggest that nearly 78% of Malay voters participated, compared with 59% of Chinese voters and 58% of Indian voters.
Although Chinese support for PH among those who voted appears relatively resilient, the weaker participation should worry DAP.
Chinese voters are not PH's permanent electoral fixed deposit.
They have expectations concerning education, economic opportunities, institutional reform and fair governance.
Fear of PAS may motivate some voters. But fear is not a substitute for trust, and disappointment can be expressed through silence at the ballot box.
Now consider BN-PN.
In 2021, BN and PN collectively received 200,472 votes while contesting separately. In 2026, their combined tally reached 308,668.
That represents an impressive 54% increase in absolute votes.
However, their combined popular vote share moved only marginally, from nearly 62.7% to 63.1%.
The alliance achieved a landslide in seats without achieving a comparable breakthrough in its combined share of the electorate.
This is not to diminish its victory. It is to distinguish electoral consolidation from a genuine expansion of political appeal.
And here lies BN-PN's greatest contradiction.

If its political identity increasingly revolves around Malay nationalism and religious conservatism, how does it intend to persuade Chinese, Indian, Sabah and Sarawak voters that their interests will be equally protected?
MCA and MIC may have won constituencies, but isolated victories do not automatically demonstrate a nationwide recovery of non-Malay confidence.
If Umno's ambition is merely to become more Malay than PAS, what exactly is MCA's future role? A political partner or a decorative guest at victory celebrations?
Defending Malay interests should never require making other communities feel politically expendable.
Malaysia's future cannot be secured by making one community believe that another community's progress represents its own defeat.
So what should PH do?
First, abandon the assumption that government performance automatically produces electoral loyalty.
I would propose an independent, constituency-level voter confidence audit, particularly among rural Malays, younger voters and the lower-middle-income population.
Ask those who rejected PH one simple question: what would convince you to reconsider?
Then publish measurable commitments on wages, housing, employment and living costs, with progress assessed every six months.

Second, PH must rebuild its political language. Ordinary Malaysians do not wake up thinking about coalition arithmetic. They wake up worrying about groceries, school expenses, wages and their children's future.
Third, stop treating criticism as hostility. Sometimes the harshest critics are identifying problems that loyal supporters refuse to acknowledge.
BN-PN should undertake an equally uncomfortable exercise: test its policies and political messaging among voters who do not share its ethnic or religious identity.

If the alliance cannot convince a substantial number of non-Malays that they have a secure future under its leadership, it risks becoming a powerful regional force with a national credibility problem.
The elections in Johor, Negeri Sembilan and Melaka offer valuable lessons, but they are not a reliable national forecast.
Umno should remember what happened after its victories in Melaka in 2021 and Johor in 2022.
Confidence turned into pressure for an early general election. Yet GE15 delivered BN its worst parliamentary performance up to that point.
Winning several states does not mean the keys to Putrajaya are already in your pocket.
Malaysia's electoral landscape is shaped by different demographics, local personalities, regional identities and economic expectations.
There is another reality politicians rarely admit openly: patronage, financial assistance and personal obligations remain influential in electoral politics.
Malaysians understand the saying, "orang berbudi kita berbahasa" ... kindness deserves appreciation.
But gratitude should never become political indebtedness.
A RM100 handout may ease household expenses today. A poor government can impose economic costs on an entire generation.

Ultimately, PH must learn to attract new voters rather than merely retain old supporters. BN-PN must learn to build confidence across communities rather than simply consolidate Malay political strength.
Neither side can claim to have solved Malaysia's political future.
An election determines who governs for five years. But the consequences of choosing the wrong leaders may be inherited for five generations.
Perhaps that is the greatest tragedy of Malaysian politics — our politicians are obsessed with counting the seats needed to capture power.
The people should be counting the price their children may eventually pay for it.
Ahmad Zaharuddin Sani Ahmad Sabri is an analyst with Global Asia Consulting.

71bfc93bc2f23df1: FRANKFURT: The European Central Bank warned Monday of growing risks from an "abrupt repricing" in markets and big losses if investor sentiment about artificial intelligence sours.
The comments from the ECB's vice president Boris Vujcic add to mounting concerns about the sector as investors increasingly question whether massive AI spending will pay off.

Jitters and market swings have been fuelled by the scandal that toppled Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang last week, and the Democratic wins in the US midterm elections that could spark greater oversight of AI technologies.
Vujcic said the "rapid expansion of AI is creating new challenges for financial stability" in the 21-nation eurozone.
"A reassessment of the AI narrative may trigger an abrupt repricing in markets and significant valuation losses," he warned in a speech in Frankfurt.
Initial public offering volumes relative to US GDP are on track to exceed the levels seen at the height of the dot-com boom of the late 1990s, Vujcic noted.
Shares in the AI titan Anthropic are expected to start trading on Wall Street on Thursday, in what could be the second-largest IPO in history.
"Historically, such surges have often coincided with market peaks, pointing to the risk of excessive investor optimism," Vujcic said.
Market falls after the Democratic sweep of Congress in the US midterms, which stoked regulatory concerns, "serve as a reminder to remain cautious about AI valuations," he said.
An AI-linked market crash represents a major risk for the eurozone because investment funds in the region had become more exposed to the sector, he added.
022548738f84fd7f: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 16 — The Housing and Local Government Ministry (KPKT) has allocated RM3.362 million to strengthen stray dog management nationwide through financial assistance to local authorities, awareness campaigns and the construction of adoption centres.

Deputy Housing and Local Government Minister Datuk Aiman Athirah Sabu said the allocation included a one-off grant of RM902,471 for local authorities to purchase euthanasia medication and equipment to capture stray dogs.
She said the allocation comprised RM58,841 for 28 local authorities in 2021, RM65,630 for 29 in 2022, RM140,000 for 31 in 2025 and RM638,000 for 71 local authorities in 2026.

"…we have also allocated funds for the Stray Animal Management Campaign, which was launched in 2024. A total of RM180,000 was allocated that year, followed by RM130,000 in 2025 and RM150,000 this year, bringing the total to RM460,000,” she said during a Special Chamber session in the Dewan Rakyat today.

Her response followed a question from Syahredzan Johan (PH-Bangi) on efforts to improve the sustainable management of stray dogs nationwide and the ministry's provision of financial assistance to local authorities for stray animal control.

KPKT had also provided RM2 million this year for two adoption centres overseen by Johor Bahru City Council and Sandakan Municipal Council, through its Local Government Department (JKT), Aiman Athirah said.
On the approach to managing stray dogs, she said the ministry followed a four-pronged policy known as trap, reclaim, rehome and dispose.

"Since September, the ministry has directed all local authorities to step up enforcement efforts, including conducting checks on dog ownership and licensing in residential areas to ensure owners comply with the dog licensing by-laws in force in their respective jurisdictions,” she said.
She said local authorities nationwide received 45,804 complaints about stray dog disturbances last year, and 24,195 operations resulted in 80,412 stray dogs being caught.

"Of these, some were handed over to the Department of Veterinary Services, while others were reclaimed by their owners or adopted through dog adoption programmes. These figures reflect KPKT's and local authorities' continued commitment to controlling and managing stray dogs,” she said.

She said the ministry acknowledged the proposal to introduce a more comprehensive national framework for managing stray animals, but any move to strengthen existing mechanisms would be undertaken in phases involving multiple agencies.

She added that KPKT welcomed suggestions from non-governmental organisations on improving stray animal management nationwide, particularly through adoption programmes, shelter facilities and public education.

“We recognise the frustration, distress and disappointment experienced by affected customers, particularly those who have purchased tickets in good faith and subsequently encountered difficulties gaining entry or accessing their allocated seats.
“The security of our ticketing platform, the integrity of ticket transactions and the protection of our customers remain our highest priorities,” GoLive said in the statement.

Explaining the mechanics behind the gate rejections, the ticketing firm revealed that primary buyers who resold their passes subsequently attempted to gain entry using duplicate copies of the same tickets.
“The original purchasers also attempted to attend the events using the same tickets.
“As each QR code allows only one successful scan, the first person to present the ticket was granted entry, while subsequent scans were rejected,” they said.
Investigators also discovered instances where scalpers doctored digital tickets, superimposing premium seating tiers or fabricated section numbers over lower-category passes with valid barcodes.

While the authentic barcode granted general access through the turnstiles, the manipulated visual details resulted in secondary buyers attempting to occupy seats already allocated to legitimate patrons. The operator cautioned that a scannable QR code alone provides no guarantee of a ticket’s authenticity or assigned seat legitimacy.
Urging music fans to purchase passes exclusively through its official portal, GoLive warned against sourcing tickets from social media accounts, peer-to-peer groups, or online marketplace platforms.
The company strongly advised ticket holders against sharing account credentials, posting unobscured ticket screenshots online, or clicking suspicious links that could compromise personal devices.
GoLive said that it is working alongside event organisers and venue security teams to resolve ticketing disputes while cooperating with law enforcement where criminal fraud is established.

The controversy underscores the persistent challenge of predatory scalping confronting Malaysia as it cements its reputation as a premier regional concert hub. Similar friction surfaced during ticketing for BTS WORLD TOUR ‘ARIRANG’ in Kuala Lumpur, where speculative listings flooded secondary platforms at heavily inflated valuations even before official presales commenced.
