2b12e0e01ef46ecb: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov xx — My Chemical Romance (MCR), one of the most influential rock bands of the 21st century, are back on tour with Malaysia among their stops.
MCR are set to bring The Black Parade 2026 tour to the TM National Stadium in Bukit Jalil on November 19 and 20.

Their Southeast Asian tour was originally scheduled for April and May this year but was postponed, with the band citing logistical considerations and the need to ensure the smooth execution of the regional leg.
The shows will mark their first performances in Malaysia in nearly 19 years, with the band once again bringing songs from their third studio album, The Black Parade, to local audiences.
The album celebrates its 20th anniversary this year, and much has happened since the band’s Malaysian debut in 2007.
MCR recap
Formed in New Jersey, US, in 2001, MCR comprise frontman Gerard Way (vocals), Mikey Way (bass), Ray Toro (lead guitar) and Frank Iero (rhythm guitar).
The band emerged with a distinctive blend of punk energy and emotionally charged songwriting that resonated with audiences worldwide.
Their mainstream breakthrough came with their second studio album, Three Cheers for Sweet Revenge, which includes hits such as I’m Not Okay (I Promise), The Ghost of You and Helena.
However, it was their landmark third album, The Black Parade, released in 2006, that cemented their legacy.
The concept album merged glam-rock spectacle with emo intensity through tracks such as Welcome to the Black Parade, Famous Last Words and I Don’t Love You.

After releasing their fourth and most recent studio album, Danger Days: The True Lives of the Fabulous Killjoys, in 2010, the band went on hiatus in 2013 before reuniting in 2019, returning to live performances after a six-year break.
Long live ‘The Black Parade’
View this post on Instagram
Since their reunion, MCR have continued to attract large audiences, particularly with their Long Live: The Black Parade stadium tour, which began in 2025.

The tour’s 2025 North American leg grossed approximately US$88.6 million (RM362 million) across 11 reported performances, selling over 448,000 tickets, according to box-office figures compiled by Touring Data.
The band have since extended the tour into 2026, taking their The Black Parade production to audiences across South America, Mexico, Southeast Asia, Europe and the United States.
MCR have also taken their stadium performances a step further with an elaborate theatrical production built around an expanding fictional universe.

This includes transforming venues into the fictional world of DRAAG, an authoritarian state in which the band are presented as ‘The Black Parade’, while incorporating mythology surrounding MOAT, a reconditioning facility where the band’s characters were held captive.

The production was brought to life with the help of TAIT, a US-based live-event production and engineering company headquartered in Lititz, Pennsylvania, which designed and built various staging, scenic and automated elements for the tour.
The company has previously worked with artists such as BTS member J-Hope on his Hope On The Stage tour.
“For their monumental return to the stage, MCR transformed stadiums into the fictional country of DRAAG – a surreal domain inspired by an old Russian train station and Gerard Way’s offbeat vision.
“TAIT helped transform each venue into a retro-futurist landscape of punk pageantry and cinematic storytelling,” TAIT wrote on its website.

Among the elements TAIT designed and built were a deep red main stage framed by distressed marble portals, a circular B-stage that brought the band closer to the audience, and a mechanical lift that raised the drum riser during performances.

The design also incorporated burning panels and pyrotechnic troughs to create a fire effect during Famous Last Words, alongside a manually operated firing-squad display that complemented the show’s dystopian themes.
Adding another layer to DRAAG’s fictional world is Keposhka, a writing system developed by Gerard Way and comic-book letterer and typographer Nate Piekos.

Inspired by Cyrillic lettering, historical propaganda posters and brutalist architecture, Piekos created 14 fonts for the project, which feature across the tour’s promotional materials, stage visuals and audience signs.
Beyond the stadium production, MCR have also expanded the album’s anniversary celebrations through Prelude to The End, an animated short film created with visual artist Lauren Tsai.

Drawing from Tsai’s own fictional universe and incorporating the album’s opening track, The End, the film offers another interpretation of the themes of creativity, identity and resistance that have long accompanied the band’s work.
Pop Shuvit to open
Malaysian rock band Pop Shuvit will once again share the stage with MCR when they open for the American rockers at the upcoming Kuala Lumpur shows.
The announcement marks a reunion of sorts, nearly 19 years after Pop Shuvit supported MCR during the latter’s first Malaysian concert at Stadium Merdeka in December 2007.
Beyond their shared stage history, MCR guitarist Ray Toro has also collaborated with several Malaysian musicians.
In 2023, Toro produced and featured on Pop Shuvit’s single Space Between Us, which also featured Butterfingers frontman Emmett on vocals.

Toro had previously contributed to Destination Nowhere in 2019 by Project E.A.R., a collaborative project featuring Malaysian musicians including Emmett and members of Pop Shuvit, alongside artists from other parts of Asia.

d3d418d2e089b8d3: NOVEMBER 16 — The world is entering an era when the use of military force is increasingly treated as an instrument of first resort rather than the last. Yet the more wars proliferate, the more urgent it becomes to strengthen the international conventions that restrain them. The world does not need fewer Geneva Conventions. It needs more of them. Come hell or high water.

The four Geneva Conventions of 1949 emerged from the devastation of the Second World War. Their fundamental purpose was to establish that even warfare must have limits. Civilians must be protected. Prisoners of war must be treated humanely. The wounded and sick must receive medical care. Hospitals and humanitarian personnel must not become deliberate targets.

These are not optional expressions of goodwill. They are legal obligations rooted in international humanitarian law. Yet the conflicts of the twenty-first century have exposed how difficult it has become to enforce these obligations. From Ukraine to Gaza, from Sudan to the wider Middle East, civilian populations have endured enormous suffering. The destruction of essential infrastructure, displacement of communities and interruption of humanitarian assistance have raised profound questions about the effectiveness of existing international mechanisms.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Displaced Palestinian children search of items that could be used as fuel for cooking amid a pile of garbage next to destroyed buildings at the Bureij camp for refugees in the central Gaza Strip October 6, 2025. — AFP pic

The problem is not necessarily that international humanitarian law has become obsolete. Rather, the mechanisms for ensuring compliance have not kept pace with the changing nature of warfare. The original Geneva Conventions were designed primarily around the realities of conventional warfare. Their Additional Protocols subsequently expanded protections, including those relating to civilians in international and certain non-international armed conflicts.
But warfare has changed dramatically.

Autonomous weapons, artificial intelligence, cyberattacks, drones and attacks against critical infrastructure have created new dimensions of vulnerability. A cyberattack against an electricity grid can disable hospitals without a single bomb being dropped. An attack against desalination facilities can deprive millions of people of drinking water. The disruption of maritime transportation through strategic waterways such as the Strait of Hormuz or the Red Sea can threaten food and energy security far beyond the immediate battlefield.

These developments require more than rhetorical reaffirmations of existing conventions. They require serious international negotiations on additional rules, clearer interpretations of existing obligations, stronger verification arrangements and credible enforcement mechanisms.

Artificial intelligence makes this particularly urgent. If military systems become increasingly autonomous, the question of human responsibility cannot be left unresolved. No government should be able to evade accountability merely because a military decision was delegated to an algorithm. The principle of meaningful human control over decisions involving lethal force deserves sustained international attention.

The history of international relations demonstrates that major wars often emerge not merely from disputes over territory or power, but from the gradual collapse of restraints on state behaviour. The First World War demonstrated the consequences of alliance commitments, militarisation and diplomatic failures. The Second World War demonstrated the catastrophic consequences of aggressive expansionism, racial supremacy and the systematic destruction of civilian populations.

The United Nations and the Geneva Conventions were among the institutional responses to these experiences. They were designed to prevent the recurrence of such catastrophes. Yet international institutions cannot survive on historical prestige alone. They must be strengthened by contemporary political commitments. The United States, China, Russia, the European Union and other major powers have particular responsibilities because their military capabilities and geopolitical influence affect the international system.

However, the development of humanitarian rules cannot become the exclusive preserve of the strongest states. The world cannot afford another arrangement resembling Yalta, where powerful governments negotiate the fate of smaller countries without their meaningful participation. Any renewed Geneva process must be inclusive.

For Asean, the strengthening of international humanitarian law is not an abstract diplomatic exercise. South-east Asia has experienced colonialism, occupation, revolutionary warfare, interstate conflicts and prolonged internal instability. Its member states understand the consequences of allowing military confrontation to overwhelm political dialogue. Asean has also spent decades developing institutions intended to encourage consultation, confidence-building and peaceful dispute resolution. These include the Asean Regional Forum, the East Asia Summit and the Asean Defence Ministers’ Meeting-Plus. Such institutions cannot replace the Geneva Conventions. But they can help build the political conditions necessary for their implementation.

Asean should therefore consider advancing a regional initiative supporting the modernisation and stronger enforcement of international humanitarian law. This initiative should involve not only the major powers but also smaller and medium-sized powers whose populations are frequently exposed to the consequences of conflicts they did not initiate. Indeed, the Indo-Pacific cannot be governed exclusively through military alliances and strategic competition. It requires a stronger architecture of humanitarian restraint. This is where Asean Will must become more important than diplomatic habit. Asean must demonstrate the collective determination to defend principles that protect civilians regardless of which major power is involved.

The moral foundations of humanitarian protection are not confined to Western international law. Islamic traditions of warfare contain important principles concerning the protection of non-combatants, the humane treatment of captives and restrictions on unnecessary destruction. Confucian political thought emphasises humane governance, moral responsibility and the obligation of rulers to exercise power with restraint. Western philosophical traditions, from Aristotle to the development of just-war thinking, have similarly examined the relationship between force, justice and political responsibility.
These traditions are not identical. Nor should their historical differences be overlooked. Nevertheless, they provide important intellectual resources for building a wider international consensus.

The Geneva Conventions should therefore be understood not as the exclusive achievement of any single civilisation, but as part of humanity’s continuing effort to limit cruelty. An international humanitarian order becomes stronger when its legitimacy is recognised across civilisations.

Military deterrence remains a feature of international relations. States will continue to maintain armed forces and defend their sovereignty. But military capabilities alone cannot produce a durable international order. The accumulation of weapons does not automatically generate political trust. Nor can military superiority resolve every historical grievance, territorial dispute or ideological disagreement.

Diplomacy is indispensable precisely because states disagree. International conventions provide a framework through which adversaries can establish minimum standards of conduct even when they cannot reach agreement on larger political questions. This is the enduring importance of Geneva. It is possible for governments to remain strategic competitors while accepting common humanitarian obligations. Indeed, the greater their rivalry, the more necessary these obligations become.

A renewed international initiative should concentrate on five priorities. First, strengthening compliance with existing Geneva Conventions, including independent investigation of alleged violations. Second, clarifying humanitarian protections in cyberwarfare and military applications of artificial intelligence. Third, reinforcing protections for hospitals, schools, water systems, electricity networks and other infrastructure essential to civilian survival. Fourth, improving humanitarian access and accountability in conflicts involving both states and non-state armed groups. Fifth, ensuring that smaller and medium-sized powers, regional organisations and representatives of affected populations participate meaningfully in the development of future rules.

Not every challenge requires an entirely new treaty. Some can be addressed through stronger implementation of existing law, additional protocols, interpretive agreements and institutional reforms. What matters is that international humanitarian protection does not remain static while the technologies and consequences of warfare continue to evolve.

The central challenge of our time is not merely the distribution of power among the United States, China, Russia and other major actors. It is whether international society can preserve a minimum standard of humanity amid intensifying geopolitical competition.
Without such standards, every conflict risks becoming a contest in which civilian suffering is treated as an unavoidable instrument of strategic pressure. That would be a dangerous regression.

The Geneva Conventions were created because earlier generations witnessed what happened when warfare was allowed to escape moral and legal restraints. Their achievement must not be squandered. The world needs more Geneva diplomacy, stronger humanitarian conventions and greater willingness to hold all parties accountable under international law. Malaysia and Asean should contribute to this effort by bringing together the major powers, smaller states, international organisations and civilisational traditions in a sustained dialogue.

The objective is not to abolish geopolitical competition overnight. It is to ensure that competition never becomes an excuse for abandoning humanity. Come hell or high water, the world needs more Geneva Conventions, not fewer. For when international humanitarian law collapses, it is not merely diplomacy that fails. It is civilisation itself.

* Phar Kim Beng, PhD, is Professor of Asean Studies at the International Islamic University of Malaysia and Director of the Institute of International and Asean Studies (IINTAS). Shahiran Kamaruzaman is an independent researcher.

49c5105a2d4acae9: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 16 — Malaysia’s broader data-centre industry is expected to be less exposed to proposed United States (US) restrictions on remote access to advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips.

“Rather, the measures could increasingly differentiate operators based on customer profiles, regulatory compliance and end-use transparency.

“In a more restrictive or worst-case scenario, this could lead to delays or cancellations of planned AI DC investments.

a7623fa46c90cf7a: Officials claim the measure ‘protects society,’ but civil society organizations see a threat to freedom of expression
Originally published on Global Voices
Post-election protests in Maputo, Mozambique, in 2025. Photo by Wilson Thole. Used with permission.

Civil society organizations in Mozambique, such as the Center for Democracy and Human Rights (CDD), submitted a document to the Ombudsman contesting the constitutionality of Decree No. 48/2025, issued in December 2025, which establishes control mechanisms and potential blocks on access to telecommunications networks in the country.<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->

According to the portal Moz24h, journalists and experts are concerned that the measure could threaten rights such as freedom of expression, access to information, and communication, particularly in contexts of social mobilization or political tension. The challenge arises in an environment still heated from the conflicts following the 2024 elections.

Activists and civil society actors argue that the decree could enable restrictions on access to the internet and digital platforms — tools that have become increasingly central to the circulation of information, the organization of protests, and civic participation. The approved text allows the state to suspend telecommunications services for up to 48 hours without needing a court order, reports Deutsche Welle.

Also, according to civil society organizations, the decree grants broad powers to authorities to intervene in telecommunications networks on grounds of national security or the maintenance of public order.<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->

By appealing to the Ombudsman, the organizations are requesting an analysis of whether the decree is compatible with the Constitution of the Republic of Mozambique, as well as Mozambique’s international commitments regarding human rights and freedom of expression.

In March 2026, the Minister of Communications and Digital Transformation, Américo Muchanga, denied that the measure restricted rights. He defended it as a way to protect society in critical moments, strengthening the state’s capacity to manage crises and protect critical telecommunications infrastructure.
Experts diverge in their reading
In discussions with Global Voices, various experts presented different interpretations of its potential impacts.

One researcher, who asked not to be identified for security reasons, recalls that several democracies around the world have legal mechanisms allowing temporary restrictions on communications. For the researcher, political contexts where social demonstrations are frequently interpreted as threats to stability can make the application of this type of legislation particularly sensitive. He notes:

O que foi feito neste decreto é tentativa de legalizar toda e qualquer ação que o governo possa ter em uma situação de protesto social. Na França existe, no Brasil existe, nos Estados Unidos existem. Em qualquer parte em que exista alguma democracia, que chamamos a dita democracia consolidada, existem dispositivos estatais, governamentais, que limitam o acesso às comunicações, quando se entende que eles violam o direito de outras pessoas ou imposições em causa do próprio Estado. Não é o decreto o problema. O problema é como pode ser aplicado. O nosso problema é que não há tolerância. Tudo aquilo que parece ser protesto é visto como tentativa de subversão, tentativa de colocar em causa a ordem. É um problema histórico de governança e questão central na interpretação também do próprio decreto.

What was done in this decree is an attempt to legalize any and all actions the government might take in a situation of social protest. It exists in France, it exists in Brazil, and it exists in the United States. Anywhere there is some form of democracy, what we call so-called consolidated democracies, there are state, governmental mechanisms that limit access to communications when it is understood that they violate the rights of other people or impose demands against the state itself. The decree is not the problem. The problem is how it can be applied. Our problem is that there is no tolerance. Everything that looks like a protest is seen as an attempt at subversion, an attempt to jeopardize order. It is a historical problem of governance and a central issue in the interpretation of the decree itself.

Meanwhile, activist and journalist Nadio Taimo emphasizes that the decree comes at a time when Mozambique’s digital civic spaces face growing pressure. According to him, internet access has become fundamental for the circulation of information and the exercise of freedom of expression. Taimo observes that many media outlets migrated to digital platforms because of the high costs of traditional printing, making the online environment an important space for news dissemination, public debate, and social mobilization. In this context, potential blocks on internet access could significantly limit access to information.

Já temos uma expansão, uma onda crescente de jornais eletrônicos. Já não imprimimos jornais, devido aos custos. Migramos para a era digital, logo, há aqui um bloqueio de acesso à informação, e até o próprio espaço de opinião, de promoção da liberdade de expressão, pode ser limitado. Os órgãos de comunicação social são todos, a maior parte deles, do governo, e controlados, e nos é fechado o espaço cívico, o espaço físico, nas ruas, quando nos proíbem de realizar marchas.

We already have an expansion: a growing wave of electronic newspapers. We no longer print newspapers due to costs. We migrated to the digital era; therefore, there is a block on access to information here, and even the very space for opinion, for promoting freedom of expression, can be limited. The media outlets are all — most of them — government-owned and controlled, and our civic space, the physical space in the streets, is closed to us when they prohibit us from holding marches.
The activist further adds that the decree could formalize practices that, according to civil society organizations, have already occurred during moments of political tension:
Este documento é apenas uma formalização de uma intenção política de bloqueio da internet, que já vinha sendo aplicada, só que não havia uma formalização legal.
This document is merely a formalization of a political intention to block the internet, which was already being applied, only without a legal framework.
Precedent cases: Protests and control

The debate over telecommunications control in Mozambique is also linked to previous episodes of social mobilization. In February 2008 and September 2010, mass protests in the cities of Maputo and Matola were triggered by the rising cost of living, particularly the prices of transport and essential goods. During those demonstrations, mobile phones and text messages were widely used to mobilize and coordinate actions. In response, the government at the time promoted stricter communications regulation measures, including mandatory SIM card registration for all users.

New protests broke out again in November 2012 as young people protested the fare hikes for urban semi-collective transport, locally known as chapa-100. Swift intervention by police forces in areas with the highest concentration of protesters prevented the demonstrations from spreading.

These episodes occurred during defining moments of social demand by Mozambican youth in the post-independence period (1975), reflecting frustrations over economic inequalities, unemployment, and the rising cost of living amid economic liberalization. In this scenario, urban culture also played an important role in expressing social discontent. Artists like the rapper Azagaia became influential voices among young people, with social critique songs widely broadcast during demonstrations and across digital platforms.
A regional trend of internet shutdowns

The debate in Mozambique is not an isolated situation. International digital monitoring organizations have documented numerous cases of internet shutdowns in African countries in recent years, often linked to electoral processes, popular protests, or internal conflicts. In Angola and Guinea-Bissau, for instance, blocking or restricting internet access has been utilized by governments during periods of political instability.<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->

Human rights organizations and digital freedom advocacy groups argue that shutdowns limit access to information, hinder the work of journalists, and restrict civic participation, while digital governance experts warn that such measures can have significant impacts not only on public debate, but also on the livelihoods of the civilian population.

Despite the ratification of the aforementioned decree in Mozambique, its practical application has not yet been documented, making it difficult to assess its potential effects in practice. Concurrently, the Constitutional Council has not yet ruled on civil society organizations’ position regarding the decree’s potential unconstitutionality, contributing to a landscape of legal and institutional uncertainty.

5b065f5caeea076e: WASHINGTON: The weekend US air traffic outage ranks as the worst in 35 years for flight cancellations caused by a technology issue, surpassing Southwest Airlines’s 2022 systems meltdown, according to travel app Flighty.

With every US carrier affected by the four-hour nationwide stoppage on Friday, the number of flight cancellations had exceed 17,000 by Sunday, aviation data providers including Flighty and Cirium said. That surpassed the 16,900 scrapped flights caused by Southwest’s tech troubles in the winter holiday of 2022.

Airlines and passengers are still reeling from the days of disruption caused by only the third nationwide ground-stop in history, and the worst since the September 2001 terror attacks. The issue has been traced to the replacement of outdated copper wire at a remote location in Arkansas and a router that started flooding the air-traffic control system with connection attempts.

Cancellations started to ease on Sunday, with more than 2,220 flights affected as of 11.15pm New York time, according to FlightAware data, though more than 10,100 services were delayed as airlines struggled to get planes and crew back on schedule.
Major airlines including Delta Air Lines and Alaska Air Group said they are anticipating a more normal service or vastly reduced cancelations Monday.

So far, American Airlines Group is the most-impacted airline by total, with more than 5,300 services scrapped since Friday, while financially-troubled JetBlue Airways was the worst hit as a proportion of flights, according to flight data provider Cirium.

The latest air traffic tech troubles also surpassed major crises like the 2024 global IT failure of CrowdStrike Holdings, which grounded flights and impacted businesses around the world. The CrowdStrike chaos triggered a further crisis for Delta at the time, after its crew-scheduling system failed.

Investors will also be keeping close tabs on geopolitical developments, with Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US and Russian counterparts Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin holding their first trilateral summit on the sidelines of the Apec gathering.
AI-linked firms continued to fall in early exchanges as the fallout from the upheaval at Nvidia courses through trading floors.
Huang, a pivotal figure in the artificial intelligence boom, resigned Thursday following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

The 63-year-old’s departure raised concerns about the chip titan, which is at the centre of a buildout that has helped propel global markets to record highs and boosted economic growth around the world.

The day looked set for a positive start after the Financial Times reported that Huang was in talks for a spectacular return to the hotseat, while several Silicon Valley titans have backed calls for his return.

There were also losses in Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore, Manila and Jakarta.
“After the bombshells dropped on markets last week, investors have had the weekend to digest the developments and reassess risk with a clearer mind,” wrote Chris Weston at Pepperstone.
“That said, I’m not convinced we’re any closer to pricing the future with a new sense of conviction.
“We’ll see whether the reinstatement trade can gather momentum,” he added.

However, he said “even if Huang were to return, alleviating the immediate key-man risk, the prospect of tighter governance requirements and additional political or regulatory constraints would remain a significant overhang”.

Nvidia is due to report its earnings Tuesday, giving a fresh view on the outlook for the AI trade, while the listing of Anthropic — creator of the Claude chatbot — will provide some insight into investors’ AI sentiment.

428730d65d2647f0: On November 14, Asia fired up its wind machines and pyrotechnics for the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia, aka Eurovision Asia. Eleven countries competed – from Bangladesh and Bhutan to Vietnam and host country Thailand. Notably absent this first year were most of the continent’s most populous nations: China, India, Japan, Pakistan and Indonesia. The format was familiar: three-minute songs performed with no more than six people permitted on stage. But there was a distinct regional inflection in the staging, costuming and language choices. Regional flavour Many of the artists wove in elements of traditional sound and traditional dress, and artists expressed gratitude to the audience with the traditional Thai gesture wai (hands together). While the original Eurovision is hosted in a combination of English and French, Eurovision Asia was delivered in English only. But most artists performed either in their own language (36%) or a combination of that language with English (54%). Only South Korea’s song was performed entirely in English. By comparison, Eurovision 2026 featured 43% of songs entirely in English, 38% in languages other than English, and 19% multilingual. Musically, it was a diverse offering. The delicate lotus leaves of Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên and her back-up dancers broke into a high-energy opening number, Em Tiên. Malaysia’s Aina Abdul finished the show with a pitch-perfect power ballad, Bluest Sky. In between, audiences were treated to Cambodian and Bhutanese ballads, Bengali a capella, South Korean K-pop and, perhaps most surprisingly, Nepali rock. Girls to the front But it was the Philippines’ Carmelle – the youngest contestant, at 19 – who won the night with Sobra-Sobra. The focus of the empowering pop song in English and Tagalog was about Filipino women’s right to be who they want to be. “It’s about how unapologetic, independent and strong Filipinas are. It describes me – not just me, but of course all the Filipinas,” Carmelle told The Guardian. Carmelle received 211 points, winning both the jury and the public vote, encompassing viewers from 183 countries and territories. With her victory, the Philippines has won the right to host Eurovision Asia in 2027. In the meantime, Carmelle will also perform at the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest in Bulgaria. Carmelle rehearsing Sobra-Sobra at the Eurovision Song Contest Asia. Eurovision Song Contest Asia Spectacle and snags Eurovision is known for its spectacle, and Eurovision Asia delivered, albeit on a more modest budget. Stage production made the most of stunning visual projections, smoke and flares. Eurovision is also known for its non-political stance, with political or ideological messages prohibited. But it has been more forgiving toward humanitarian statements. And at Eurovision Asia, Nepal’s Pratik Himal Rai used the end of his set to call for support for his country as it recovers from the August flood disaster. The show was not without its hitches. Laos’ representative, Thinla, couldn’t hear her music due to an issue with her earpiece, so footage of her technical rehearsal was shown at the end of the performances to ensure fair judgement of her act. Thai artists Mang x Daou experienced wardrobe malfunctions during their ballad Aroma, though this didn’t affect their chances in the voting – Thailand came in second place, with 169 points. Why not Asiavision? If Europe has Eurovision, why can’t Asia have Asiavision? For one, the name “Asiavision” is already taken: it’s the broadcasting network of the Asia-Pacific Broadcasting Union (ABU), which has its own song contests and festivals. But mostly, it’s about branding. Although the name Eurovision has become synonymous with the song contest, it actually refers to the European Broadcasting Union’s (EBU) pan-European telecommunications network. The Eurovision Song Contest was created in 1956 to promote the network and attract audiences across borders. (No, it was not created to unite a war-torn Europe.) The purpose of Eurovision Asia is specifically to expand the Eurovision brand and format into the region. This is a project the EBU has been attempting for more than two decades. It plans to continue the expansion of the brand through other continental editions. MANG x DAOU rehearsing for Thailand at Eurovision Song Contest Asia in Bangkok. Ralph Larmann/Eurovision The future of Eurovision Asia Staging the inaugural competition is one thing, but securing the longevity of the franchise in Asia is another matter. Buy-in from economic powerhouses Japan, China and India may be the key to its success. Negotiations were underway with China and Japan to participate this year, and organisers are optimistic that they and several others will join in 2027. The broad geographical scope of “Asia” also has the potential to draw in participants from the Middle East. But broader participation presents its own challenges. The original Eurovision is heavily associated with LGBTQIA+ acceptance and pride, which may not be well-received by certain broadcasters and their audiences within Asia. We saw this play out in the inaugural Eurovision Asia contest: Malaysian broadcaster TV3 cut drag performer Vice Ganda, the Phillipines’ jury spokesperson, from its broadcast. There was also speculation about whether Islamophobia played a role in Malaysia’s Aina Abdul’s results; despite being a favourite to win going into the contest, she finished in fourth place. Soft power and pop Like the OG Eurovision, Eurovision Asia offers great potential for soft power politics. It also has the potential to be a powerful global platform for Asian pop. The inaugural competition was a diverse showcase for the unique voices and cultures of its participants, beyond the dominant trends of J- and K-pop. Hopefully we will get a chance to see more in Manila next year. Jess Carniel does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

279fed26f5857518: HONG KONG: A resounding Democratic takeover of Capitol Hill did more than rattle Asian chipmakers.
It set off a macro realignment of foreign policy, energy, and trade that could create new winners and losers across Asian markets.
The "blue wave" in the US midterm elections on Nov 3 triggered an anti-AI market shock, sending the tech-heavy Nasdaq to its steepest fall in 19 months.
Investors feared that incoming Democratic leaders would subject AI companies to stricter scrutiny, including over data centre construction and tax breaks.
Asian equities — home to some of the world's biggest chipmakers — led the regional retreat in the week of the vote.
South Korea's KOSPI and Taiwan's TAIEX each tumbled 12%, dragging the broader MSCI Asia ex Japan index down 5%.

While Asian markets have recovered some ground, investors remain on edge after an October tech selloff driven by valuation concerns and doubts about the payoff from AI investment, fears since amplified by turmoil at Nvidia, a key engine of the AI boom.
The risk from the AI blowback is clearly concentrated in North Asia.
The CSOP-Solactive AI exchange-traded fund, the region's leading AI-focused fund, allocates 37% to Taiwan and South Korea and 26% to Japan.
KraneShares' more geographically diversified AI ETF allocates 12% to China, highlighting Asia's wide exposure to the sector.

Less tech-dependent neighbours are feeling less heat from the AI jitters. India's benchmark BSE Sensex rose 7% in the election week, while Singapore's Straits Times Index fell only 3%; both have since advanced further.
If the tech rout deepens, these markets appear better placed than the regional bourses that led gains in the first half of 2026.
Competing forges
The ramifications of the US elections for Asia extend well beyond data centres.
First, there is US policy in the Middle East. Democratic congressional control could pressure the White House to de-escalate the US-Iran war.
Indeed, president Donald Trump said that the US was unlikely to strike Iran while negotiations continued, a far cry from the more hawkish rhetoric before the elections.
Markets appear to be pricing in this policy shift. Since the midterms, benchmark Brent crude oil has fallen for a second straight week, dropping nearly 19% to below US$96 a barrel.

Cheaper energy could offer relief across Asia. Historically, around 80% of oil and 90% of gas transiting the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint were destined for ‌Asian markets, meaning this year’s Middle East conflict, which effectively closed the narrow waterway for months, has hit the region particularly hard.
The countries that stand to benefit the most from falling fuel prices include Japan, South Korea and India.

In addition to weighing on inflation and helping boost growth, declining oil prices should also be positive for Asian energy importers' trade balances, which, all else being equal, could help boost their currencies.
However, this is where countries may see greater divergence.

North Asian economies have seen their trade surpluses balloon over the past year on the back of massive AI exports. So, if oil prices and AI demand decline together, the latter could offset the former, leaving large tech exporters as net losers. That shouldn't be the case for their less tech-exposed neighbours.

Currency markets illustrate the divide. Since Nov 3, South Korea's won and the Taiwan dollar have underperformed their major Asian peers, whereas the Indian rupee, heavily exposed to oil prices but not to tech hardware exports, has appreciated sharply.
Affordability push

A widely held view in the US, echoed by leaders on both sides of the aisle, is that elevated prices were a major factor behind the Democratic landslide. Policy focused on improving affordability could therefore become more prominent in both parties' agendas.

Tariffs played a role in cost-of-living concerns, so the election results may reduce the likelihood that Trump ratchets up his aggressive trade policy, even if he could persist via executive authority.
Given bipartisan concerns about China, trade pressure on Beijing may not ease.
However, this could benefit other Asian countries that supply consumer goods, such as Vietnam, Bangladesh, Thailand, Indonesia and India.
Another key affordability issue was healthcare. Efforts by Democrats to lower healthcare costs could accelerate demand for generic drugs and outsourced manufacturing.

India could be well positioned here. The country’s generic manufacturers, including Sun Pharmaceutical Industries, produce roughly 20% of the world's generic medicines and already supply about 40% of US demand for generics.
Another winner could be contract development and manufacturing organisations (CDMOs) such as South Korea's Samsung Biologics, which provide outsourced manufacturing services to major US drugmakers.
When tailwinds converge
India appears to be the Asian market that most clearly ticks all of the above boxes.
As a net energy importer with minimal exposure to tech cycles, it could directly capture the upside of lower commodity prices, reduced trade pressure and pharmaceutical tailwinds.
It was therefore no surprise that Indian stocks outperformed after the vote.
Foreign flows have also skyrocketed in recent days, underscoring investors’ renewed confidence in a market often touted as an “anti-AI” play.
However, nothing is certain.
Should Trump leverage his executive powers to escalate Middle East conflicts, any projected relief from inflation or high energy costs would immediately vanish.
He could also shrug off voter concerns and continue to pursue his aggressive tariff agenda.

Furthermore, if strategic competition with China pushes Washington to loosen domestic constraints on AI development, capital could pivot rapidly back to North Asian hardware exporters, relegating markets like India to the sidelines.
For now, navigating Asia requires recognising that Washington's policy shifts reach far beyond the AI supply chain.
(The views expressed here are those of Manishi Raychaudhuri, the founder and CEO of Emmer Capital Partners Ltd and the former head of Asia-Pacific Equity Research at BNP Paribas Securities.)
2bd9ad18b7f61464: BEIJING: Chinese retail sales growth weakened in October, official data showed on Monday, as the world's second-largest economy struggles to prop up domestic demand and reverse a spending slump.
The 0.4% year-on-year increase, announced by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS), followed a 1.1% increase in September.
The reading also missed a Bloomberg forecast of 0.8%, despite a week-long national holiday, underscoring persistent challenges to kickstart consumer activity.
Beijing has grappled with sluggish domestic spending since the end of the Covid-19 pandemic, with stagnant activity weighing down national growth even as exports boom.
Industrial production expanded 4.8% in October, the NBS said, compared with September's 5.5% growth and short of Bloomberg's forecast of 5.3%.
China's economy remained stable in October but the "international environment" is still "characterised by significant instability and uncertainty", the NBS said in a statement on Monday.

"Domestically, the imbalance between strong supply and weak demand persists, some enterprises face operational difficulties, and the foundation for a stable, improving economy requires further consolidation," the NBS added.
Authorities are pursuing an official growth target this year of 4.5-5.0% - the lowest goal in decades.
China's economy grew slightly more than expected in the third quarter, data published in October showed, but figures still came in at 4.5%.
7afec735418a3e23: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 16 — Bursa Malaysia’s key index opened lower today, tracking Wall Street’s weaker performance last Friday, as concerns over Nvidia’s leadership uncertainty continued to weigh on market sentiment.

661877edb0aa3a98: SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 16 — Tech tycoon Elon Musk and an Uber co-founder are, as of yesterday, among more than 158,000 signatories of an open letter calling for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia chief.
The letter demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts.”

Huang resigned Thursday, ending a 33-year run at the helm of the AI giant he co-founded after revelations he had two extramarital affairs, with a woman accused of spying for China and another with a subordinate.

Alongside the SpaceX chief, the tech heavyweight signatories include Tim Sweeney, founder and CEO of video game publisher Epic Games, and Garry Tan, president of Y Combinator, San Francisco’s most renowned business incubator.

Another signatory, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, wrote that Huang had “erred, yes — to err is to be human — but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company.”
More than 7,500 signatories identify themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to 18 per cent of the company’s workforce.
The support illustrates the unique standing of the leather-jacketed executive, who is seen as a godfather of AI within the industry.
Under his leadership, Nvidia became a pivotal Silicon Valley investor, financing data centres and startups, earning it the nickname “the central bank of AI.”
But the company has also faced criticism that it has fuelled a speculative investment bubble.
Huang championed open AI models, including Chinese ones, and fought any constraints on the AI race, clashing on these issues with Claude creator Anthropic and its chief Dario Amodei.
According to the Financial Times, Huang has discussed a possible return with people close to him, and one of his allies says he is assembling a crisis team of executives to seek White House support.
On Friday, two major shareholders, investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker, urged the board to keep “all options” open.
In Washington, however, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent argued yesterday that Nvidia should look “outside” the company for its next chief.
“They need a dramatic shake-up,” Bessent said on Fox News, demanding that the company explain whether it had knowingly turned a blind eye to the smuggling of its chips to China. — AFP
e1b19cda99281fde: SYDNEY: Australia on Monday expressed concern its economy will take a hit from "manipulation" of trade in its biggest export iron ore, by its biggest customer China.
The world's top producer, Australia exported 944 million tonnes of iron ore last year, of which three-quarters were shipped to China for steel making.

The trade has withstood political disputes between the two countries, flowing even as China imposed blocks on A$20 billion (US$13.5 billion) worth of Australian coal, wine and agricultural exports in 2020 as retaliation for Canberra's call for an inquiry into the origins of Covid-19.
But China's formation of a central buying body to lower the price its steel makers pay Australian iron ore producers risks souring trade.
China's embassy did not respond to a request for comment.

Resources minister Madeleine King said on Monday the activity of China Minerals Resources Group, which has reportedly sought to block sales by Australian producers as it negotiates contracts, was against the international rules of trade.
"The export of iron ore from this country since it started in the 60s has been integral to our national economy," King told national broadcaster ABC.

"When there is movements by the biggest consumer of that product to moderate the prices in their favour, well, that is of concern to the government because it affects the budget bottom line," she said.
"The manipulation of trade is not good for our country," she added.
The government has previously said iron ore negotiations were a commercial matter.
King said on Monday she is in discussions with Australia's iron ore producers.
CMRG was formed in 2022 to centralise buying. China is the world's biggest buyer of iron ore.
Australia's iron ore exports are forecast to be A$107 billion next year, a 10% fall in value.
In an export forecast last month, Australia's industry ministry said CMRG's increasing influence "could represent a shift in market structure" with implications for iron ore price negotiations.
Miners BHP and Rio Tinto recently struck deals with CMRG, however Fortescue told investors last month its sales were 3.9 million tonnes lower because of continuing negotiations with CMRG.
If those talks are not concluded by December, the miner's operations may be impacted, Fortescue said.
432f025c9a36a30a: SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 16 — US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called on Nvidia to explain whether it knowingly allowed its most advanced AI chips to reach China yesterday, saying this was more important than ex-CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged spy for Beijing.

Speaking on Fox News Sunday Morning Futures three days after Huang resigned, Bessent said he wants to know if Nvidia used shell companies to dodge US restrictions and sell its most powerful chips to China.

But late yesterday, tech tycoon Elon Musk and several other Silicon Valley leaders added their signatures to more than 165,000 others on an open letter demanding that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts.”
The United States forbids sales to China of the most cutting-edge AI chips, hoping to stay ahead of the Chinese in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.
In late 2025, President Donald Trump did authorize sales of Nvidia chips called H200s to the Chinese — but not the most advanced chips used to run AI models reshaping modern society.
“Nothing above the H200s can be sold to the Chinese,” Bessent said.
“What’s more important here,” he said, “is to examine whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the US export restrictions.”
Bessent alluded to companies linked to Megaspeed, the Singapore-based data centre company that Huang’s alleged lover Alice Huang once worked for.
“And who knew? Because I mean, these shell companies were obvious. They were being investigated. And did Nvidia use them as a workaround to sell chips to the Chinese?”
Of Alice Huang, he said: “It doesn’t matter to me whether she’s a spy or not. You know, Jensen’s foibles are his foibles.”
Investigation deadline

Bessent said he wanted answers from Nvidia and its internal investigation of Jensen Huang’s behaviour within the next 10 days, and said the company needed “a dramatic shake-up,” which should include looking “outside” for its next chief.
The United States suspects Megaspeed helped Chinese firms get around US export controls by buying Nvidia chips for its data centers in Southeast Asia, then routing them to China.
The Justice Department is carrying out a criminal probe.
Nvidia late last month said it had investigated these allegations last year and refuted them.
The Financial Times has reported that four federal agencies pushed to have Megaspeed blacklisted by the Commerce Department run by Howard Lutnick, but the department did not do so.
“Many other departments were pushing for this, and Commerce had the pen,” Bessent said, repeating remarks he made Friday that suggest fissures in the Trump administration on this issue.

Jensen Huang and other Nvidia officials have agreed to testify in one session before representatives of three House of Representatives committees — Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and a special committee focusing on China — Republican Congressman John Moolenaar, the chairman of that select committee, said yesterday on CBS. He said no date has been set yet.

“And we think that’s going to be a very important meeting to understand to what degree privileged information was accessed, also to what degree this potential alleged Chinese spy influenced Nvidia’s philosophy,” Moolenaar said.
On Friday, two major shareholders, investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker, urged the board to keep “all options” open.
Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent successor, the company said earlier this week.
The end of Huang’s 33-year-long run at the helm of Nvidia sent its stock spiraling.
When trading closed on Friday, the stock was down more than 12 per cent over the week, wiping approximately US$573 billion (RM2.3 trillion) off its market value.
Nvidia is due to publish its quarterly report tomorrow. — AFP
d363e2d73ebadd97: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 16 — Construction, transportation and logistics, and telecommunications and media attracted net inflows from foreign institutions into Bursa Malaysia last week, according to MBSB Investment Bank Bhd (MBSB IB).

936348b61b0e5836: BERLIN: The crisis in Germany's skilled trades sector is worsening despite more favourable growth forecasts, German Press Agency (dpa) reported, citing the president of the German Confederation of Skilled Trades on Sunday.
"Our business climate index is at the level of the coronavirus pandemic, investment has fallen to the level of the financial crisis," Jorg Dittrich told newspapers of the Funke Media Group.

He warned that, if nothing was done to counter this, the trade sector would "lose between 70,000 and 80,000 jobs a year." He added that more than 150,000 jobs had already been lost in the sector over the past two years.
Skilled trades are a key part of the German economy and cover jobs ranging from construction and electrical positions to food production and health and personal care jobs.
"Many business owners lack confidence, others simply lack the financial means. And then they shut up shop," Dittrich said.
The sector was experiencing a "silent death of businesses." The high cost of living was also putting skilled trades workers under pressure.
"Anyone who spends a lot at the petrol station is more inclined to think twice about having one fewer haircut or buying one fewer cake or piece of jewellery," he added.
To halt the trend, Dittrich called for a reduction in non-wage labour costs and for the coalition to push through its promised electricity tax cut for the trades.
He warned that successful vocational training programmes were at risk of being cut.
"It is undignified how the trades sector is being treated."

d2ec6581b65c222b: International executives will gather in Kuala Lumpur on Nov 16-17 to discuss cruise opportunities in Malaysia and Southeast Asia. For Malaysia, this is a significant development.
It is the first time the event is being hosted here, reflecting the growing recognition of Malaysia's considerable potential to have a more important role in the regional cruise tourism industry.

The event, Seatrade Cruise Asia 2026, brings together more than 18 international cruise line brands, including some of the biggest names such as Royal Caribbean International, StarDream Cruises, Norwegian Cruise Line, MSC Cruises, Azamara, Disney Cruise Line and Princess Cruises.

Senior executives and industry representatives from Europe, the US and Asia will participate in discussions on the future of cruising in this region, including new itineraries, emerging destinations, home-porting opportunities, port infrastructure and the growing demand for cruise holidays among Asian travellers.

Indeed, the event is being organised across several Malaysian destinations, with Kuala Lumpur hosting the main conference, followed by activities in Penang and Langkawi. This provides an opportunity to showcase not just our ports but also the country's wider tourism attractions.
Malaysia's opportunity

For many years, Singapore has established itself as the principal cruise home port in Southeast Asia. Its strategic location, international airport connectivity, modern cruise terminals and well-developed tourism infrastructure have made it a natural starting point for many international cruise operators.
From Singapore, cruise itineraries frequently extend along the Straits of Malacca, with calls at Melaka, Port Klang, Penang and Langkawi before continuing towards Phuket in Thailand.

Another attractive itinerary, depending on the season and weather conditions, covers the eastern side of the peninsula, with destinations such as Tioman, Redang and neighbouring destinations including Koh Samui in Thailand. Further itineraries can extend towards Cambodia and Vietnam, which includes Sihanoukville, Ho Chi Minh City and Da Nang.

All these routes offer considerable opportunities for Malaysia. We have the geographical advantage of being located along some of the busiest and most established maritime tourism corridors in Southeast Asia.
We also have a diverse range of destinations, from historical cities and cultural attractions to islands, beaches, rainforests and natural landscapes.

However, geographical location alone does not guarantee success. Cruise operators are commercial businesses. They look at passenger demand, port accessibility, terminal facilities, operating costs, immigration procedures, shore excursions and the overall attractiveness of destinations before deciding where to deploy their vessels.
Growing Asian market
The timing is particularly important because the Asian cruise market is developing rapidly.

According to figures released by the Singapore Tourism Board, Southeast Asia recorded approximately 3.9 million cruise passenger visits in 2024. Singapore accounted for 48% of these visits, while Malaysia captured approximately 22%.
Together, the two countries accounted for around 70% of the growing regional market. These figures also demonstrate that Malaysia is already an important cruise destination.

However, it has also been suggested that there is considerable room to grow, particularly if we can attract more international cruise operators and encourage more Malaysians to experience cruise holidays.

The potential domestic market should not be underestimated either. Malaysia has a sizeable middle-income population, an expanding travelling public and a growing number of families looking for alternative holiday experiences.

Cruise holidays could become increasingly attractive, particularly for families who prefer an all-inclusive holiday package with accommodation, meals, entertainment and multiple destinations incorporated into one journey.
There is also an opportunity to develop more regional cruise packages catering specifically to Malaysian, Indonesian, Thai and other Southeast Asian travellers.
This is a growing market that cruise operators are looking to explore and I think Malaysia is ready for it.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
5a2587b6eab93678: Sabtu lalu, Menteri Besar Negeri Sembilan, Ismail Lasim, mengesahkan beliau telah menarik balik surat yang dihantar kepada Penyimpan Mohor Besar Raja-raja berhubung 'penyingkiran' Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir sebagai Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan.
Surat itu juga difahamkan mengesahkan sokongan sebulat suara bekas 10 anggota Majlis Mesyuarat Kerajaan Negeri terhadap Tuanku Muhriz.

Ini membawa kita kepada soalan satu juta ringgit: Bolehkah kita meletakkan kepercayaan kepada Umno Negeri Sembilan? Adakah kata-kata mereka benar-benar ikhlas? Atau adakah ini satu lagi helah untuk cuba menjatuhkan pemerintah negeri?
Teguran terbuka Tuanku Muhriz terhadap Ismail baru-baru ini secara tidak langsung menggambarkan Ismail sebagai seorang yang tidak boleh dipercayai.
Terdapat empat sebab mengapa saya masih sangsi terhadap tindakan Ismail.

1. Kenapa baru sekarang Ismail menarik balik surat itu? Teori saya ialah beliau memerlukan perkenan untuk mengadakan sidang DUN. Walaupun dari segi teori menteri besar boleh mentadbir sesebuah negeri tanpa anggota Majlis Mesyuarat Kerajaan Negeri, sidang DUN diperlukan untuk meluluskan belanjawan dan rang undang-undang.
Perkara ini menimbulkan persoalan: adakah Ismail benar-benar insaf atas tindakannya? Atau beliau hanya terdesak?
2. Tindakan Ismail ketika kontroversi itu

Tindakan Ismail menggambarkan dengan jelas mengenai beliau. Sebelum ini, Ismail berkata beliau dipaksa menandatangani dokumen untuk menurunkan Tuanku Muhriz, namun kemudian menyokong kenyataan Majlis Mesyuarat Kerajaan Negeri yang mengumumkan pemerintah negeri itu telah diturunkan.

Pada 2 Ogos, Ismail mengangkat sumpah sebagai menteri besar di hadapan Tuanku Muhriz dan melafazkan ikrar taat setia kepada baginda. Sehari selepas itu, Ismail menandatangani pengisytiharan untuk menurunkan pemerintah negeri itu.
Ada pepatah yang berbunyi, 'sekali terkena, dua kali beringat'. Namun, dalam keadaan ini, kita sepatutnya empat kali beringat.
3. Isu Undang Luak yang masih belum selesai
Masih terdapat isu membabitkan Undang Luak, termasuk beberapa orang yang telah diturunkan, serta individu yang dilantik oleh mereka sebagai Yang Dipertuan Besar yang baharu.

Kumpulan ini masih rancak dengan aktiviti mereka, dilihat tidak menunjukkan sebarang kekesalan atas tindakan mereka apabila secara terbuka mencabar notis warta Dewan Keadilan dan Undang (DKU) yang mengesahkan penyingkiran dua Undang dan seorang pemimpin adat.
Dikatakan kumpulan ini mempunyai hubungan rapat dengan Adun Umno Negeri Sembilan. Perlu diingat, tiada seorang pun Adun Umno tampil secara terbuka menolak kumpulan tersebut.
Jadi, bagaimana kita sebagai rakyat boleh menaruh kepercayaan terhadap tindakan Ismail menarik balik surat itu sedangkan Umno dipercayai masih mempunyai kaitan dengan kumpulan berkenaan?

4. Umno yang kembali bangkit berkemungkinan lebih berani untuk melakukan satu lagi tindakan serupa di Negeri Sembilan, memandangkan percubaan pertama mereka tidak berjalan seperti yang dirancang.
Tak banyak sebab untuk saya mempercayai Ismail dan Umno Negeri Sembilan ini benar-benar insaf dengan kesalahan mereka.

a8becbed55c716fd: On Saturday, Negeri Sembilan menteri besar Ismail Lasim confirmed he had withdrawn a letter sent to the Keeper of the Rulers’ Seal concerning the “removal” of Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir as the Yang Dipertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan.
The letter was also understood to affirm the unanimous support of the 10 sacked executive council members for Tuanku Muhriz.

This brings us to the million-ringgit question: can we trust Negeri Sembilan Umno? Is there any sincerity in what they say? Or is this yet another sleight of hand in an attempt to topple the state ruler?
Tuanku Muhriz's recent public rebuke of Ismail does not paint the latter as someone trustworthy.
There are four reasons why I remain wary of Ismail’s actions.

1. Why is Ismail retracting the letter only now? My theory is that he needs the ruler’s consent to convene the state assembly. While one could, on paper, administer a state without executive councillors, a state assembly sitting is needed to pass budgets and proposed laws.
Which raises this question: is Ismail really remorseful for his actions? Or is he acting out of desperation?
2. Ismail’s actions amid the controversy

They speak volumes about the man himself. He previously said he was coerced into signing a document deposing Tuanku Muhriz, only to later endorse a state executive council statement announcing the ruler’s purported removal.
On Aug 2, Ismail took his oath of office as menteri besar and pledged allegiance to Tuanku Muhriz before signing a proclamation the following day to remove the ruler.
There is a saying, “once bitten, twice shy”. In this instance though, we should be shy four times over.
3. There is still the matter of the other undangs (traditional territorial chieftains), some of whom have been removed, and the matter of the person whom they appointed as the state’s new ruler.

This faction, which is still alive and kicking, has apparently shown no remorse for its actions by openly challenging a Dewan Keadilan dan Undang Negeri Sembilan gazette notice formalising the removal of two chieftains and a customary leader.
It is said that this faction is close to Umno assemblymen in Negeri Sembilan. Mind you, none of the Umno assemblymen have come out to publicly distance themselves from this faction.
So how can we, the people, have any faith in Ismail’s retraction of a letter when Umno is presumably still linked to the said faction?

4. Has Ismail provided assurance via a written and signed declaration that he and his band of Umno men will never again conspire with others to overthrow Tuanku Muhriz? If Ismail were truly repentant, he would have gone the extra mile to show it.

Now, Umno’s decisive win at the Melaka polls will give the party some bragging rights following the controversies over former prime minister Najib Razak’s house arrest and the finances of Felda or Tabung Haji, which did not dent support for the party.
A resurgent Umno is likely to be emboldened to pull off another stunt in Negeri Sembilan, seeing as how the first one didn’t pan out exactly as they planned.
Ismail Lasim and Negeri Sembilan Umno give me very little reason to trust this mea culpa.

13c955d113761972: It began, as most modern Malaysian sagas do, not with a bang, but with a grumble. A mamak shop, that near-sacred 24-hour temple of roti canai and teh tarik, had the audacity to close its doors on Deepavali day.

The reason? To allow its staff, many of whom are Hindus, to celebrate the Festival of Lights. A simple, humane and frankly logical decision. And yet, within hours, it had ignited a firestorm on social media, transforming a shop’s holiday schedule into a national debate on race, religion and the soul of our nation.
This can only happen in Malaysia. “Mamak tutup? On Deepavali? How can a Muslim-run restaurant close for a Hindu-based celebration?” So began the stream of religious insults and slurs.

For most people, the mamak shop is more than a restaurant; it is a cultural institution, a neutral ground where everyone can sit side-by-side at 3am, arguing over football or who should be the prime minister.

But the debate triggered by the post made out the closure to be almost a betrayal of the social contract. The real fireworks began when the keyboard warriors logged on and the debate fractured along predictable, yet deeply depressing, lines.

On one side, some who described the closure as an act of placing Deepavali celebrations over Islam, an analogy that is mind-boggling. On the other side, those who celebrated the closure as a victory for inclusivity, while simultaneously weaponising it against the owners. A simple act of employee appreciation became a truncheon in the never-ending racial culture war.

The comments sections devolved into a cesspool of racial slurs and religious mockery. The practices of each community – from fasting to praying to celebrating – were dissected, mocked and used as ammunition.

This is the Malaysian paradox. We are a nation that prides itself on our diversity, our muhibbah spirit and our ability to live together. We celebrate each other's festivals with open houses and open hearts. But the moment a minor racial or religious issue is raised, the harmony ruptures and the nation's ugly, tribalistic underbelly is exposed for all to see.

The debate exposed a deep-seated insecurity, the fear of being marginalised, anxiety over the “other” and the constant, exhausting need to assert one's own identity in a multi-racial landscape. The mamak shop became a proxy for a much larger, unresolved national conversation about what it means to be Malaysian.

The fact that we lose our minds over such a small matter is precisely the problem. We have become experts at finding offence, at drawing battle lines over the most trivial of issues. A shop closure becomes a religious war. A wrong word becomes a racial slur. A difference in opinion becomes a declaration of enmity.
We are so quick to insult each other, yet so slow to extend the basic courtesy of understanding.

The next time you see a shop closed for a holiday that isn't “yours”, take a breath. Instead of reaching for your phone to type a scathing comment, maybe reach for a packet of murukku from a Hindu neighbour.
The mamak shop will reopen, but the damage done by our own intolerance, the scars we inflict on our national psyche with every hateful comment, are far harder to heal.
Only in Malaysia can a day of light be turned into a war of darkness. Sadly, that is the most Malaysian thing of all.

afff4032dd146415: Israel’s laws are built to entrench ethnic domination, and international courts are under attack for noticing
Originally published on Global Voices
Roadblocks at the entrance to Shuhada Street in Hebron, Palestine. Photo by Travel 2 Palestine on Flickr (CC BY 2.0).

Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank are subject to Israeli civil law. Palestinians who suffer their violence and occupation are subject to Israeli military law. The two face two different legal systems.

Palestinian, Israeli and international rights groups, and UN findings, have long argued this is not a malfunction of Israeli justice but its design, and that the international system meant to check, and failed to do so, is being taken apart.
Two legal systems, one occupation
For years, Israeli military data has shown conviction rates for Palestinians in Israeli military courts to be anything between 99.74 and 96 percent.

A May 2025 report by Adalah, the legal center for Palestinian citizens of Israel, documents how Israel moved settlement governance in Area C under civilian authority while Palestinians remain under military rule. Adalah calls the arrangement a system of apartheid and de facto annexation.

Inside Israel, the Knesset keeps adding to the structure. Adalah’s Discriminatory Laws Database listed over 65 laws that discriminate against Palestinian citizens of Israel or residents of the occupied territory in 2017. Its November 2025 report reviews more than 30 further laws passed between October 7, 2023 and July 27, 2025, which Adalah says rest on the principle of Jewish ethno-national supremacy that the 2018 Nation-State Law enshrined.

In March 2026, the Knesset passed a death penalty law with 62 votes. Adalah and four other Israeli rights groups argue its wording excludes Israeli Jewish perpetrators of similar offenses, so that in practice it applies only to Palestinians. They have petitioned the Supreme Court to annul it.
Impunity as procedure

The Israeli group Yesh Din has tracked police investigations into settler violence against Palestinians since 2005. Of the files it monitored through 2025, 93.6 percent ended without an indictment, and only about 3 percent ended in a full or partial conviction. Most closures cited an unidentified suspect or insufficient evidence, which Yesh Din attributes to police failures. In roughly half of the nearly 30 mass settler attacks it documented between 2023 and late 2025, soldiers or police were present.

Soldiers face similar odds. In March 2026, the military’s top lawyer dropped charges against five reservists accused of severe sexual and physical abuse against a Palestinian detainee at the Sde Teiman detention camp. Yesh Din said only two indictments existed over soldiers’ conduct in the Gaza war.
Courts have not interrupted the pattern. In March 2025, Israel’s Supreme Court unanimously rejected a petition by five Israeli rights groups seeking unimpeded humanitarian aid into Gaza.
The UN Commission of Inquiry concluded in September 2025 that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, joining findings by Amnesty International and B’Tselem.

In October 2026, the commission added that Israel committed crimes against humanity in the West Bank, including extermination, and that military operations since January 2025 caused the largest displacement there since 1967.
Sanctioning the world courts

In July 2024, the International Court of Justice ruled that Israel’s presence in the occupied territory is unlawful and must end as rapidly as possible. It also found that Israel’s legislation and measures breach Article 3 of the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination (ICERD), which prohibits racial segregation and apartheid. In September 2025, UN experts criticized the failure to act on the General Assembly resolution that followed the ruling.

Meanwhile, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defense minister Yoav Gallant in November 2024. In December 2025, its Appeals Chamber rejected an Israeli challenge and left the warrants in force.

The reaction to the warrants, like that to the UN findings regarding apartheid, genocide and crimes against humanity perpetrated by Israel, has contributed to the failure of international law in delivering justice.

By August 2026, nine of the court’s 18 judges and both deputy prosecutors were sanctioned by the US. On October 9, 2026, the US sanctioned the ICC itself, citing its jurisdiction over US nationals abroad, after earlier sanctions on three Palestinian human rights groups and UN special rapporteur Francesca Albanese. Human Rights Watch and three other groups have sued in US federal court, and say the aim of the sanctions is to shield US and Israeli officials from prosecution.
A system, not an anomaly

None of this is an aberration of the post-October 7 period, a rogue government or a failure to apply the rules. Adalah traces these laws to Israel’s constitutional and political culture, built on Jewish ethno-national supremacy, and notes that, unlike apartheid South Africa or Jim Crow in the US, “most of the laws cited in the report use neutral legal language.”

The UN Commission of Inquiry reaches the same conclusion from another direction. It traces the root causes back to 1947–1948 and says the aim of seizing maximum land while minimizing the Palestinian population stems from Israel’s colonizing policies.

That is how settler colonial states have always worked. Law does not sit outside the project. It is the project’s instrument. Military rule in the West Bank rests on emergency regulations the British Mandate wrote in 1945 to subdue the local population. Declaring “State land” has been, in Adalah’s words, the primary legal mechanism for taking Palestinian land since the late 1970s. Each layer converts dispossession into a legal procedure: a permit denied, a file closed, a petition dismissed, a statute passed.

Seen this way, the evidence describes one logic working across three levels. Statutes define who holds rights. Police, prosecutors and courts decide whom those rights protect. And the Israeli state has moved to shield itself from outside scrutiny, backed by a US government that now sanctions the institutions that try to apply international law.
A state built to secure one people’s dominance over another people’s land will produce exactly this legal order.
Written by Walid El Houri
